teaching.text: Read *She may have been reading the report when the call came* and count what the clause does at once. It presents the reading as possible rather than actual, places it before the moment of judgement, keeps it in progress, and anchors it against a past interruption. All of that comes from the verb and the small words clustered around it. The verb is the clause’s engine, and a description of English syntax keeps returning to it even when the topic is the noun phrase or the clause.

Two tracks run through the chapter. One follows form: the six inflectional shapes of a lexical verb, the special paradigms of auxiliaries, and the difference between a verb form and the construction it builds. The other follows meaning: tense and time, perfect and progressive, mood and modality, and the several expressions that place a situation in future time.

The tracks meet in the auxiliary chain. Modal, perfect, progressive and passive can stack in a fixed order, each one selecting the shape of the next verb. See that order clearly and the individual meanings stop looking like a list of labels; they become positions in a system a speaker can combine.

*She is writing a novel* and *She began writing a novel* run the same words past the same point, yet the grammar divides them differently. In the first, *is* heads the finite clause and *writing a novel* is its non-finite complement. In the second, *began* heads the finite clause and *writing a novel* is a catenative complement. The predicate of each clause is a verb phrase, its head a verb, and that head decides which other elements are required, permitted or excluded.

So *is writing* is not a constituent. The auxiliary heads one clause; the lexical verb heads a subordinate clause embedded inside it. Longer chains repeat the pattern: *She may have been reading* stacks a modal, a perfect auxiliary, a progressive auxiliary and a lexical verb, each adding a layer rather than a word to a flat string.

*Having finished the report, she left* opens with a participial clause; *to finish the report* is an infinitival one. Both are verb phrases with a verb at the head, and neither carries primary tense on its own. The rest of the chapter separates the forms verbs take from the constructions those forms build.
Layers in a verb phrase
Finite clause | Auxiliary verb | She is writing a novel.
Non-finite complement | Lexical verb | writing a novel
Perfect auxiliary | have | has written
Progressive auxiliary | be | is writing
Passive auxiliary | be | was written
She is writing a novel. — Is heads the clause; writing heads the non-finite complement.
She began writing a novel. — Began heads the clause; writing is a catenative complement.
She may have been reading. — Modal may, perfect have, progressive be, lexical read: four layers.

Line up *take, took, takes, take, taking, taken* and the paradigm looks untidy: six forms, five shapes, and *take* doing duty twice. *Want* and *hit* are untidier still, with syncretism collapsing several forms onto one pronunciation. The grammar nevertheless recognises six positions, because the preterite and the past participle behave differently even when they sound identical.

Primary and secondary forms do different work. A past participle follows perfect *have* and passive *be*; a gerund-participle follows progressive *be* and heads a range of non-finite clauses; the plain form turns up in imperatives, subjunctives, *to*-infinitivals and bare infinitivals. Those are constructions, not further inflectional forms. Calling imperative and subjunctive separate paradigms would mistake a clause type for a shape of the verb.

*He left* is finite; *to leave*, *having left* and *left behind* are not. Finiteness is a property of clauses and VPs, not of verb forms in the abstract. A finite clause is headed by a primary form, or by a plain form in an imperative or subjunctive; a non-finite clause is headed by a gerund-participle, a past participle, or a plain form in an infinitival. Auxiliaries add negative forms such as *isn’t* and *couldn’t*. Modals lack the secondary forms altogether, and *must* has no preterite.
The six-form paradigm
Preterite | took | wanted | hit
Third singular present | takes | wants | hits
Plain present | take | want | hit
Plain form | take | want | hit
Gerund-participle | taking | wanting | hitting
Past participle | taken | wanted | hit
She wanted the car. — Preterite: the first verb of a canonical finite clause.
She had wanted the car. — Past participle after perfect have.
The train approaching Platform 3 is late. — Gerund-participle heading a non-finite clause that modifies train.

Why participle and adjective are distinct: A word like broken can be a verb form or an adjective. In *It was broken deliberately* it denotes an event and is a passive verb. In *It didn’t look broken* it denotes a state and is an adjective. Tests with objects, seem and degree modifiers help separate the two without relying on the spelling.

*He has seen it* gives four tests in one clause. Negate it and *not* follows *has* directly; invert it and *has* moves in front of the subject; continue with *and I have too*; stress it and the polarity becomes emphatic. A lexical verb manages none of these without help: *He did not see it*, *Did he see it?*, *He saw it and I did too*, *He DID see it*. Negation, inversion, code and emphasis give the NICE constructions their name, and they identify auxiliaries by syntax rather than meaning.

Dummy *do* is semantically empty. It exists to supply the auxiliary position that those four constructions demand. Because the test is syntactic, *be* counts as an auxiliary even when it merely links subject and complement: *They are cheap* yields *They are not cheap* and *Are they cheap?* Auxiliary *have* behaves the same way, while lexical *have* takes *do*: *They had a fight* gives *They didn’t have a fight*.

*She is writing a novel* does not split into a subject plus a flat *is writing* predicate: *is* heads the clause and *writing a novel* is its complement. Auxiliaries are heads, not dependents. The same analysis explains the shape of questions: *Has she been writing?* moves one auxiliary into the prenucleus and leaves the rest of the clause as the nucleus. Subject-auxiliary inversion is not subject postposing, where a lexical verb precedes its subject, as in *In the corner stood a small table*.

Several kinds of fronted element trigger inversion. Closed interrogatives invert obligatorily; open interrogatives invert when a non-subject wh-phrase is fronted; exclamatives invert optionally. Initial negatives, *only* with clause scope, and *so/such* belong to the same family, and conditional inversion in *Had he seen it, he would have reported it* completes the set.
The NICE constructions
Negation | He has not seen it. | He saw not it.
Inversion | Has he seen it? | Saw he it?
Code | He has seen it and I have too. | He saw it and I saw too.
Emphasis | He HAS seen it. | He SAW it.
He has not seen it. — Auxiliary have takes not directly.
He did not see it. — Lexical see needs supportive do.
Has he seen it? — The auxiliary inverts with the subject.
He has seen it and I have too. — Code: have stands for the understood predicate.
Test for an auxiliary
Put not immediately after the verb and see whether the result is grammatical.
Form a closed interrogative and see whether the verb can precede the subject.
Add a tag or a code continuation and see whether the verb can stand alone.
Stress the verb and see whether it can carry emphatic polarity.
If the verb passes the NICE tests, it is an auxiliary. If it needs do, it is lexical.

Stack the auxiliaries and an order emerges: modal, perfect *have*, progressive *be*, passive *be*, lexical verb. Each one selects the form of what follows. A modal takes a plain form, perfect *have* a past participle, progressive *be* a gerund-participle, passive *be* a past participle. *She may have been reading* therefore reads as modal, perfect, progressive, lexical, with each verb shaping the next.

*She may can swim* fails. Core modals are mutually exclusive in Standard English. The same defectiveness keeps them out of infinitival and perfect positions: *to can swim*, *having could swim* and *has must swim* are all excluded. *Be*, *have* and *do* are not defective in that way, while *need*, *dare*, *have*, *do* and *use* split their time between auxiliary and lexical behaviour.

*She has probably been working* puts *probably* between the perfect auxiliary and its progressive complement; *They may well have been waiting* keeps *may* as head while *well* colours the modal judgement. Adverbs can sit inside the chain without breaking its dependencies.
Order and selection in the chain
Modal | Plain form | may go
Perfect have | Past participle | has gone
Progressive be | Gerund-participle | is going
Passive be | Past participle | was seen
Supportive do | Plain form | did go
She may have been reading. — Modal + perfect + progressive + lexical verb.
The report may have been checked. — Modal + perfect + passive + lexical verb.
She has been working. — Perfect + progressive + lexical verb.
They had been warned. — Perfect + passive + lexical verb.
Trace the chain
Find the first auxiliary after the subject.
Identify its category: modal, perfect, progressive or passive.
Check the form of the next verb against the selection in the table.
Continue until the lexical verb; the last verb heads the most embedded clause.
The chain is layered, not a flat sequence. Each auxiliary takes the following clause as its complement.

English marks two primary tenses by inflection, present and preterite, and neither stays inside its obvious time zone. The present can report a timeless truth, a habit, a historic narrative, a scheduled future event, or a future situation in a subordinate clause. The preterite can soften a request, backshift a report, or mark a hypothesis as remote. Form and time are correlated, but the correlation is loose enough to be interesting.

*If I lived there tomorrow* does not put the living in the past; it presents a future possibility as remote. Tense is grammatical; time is semantic. The present typically locates a situation as simultaneous with the time of orientation, the preterite typically as anterior, and context supplies the rest. *I wondered whether you could help* uses the preterite to make the request less direct.

Take *She said she was tired*: *was* is interpreted relative to the past reporting verb, not to the moment of speaking. *He believes she is ill* shifts the reference to his belief rather than the speaker’s present. A single timeline running from the speaker’s now cannot capture those shifts.
Primary tense and its uses
Present | Present time; timeless truths; habits | Historic present; futurate; subordinate future
Preterite | Past time | Politeness; backshift; modal remoteness
Present perfect | Past situation with present relevance | Experiential, resultative or recent past
Past perfect | Situation before a past reference point | Backshifted reported speech
The train leaves tomorrow. — Present tense, future time: the present futurate.
If I lived there, I would walk to work. — Preterite form, present hypothesis: modal remoteness.
She said she was tired. — Preterite form, backshifted report.
I wondered whether you could help. — Preterite form, polite request.

Why there is no future tense: Will and shall behave like modal auxiliaries, not like a third tense inflection. They share the syntax and meaning range of can, may and must, and they combine with past and present forms rather than replacing the primary tense system. English expresses future time in many ways, but it does not mark it with a dedicated tense.

*She has finished* and *She had finished before I arrived* both place a situation before a reference point; the difference is where that point sits. The perfect is the secondary past tense, built from *have* plus a past participle. Its reference point is often the moment of speaking, but it can be a past moment, as in the second example, or a future one, as in *She will have finished by Friday*.

*She has lived in Berlin ever since she married* forces the continuative reading: the living runs from the past up to the reference point. Remove the duration phrase and *She has lived in Berlin* defaults to non-continuative, with the living located at some indefinite time within the relevant span. A duration expression such as *ever since* or *for* usually forces the continuative reading, which is also restricted to atelic situations.

The present perfect differs from the simple preterite by keeping a past situation tied to the present. The tie can be experiential (*I have seen that film*), resultative (*She has written the report*, so the report now exists), or recent (*He has just left*). Past-time adjuncts such as *yesterday* or *two minutes ago* normally exclude the present perfect because they place the situation wholly in the past.

*She may have left* puts the leaving before the modal judgement. *She must have been working* stacks perfect and progressive to present a past ongoing situation inferred from evidence. The order of the auxiliaries keeps those meanings apart: modal first, perfect second, progressive third.
Uses of the present perfect
Continuative | She has lived here for years. | The situation continues up to now.
Experiential | I have seen that film. | The experience exists within the relevant span.
Resultative | She has written the report. | The result is available now.
Recent past | He has just left. | The event is close to now.
She has lived in Berlin ever since she married. — Continuative: the living extends up to now.
She has lived in Berlin. — Default non-continuative: at some time within the relevant span.
She had finished before I arrived. — Past perfect: anterior to a past reference point.
She may have left. — The perfect is inside the scope of the modal.
Locate the perfect
Find have or had and check that the next verb is a past participle.
Identify the reference point: speaking time, a past time, or a future time.
Ask whether the situation extends up to that point or lies wholly before it.
Check whether a duration expression forces the continuative reading.
The perfect is a secondary past tense, not simply a past-time marker. Its reference point comes from the surrounding clause.

*The flag is red* holds steady; *She walked in the park* goes on without a natural endpoint; *She reached the summit* is over in an instant. Aspect describes that internal temporal shape, and the shape depends on the kind of situation. States are static, like *She knows the answer*. Occurrences are dynamic, dividing into activities, accomplishments and achievements: activities are durative and atelic, accomplishments durative and telic (*She wrote a novel*), achievements punctual.

Multiplicity adds another layer. *She knocked once* is singulary; *She knocked repeatedly* is iterative; *She usually walks to work* is a serial state built from repeated subsituations. A whole can have a different aspectual character from its parts, so a habitual sentence may behave like a state even though every instance is an activity.

Perfective and imperfective aspectuality divide the viewpoint. Perfective presents a situation as a complete whole, seen from outside; imperfective presents it from within, focusing on an internal phase or interval. English marks neither with a dedicated inflection. Simple present and preterite can receive either interpretation, while the progressive is a special imperfective construction.
Situation types
State | The flag is red. | Normally resists progressive; simple present is natural.
Activity | She walked in the park. | Durative, atelic; for an hour is natural.
Accomplishment | She wrote a novel. | Durative, telic; in an hour is natural.
Achievement | She reached the summit. | Punctual; normally resists progressive and for an hour.
She wrote a novel. — Accomplishment: bounded object gives a terminal point.
She wrote novels. — Activity: unbounded object, no inherent endpoint.
She reached the summit. — Achievement: punctual change of state.
She was reaching the summit. — Extendable achievement: the progressive stretches the approach.

*She was reading the letter when the phone rang* puts the reading around the moment of the call. *Be* plus a gerund-participle presents the situation as in progress at the relevant time, viewed from within, durative and dynamic. The progressive does more than add duration; it changes the viewpoint, and the change has consequences for what the clause entails.

Entailment and implicature pull in different directions. *I was working* entails *I worked*: an activity in progress has really happened. *She was writing a novel* does not entail that she finished it, though it usually implicates as much. *The train was arriving* stretches a punctual achievement into an approach. Context can cancel the implicatures, but it cannot cancel the entailment.

States generally resist the progressive, which is why *The flag is being red* sounds wrong. The restriction is not absolute, since context can present a state as temporary or dynamic. Nor is the progressive always aspectual. It can supply narrative background, make an interpretation explicit (*I was referring to you*), or present a future arrangement (*We’re meeting tomorrow*).
She was writing a novel. — Accomplishment in progress: completion is not entailed.
I was working. — Activity in progress: the activity did take place.
The train was arriving. — An achievement presented as an approach.
I was referring to you. — Interpretive use: the progressive clarifies what the earlier words meant.
Ask what the progressive adds
Identify the situation type: state, activity, accomplishment or achievement.
Ask whether the progressive presents an internal phase or a complete event.
Check whether completion is entailed or only implicated.
Look for a non-aspectual use: background, interpretation, arrangement or politeness.
The progressive is not a general marker of ongoing time. Its meaning depends on the situation and on the surrounding discourse.

*I wish she were here* preserves a fossil: *were* is a residual irrealis form, almost the last inflectional mood English has. The main system is analytic, carried by modals such as *can*, *may*, *must*, *will* and *shall*. Modality itself is broader than those auxiliaries, reaching into adjectives, adverbs, verbs, nouns, clause type and past tense.

Three dimensions organise modal meaning. Strength sets necessity against possibility. Kind separates deontic modality (obligation, permission, prohibition), epistemic modality (commitment to truth) and dynamic modality (ability, disposition and other participant properties). Degree measures how strong the judgement is, and modals can reinforce or clash with one another in modal harmony.

Negation shows how much scope matters. *You mustn’t eat it all* puts the negation inside the modal: it is necessary that you not eat it. *You needn’t eat it all* puts it outside: it is not necessary that you eat it. *May not* and *can’t* repeat the contrast, and the perfect raises the same question in *may have left*.
Three dimensions of modality
Strength | Necessity vs possibility | must vs may
Kind | Deontic, epistemic, dynamic | You must go; It must be true; She can swim
Degree | Strong, medium, weak | must, should, might
Scope | Modal over negation vs negation over modal | mustn’t vs needn’t
You must come in immediately. — Deontic: obligation.
It must have been a mistake. — Epistemic: inference about the truth of the proposition.
Liz can drive better than you. — Dynamic: ability.
You needn’t eat it all. — External negation: it is not necessary that you eat it all.

*She may can swim* fails, and the failure reveals a small, tightly behaved class. The core modals are *can*, *may*, *must*, *will* and *shall*, with *ought*, *need* and *dare* at the edges. They lack secondary forms, *must* lacks a preterite, they take a plain-form complement, and they cannot combine with one another in a single Standard English chain. Their meanings overlap, so one form can carry different kinds of modality in different contexts.

*Must* carries strong necessity, deontic or epistemic. *May* handles possibility and permission; *can* handles ability, possibility and permission with a strong dynamic bent. *Will* stretches from epistemic prediction through dynamic volition to deontic insistence. *Shall* is mainly deontic and formal, at home in first-person offers and suggestions, while *should* and *ought* sit at medium strength, expressing necessity or expectation.

The preterite forms *could*, *might*, *would* and *should* are not simply past tenses. They can mark past time, backshift in reported speech, or modal remoteness. *Could* is the past of *can* in ability contexts, but in *Could you help?* it signals politeness. *Would* can mark habitual past behaviour, a future-in-the-past, or a remote conditional. *Should* has developed idiomatic deontic and evaluative uses that do not reduce to past tense.
Core modals and typical meanings
can | Ability, possibility, permission | She can swim.
may | Possibility, permission | It may rain.
must | Necessity, strong inference | You must go; It must be true.
will | Prediction, volition, insistence | They will arrive tomorrow.
shall | Deontic, formal offer or suggestion | Shall I open the window?
should | Medium necessity, expectation | You should apologise.
ought | Medium necessity, expectation | You ought to apologise.
You must help him. — Deontic necessity: an obligation is imposed.
He must have written it himself. — Epistemic necessity: the conclusion is inferred.
She can drive better than you. — Dynamic possibility: ability.
Could you help? — Preterite form used for politeness, not past time.

Do not read one meaning from the form: The same modal can be deontic, epistemic or dynamic. The context, the scope of negation and the kind of situation decide which reading is salient. A label such as “modal of obligation” is a description of one use, not the meaning of the form in every sentence.

Scope decides what a negative or a perfect applies to. *She may not have read it* can mean that it is possible she did not read it, with the negation inside the scope of *may*. *She can’t have read it* normally means that it is not possible that she read it, with the negative outside the modal. The words’ tense has not changed; the structure of the judgement has.

*She may have left* puts the perfect inside the modal’s scope, so the possibility concerns a past leaving. *She must have been working* makes the judgement about a past progressive situation. Reversing the order is not a stylistic preference; it changes which proposition is modalised.

Modal meaning also lives outside the auxiliaries. *Have to*, *have got to*, *be able to*, *be allowed to*, *be likely to* and *be going to* are fixed expressions with modal or future meaning. Lexical verbs such as *permit*, *require* and *insist*, adjectives such as *possible* and *necessary*, adverbs such as *perhaps*, and nouns such as *permission* and *obligation* all belong to the wider modal domain. They differ in register, inflection and syntax even where their meanings overlap with a core modal.
Modal alternatives
have to | must | Takes do-support; common in all registers
have got to | must | Informal; fixed perfect form
be able to | can | Supplies missing forms such as infinitives and perfects
be allowed to | may / can | Explicit permission; full inflectional range
had better | should | Fixed expression with a bare infinitival complement
be going to | will | Future time with present focus or intention
You mustn’t eat it all. — Internal negation: it is necessary that you not eat it all.
You needn’t eat it all. — External negation: it is not necessary that you eat it all.
She may have left. — The perfect is within the modal’s scope.
She has to leave. — Have to expresses necessity with a lexical verb.
Find the scope
Paraphrase the modal with a lexical expression such as it is necessary or it is possible.
Decide whether the negative belongs in the subordinate clause or the main clause.
Check whether a perfect auxiliary falls inside or outside the modal judgement.
Compare the result with the likely context; modal scope is often disambiguated by discourse.
The position of negation and perfect reveals which proposition the modal qualifies.

English has no future tense, only a repertoire for talking about future time. Modal *will* and *shall*, *be going to*, the present futurate, the progressive futurate, imperatives, mandative clauses and non-finite complements all do the job. *The match starts tomorrow*, *We’re meeting at six*, *She is going to resign* and *I will call you* place a situation in the future by different means.

*Will* is a modal auxiliary, not a tense marker. It expresses epistemic prediction, dynamic volition or deontic insistence, and *would* carries past, backshifted and remote uses. *Be going to* has a stronger present focus: intention, arrangement or imminent development. In the preterite, *was going to* commonly implicates that the intended situation did not happen.

The present futurate handles schedules and planned events: *The train leaves at six*. The progressive futurate presents an arrangement as already under way: *We’re flying to Rome tomorrow*. In subordinate clauses the present often carries future meaning: *If she arrives early, we’ll start*. None of these needs a future inflection, because future time is a semantic relation, not a grammatical category in English.
Ways to express future time
will + plain form | I will call you. | Prediction, willingness or insistence
be going to | She is going to resign. | Intention, arrangement or present evidence
Present futurate | The match starts tomorrow. | Schedule or fixed plan
Progressive futurate | We’re meeting at six. | Arrangement already in place
Imperative | Take this umbrella. | Directive with future actualisation
Subordinate present | If she arrives, we’ll start. | Future condition
The train leaves at six. — Present futurate: a scheduled event.
We’re flying to Rome tomorrow. — Progressive futurate: an arrangement.
She is going to resign. — Present evidence or intention, with present focus.
If she arrives early, we’ll start. — Present tense in a subordinate clause with future reference.
Choose the future expression
Ask whether the sentence presents a prediction, an intention, an arrangement or a schedule.
Check whether the situation is viewed from the present or from a past reference point.
Use be going to when present evidence or intention is central; use will for a modal prediction.
Remember that the present tense can refer to future time in schedules and subordinate clauses.
Future time is expressed by a family of constructions, not by a single future tense.

Tense and aspect do more in a text than locate events. Narrative uses the preterite to carry the main sequence forward and the progressive to supply background: *She was working in the garden when the police arrived*. The perfect ties a past event to a later reference point and often explains a present state: *The road is closed because a tree has fallen*.

The historic present shifts a narrative into the present for immediacy. Backshift anchors a subordinate clause to the reporting time rather than the speaker’s now. Free indirect style moves between these viewpoints without quotation marks. None of these effects needs a new tense form; they arise from tense, aspect and context interacting.

Take *Having finished the report, she left*: the perfect participle places the finishing before the leaving. *With the windows open, the room stayed cool* is a verbless clause describing a circumstance. Non-finite and verbless clauses often have no primary tense at all; the matrix clause, the aspect of the non-finite form and the wider discourse supply the temporal interpretation.
She was working in the garden when the police arrived. — Progressive background; preterite event.
The road is closed because a tree has fallen. — Present perfect explains a present state.
Having finished the report, she left. — Perfect participle locates the finishing before the leaving.
With the windows open, the room stayed cool. — Verbless clause supplies a circumstance.

Four systems organise the English verb. Primary tense contrasts present and preterite; secondary tense contrasts perfect and non-perfect; aspect contrasts progressive and non-progressive; mood contrasts modal and non-modal. Each has its own forms and its own characteristic meaning, and all four meet in the auxiliary chain.

That chain runs modal, perfect, progressive, passive, lexical verb. Each auxiliary selects the form of its complement and adds a layer of meaning, while the verb’s subclass decides which complements the clause requires. Tense, aspect and modality are not three names for time; they are separate systems whose interaction produces the temporal and evaluative effects of ordinary prose.

A practical method: find the finite verb, list the auxiliaries in order, then ask what each layer contributes. Is the clause modalised? Is the situation perfect or non-perfect, progressive or non-progressive? Is the verb lexical or auxiliary? Is future time carried by *will*, *be going to*, a present futurate or a subordinate present? Answering those questions turns a long verb chain into a readable structure.

A verb checklist: Find the head of the clause and the auxiliaries that precede it. Check the form selected by each auxiliary. Identify primary tense, then perfect, progressive and mood. Finally, ask what kind of situation the clause describes and how the surrounding discourse anchors it in time.

Take *She may have been reading the report when the call came*. The finite clause is headed by the modal *may*. Its complement is the perfect clause *have been reading the report when the call came*, whose head is *have*. The perfect takes the progressive clause *be reading the report when the call came* as its complement, and progressive *be* takes the gerund-participle *reading*.

The modal expresses possibility; the perfect locates the reading before the modal judgement; the progressive presents the reading as ongoing at the time of the call. The lexical verb *read* takes the object *the report*, and the adjunct *when the call came* locates the reading in time. Each layer has a distinct job, and the order of the auxiliaries keeps those jobs separate.

When you meet a long verb chain, read it from left to right. Identify the first auxiliary, then check the form of the next verb, and continue until the lexical verb. The first auxiliary carries the clause’s primary tense or mood; the later auxiliaries add perfect, progressive or passive meaning.

Next, ask what kind of situation the lexical verb describes. An activity, an accomplishment, an achievement and a state interact differently with the progressive and with duration phrases. The same verb can shift category when its object or complement changes, as in *write a novel* and *write novels*.

Finally, separate form from meaning. A present tense can refer to future time, a preterite can express politeness or remoteness, and a modal can express obligation, inference or ability. The context, the scope of negation and the kind of situation decide which reading is active.

In *She may have been reading the report when the call came*, *may* is a modal auxiliary expressing epistemic possibility. *Have* marks the perfect, locating the reading before the modal judgement. *Be* marks the progressive, presenting the reading as ongoing at the time of the call. *Reading* is the lexical verb and takes *the report* as its object.

Lexical verbs have six inflectional forms; auxiliaries have special paradigms and special syntax. The NICE constructions identify auxiliaries, and do-support supplies an auxiliary when a lexical verb lacks one. Auxiliaries form a fixed chain: modal, perfect, progressive, passive.

Tense, aspect and mood are separate systems. The perfect is a secondary past tense, the progressive presents an internal view, and modality covers necessity, possibility and related meanings. Future time is expressed by several constructions, not by a dedicated future tense.

key_terms.definition: A verb belonging to the open class of ordinary verbs, as opposed to an auxiliary.
A verb with special syntax, including negation, inversion, code and emphasis.
An auxiliary such as can, may, must, will or shall that marks mood rather than tense.
The uninflected verb form used after modals and dummy do, and in imperative, subjunctive and infinitival constructions.
The primary past-tense verb form, as in took or wanted.
The verb form used after perfect have and passive be, as in taken or written.
The verb form in -ing, used after progressive be and in various non-finite clauses.
A clause headed by a primary verb form, or by a plain form in an imperative or subjunctive.
The four auxiliary-sensitive constructions: negation, inversion, code and emphasis.
The use of dummy do to supply an auxiliary for negation, inversion or emphasis.
A grammatical system that locates a situation, or part of it, in time.
A grammatical system concerned with the internal temporal structure of a situation.
The grammatical marking of modality, chiefly through modal auxiliaries in English.
The secondary past tense marked by have plus a past participle.
The aspect marked by be plus a gerund-participle, presenting a situation as in progress.
Whatever a clause expresses: an action, process, event, state or relation.
The meaning side of aspect: how a situation is viewed internally or as a whole.
Meaning concerned with necessity, possibility and the speaker's attitude to factuality or actualisation.
Modality of obligation, permission and prohibition.
Modality concerned with the speaker's commitment to the truth of a proposition.
Modality concerned with abilities, dispositions and other properties of participants.
The use of a past tense in reported speech to mark anteriority relative to the reporting time.
The use of a past tense form to present a situation as less likely, less direct or hypothetical.
A semantic time reference that English expresses through several constructions rather than a dedicated future tense.
A fixed expression with modal meaning, such as have to, had better or be able to.
A verb that takes a non-finite clause complement, often in a recursive chain.

teaching.text: *The committee gave the designer an award for the new bridge* looks like a verb followed by a queue of phrases. The grammar sees something more precise: a subject outside the verb phrase, two internal objects, and a prepositional complement explaining what the award was for. The verb selects that arrangement, and the arrangement is what this chapter describes.

The chapter begins with the architecture of the clause: the major functions, the split between core and non-core complements, and the five canonical patterns. From there it turns to meaning, taking up semantic roles, the subject’s cluster of properties, objects and predicative complements. The final sections widen the view to prepositional verbs, particles, idioms, light verbs and verbs that live in several complementation patterns at once.

Two questions are worth asking together: what function does this expression perform, and what role does its referent play in the situation? The answers are related but not identical. Keeping them apart lets a description handle a passive, a ditransitive alternation or a prepositional verb without collapsing syntax into meaning.

*He always reads the paper before breakfast* contains three kinds of dependent, and only one of them fills a slot the verb demands. *Reads* is the predicator, the verb phrase that heads the clause. *The paper* is a complement, licensed by the verb. *Always* and *before breakfast* are adjuncts, adding information without completing the verb’s requirements.

The subject belongs with the complements but sits apart from them. It is external to the verb phrase, while objects and predicative complements are internal, which is why a canonical clause divides first into subject and predicate. The subject also carries a cluster of distinctive properties: position, case, agreement, inversion, tag formation and coordination behaviour.

*He looked at the paper*, *He seemed quite competent* and *He said that she was right* show complements in three forms: PP, adjective phrase and clause. Not every complement is an NP. Ask instead whether the verb licenses the dependent, and how that dependent fits the verb’s meaning.
Clause functions
Predicator | Verb phrase | reads
Subject | NP, external to the VP | He
Direct object | NP, internal to the VP | the paper
Predicative complement | AdjP or NP | quite competent
Adjunct | AdvP, PP or clause | before breakfast
He reads the paper. — The paper is an NP object.
He looked at the paper. — At the paper is a PP complement, not an object.
He seemed quite competent. — Quite competent is a predicative complement.

*Kim gave Pat the key* and *Kim gave the key to Pat* describe one transfer with two different structures. In the first, *Pat* and *the key* are core complements, directly related to the verb and prototypically NPs. In the second, *to Pat* is still a complement of *give*, but it is non-core, realised by a PP, and *Pat* inside it is an oblique: an NP related to the verb only through the preposition.

The preposition contributes to the oblique’s semantic role; in *to Pat*, *to* marks the recipient. That does not make *Pat* an indirect object, because the syntactic relation differs: the NP sits inside a PP complement rather than acting as a direct complement of the verb. The two sentences are related in meaning, not in structure.

*Read* is intransitive in *She read*, transitive in *She read the letter*: same lexeme, different valency. Valency counts the syntactic complements a verb takes in a given use, not the semantic participants. A verb can be bivalent with a subject and object, or monovalent with a subject alone.
Core and non-core complements
Subject | NP, external | Kim
Direct object | NP, internal | the key
Indirect object | NP, internal | Pat
Predicative complement | AdjP or NP | quite competent
Non-core complement | PP | to Pat; in the box
Oblique | NP inside a PP | Pat in to Pat
Kim gave Pat the key. — Pat is an indirect object; the key is the direct object.
Kim gave the key to Pat. — To Pat is a PP complement; Pat is an oblique.
Kim gave the key. — The indirect object is omissible here; the direct object remains.

Why valency is a property of uses: A verb is not permanently transitive or intransitive. Many verbs occur in several patterns, and the pattern can change the meaning. Describing valency means describing a use in a construction, not attaching one fixed label to the lexeme.

*She smiled*, *He washed the car* and *They gave me the key* are intransitive, monotransitive and ditransitive. The five patterns are shapes, not definitions of verbs. Add a predicative complement and the clause becomes complex: *This seems a good idea* is complex-intransitive, *I consider this a good idea* complex-transitive.

The labels describe clauses and verb uses, not lexemes in isolation. A verb can appear in more than one pattern, so the construction decides the label. Take *read*. *She read for a while* is intransitive; add *the letter* and it becomes monotransitive; add *us a story* and it is ditransitive.

A predicative complement makes the clause complex because it adds a second predication inside the same clause. *This seems a good idea* predicates *a good idea* of the subject; *I consider this a good idea* predicates it of the object. The relation is the same; the predicand has moved.
Canonical clause patterns
Intransitive | S + P | She smiled.
Monotransitive | S + P + Od | He washed the car.
Ditransitive | S + P + Oi + Od | They gave me the key.
Complex-intransitive | S + P + PCs | This seems a good idea.
Complex-transitive | S + P + Od + PCo | I consider this a good idea.
She smiled. — Intransitive: no internal core complement.
They gave me the key. — Ditransitive: indirect object plus direct object.
This seems a good idea. — Complex-intransitive: predicative complement oriented to the subject.
I consider this a good idea. — Complex-transitive: object plus object-oriented predicative complement.
Name the pattern
Find the subject and the predicator.
Identify the internal complements that follow the verb.
If there is an object, decide whether there is also a second object or a predicative complement.
Check whether the extra complement ascribes a property. If it does, the clause is complex.
The pattern is defined by the functions present, not by the number of words after the verb.

*Kim heard an explosion* and *The noise frightened Kim* place Kim on opposite sides of the same event: perceiver in one, affected party in the other. Roles track those differences. An agent is a prototypical conscious causer; a patient is affected by an action; an instrument is used by an agent; an experiencer feels or perceives; a stimulus arouses the feeling or perception. Theme is a broad role for entities involved without being agents or patients, and goal, source and recipient describe endpoints, starting points and receivers.

*Kim heard an explosion* has an experiencer subject; *They like me* has a stimulus object. Roles are not fixed by grammatical function. A single argument can carry more than one role: in *Kim bought the car from Pat*, Kim is both agent and goal, while Pat is both agent and source.

*Kim shot Pat* and *Pat was shot by Kim* describe the same situation with the same roles but present it from different perspectives. Presentational status is a separate dimension. In symmetric pairs such as *Kim married Pat* and *Pat married Kim*, the roles stay the same and the difference is entirely one of perspective. Passive does this, but it is not the only construction that can.
Common semantic roles
Agent | Conscious causer | Kim signed the letter.
Patient | Affected entity | They hit me.
Instrument | Entity used by an agent | I cut the lace with a knife.
Experiencer | One who feels or perceives | He heard a bang.
Stimulus | What arouses feeling or perception | The noise frightened me.
Theme | Entity involved in a situation | The key is on the table.
Goal / source | Endpoint / starting point | to Paris; from Berlin
Kim heard an explosion. — Subject as experiencer; object as stimulus.
The knife cut the lace. — Subject as causer, not an agent using an instrument.
Kim gave the key to Pat. — Pat is the recipient, expressed as an oblique.
Pat was shot by Kim. — Same roles as the active, different presentational status.

*The minister knows the candidates* shows the subject’s position and agreement in one stroke: the NP comes before the predicator, and *knows* agrees with it. Other properties cluster around those. The subject controls the pronoun in a tag (*The candidates know, don’t they?*), takes nominative case where a pronoun shows it, moves after the auxiliary in closed interrogatives, and plays a distinctive part in open interrogatives.

*The parcel was opened by Kim* has *the parcel* as subject although it is the patient, not the agent. Those properties identify the subject even when the clause is non-canonical. *There is one nurse here* has dummy *there* as subject and *one nurse* as displaced subject. *More important are the moral objections* has *the moral objections* as postposed subject.

*This one I’m giving to Jill* has *this one* as topic and *I* as subject. Subject and topic are different jobs. Passive, existential, extraposition and preposing constructions let a speaker choose which element is presented as subject and which as topic.
Subject properties
Category | Prototypically an NP | The minister knows the candidates.
Position | Before the predicator | The minister knows them.
Case | Nominative pronoun in formal finite clauses | I know them.
Agreement | Verb agrees with the subject | The candidates know.
Inversion | Subject follows the auxiliary in questions | Do the candidates know?
Tags | Tag pronoun matches the subject | The candidates know, don’t they?
The parcel was opened by Kim. — The parcel is subject, even though Kim is the agent.
There is one nurse here. — Dummy there is subject; one nurse is displaced subject.
More important are the moral objections. — The moral objections is the postposed subject.
The others you know, don’t you? — The tag pronoun matches the subject you, not the preposed object.
Test for the subject
Form a closed interrogative and see which element moves after the auxiliary.
Add a tag and see which pronoun the tag uses.
Check agreement with the finite verb where the form distinguishes it.
Check whether a pronoun with case contrast appears in the nominative.
The subject is the element with this cluster of properties, not simply the first NP in the clause.

*Kim gave Pat the key* contains two internal complements, and only one of them is the thing given. *Pat* is the indirect object, characteristically the recipient; *the key* is the direct object, the patient or affected entity. Put the recipient inside a PP, as in *Kim gave the key to Pat*, and *to Pat* becomes a PP complement rather than an indirect object.

*I used a knife* requires its object; *He lent his car* allows it to be left out. Most objects are NPs, but their obligatoriness varies with the verb. A related passive gives a useful test: if an NP complement can become the subject of a passive, it is an object. The test is sufficient, not necessary, because some objects resist passivisation.

*Pat was given the key* and *The key was given to Pat* show that either object of a ditransitive can become the passive subject. The indirect object is usually the more expendable of the two. Languages with a distinct dative case do not necessarily allow that freedom.

*We thought it necessary to postpone the meeting* has *it* as object and *to postpone the meeting* as extraposed object. Objects can be extraposed. The clause behaves semantically like an object without occupying the object position syntactically.
Object properties
Typical form | NP | NP
Core status | Internal core complement | Internal core complement
Typical role | Patient or affected entity | Recipient
Passive test | Often becomes passive subject | Can become passive subject in English
Omissibility | Often obligatory | Often omissible
They gave me the key. — Me is the indirect object; the key is the direct object.
They gave the key to me. — To me is a PP complement, not an indirect object.
The key was given to me. — The direct object becomes the passive subject.
I was given the key. — The indirect object can also become the passive subject.
We thought it necessary to postpone the meeting. — It is the object; the clause is an extraposed object.

*Kim seemed uneasy* and *He found Kim intolerant* both say something about Kim, but the predicand sits in a different place. A predicative complement expresses a property predicated of another element, its predicand. In the first sentence the predicand is the subject; in the second it is the object. The predicand is not the subject of the complement; it is the element the complement applies to.

Three tests separate a predicative complement from an object. Form is the first: a PC can be an AdjP (*nice*) or a bare role NP (*treasurer*), while an object is normally an NP. The passive is the second: *A minister was become by Ed* is impossible, so the PC does not become a passive subject. Case is the third: formal style allows *It was he who wrote it*, with a nominative pronoun.

Depictive and resultative readings describe different moments. *Kim seemed uneasy* characterises the predicand while the situation holds; *He found Kim intolerant* does the same for the object. Those are depictive readings. *Kim became angry* and *He made Kim happy* describe the state reached when a process ends: resultatives, which typically need a verb of change to supply the endpoint.

Obligatory and optional complements differ in how tightly they integrate. Take *He looked young*: the sense of *look* requires the complement. *He died young* is different; *young* is a predicative adjunct rather than a complement. Same form, different degree of attachment.
Predicative complements and objects
Form | AdjP, bare role NP, or ordinary NP | Normally NP
Meaning | Property predicated of a predicand | Participant in the situation
Passive test | Fails | Often passes
Pronoun case | Nominative possible in formal style | Accusative
Kim seemed uneasy. — Subject-oriented depictive PC.
He found Kim intolerant. — Object-oriented depictive PC.
Kim became angry. — Resultative PC: the state reached at the end.
He made Kim happy. — Object-oriented resultative PC.

*Ed was quite competent* is the plainest copular clause: *be* relates a predicative complement to the subject, and the complement says what Ed was like. The construction covers several relations. Sometimes *be* does little beyond carrying tense; sometimes it identifies a value.

Two uses of *be* pull in different directions. Ascriptive *be* applies a property: *This is a good idea*, *Ed is competent*. Specifying *be* identifies a value: *The only problem is the cost*. Reverse a specifying clause and the relation survives, *The cost is the only problem*; reverse an ascriptive one and it does not.

Copular clauses form a family, not a single pattern. *Seem*, *become*, *remain*, *look* and *feel* take predicative complements with different degrees of obligatoriness and different semantic effects. *Become* is resultative, *remain* continuative, *seem* evidential. Calling them all copular does not make them interchangeable with *be*.
This is a good idea. — Ascriptive: a property is applied to this.
The only problem is the cost. — Specifying: the complement identifies the problem.
The cost is the only problem. — The specifying relation allows reversal.
Ed became angry. — Resultative copular clause.

*Refer* insists on *to*: *refer to her article*. *Blame* selects *on* in *blame the accident on me*. In both, the preposition belongs to the verb’s lexical requirements rather than marking place or time freely. That is what separates *refer to* from *fly to Boston*, where *to* is an ordinary goal preposition.

Mobile and fixed prepositions behave differently under movement. A mobile one fronts with its complement and coordinates like any ordinary preposition: *the article to which I referred*, *I referred to her article and to several others*. A fixed one stays put: *the letters across which I came* is impossible, and only *the letters which I came across* works.

The distinction reaches adjunct placement and passives. A mobile preposition allows an adjunct between verb and PP: *I referred repeatedly to her article*. A fixed preposition generally does not: *I came eventually across these letters*. Prepositional passives are possible with some combinations and not others, depending on how tightly verb and preposition have fused.
Specified and unspecified prepositions
Unspecified | fly to Boston | Goal preposition; contrasts with from, towards, over
Mobile specified | refer to her article | Can front with its complement; allows adjunct insertion
Fixed specified | come across some letters | Resists fronting and adjunct insertion; stranding preferred
the article to which I referred — Mobile preposition fronted with its complement.
I referred repeatedly to her article. — An adjunct can intervene before the mobile preposition.
the letters which I came across — Fixed preposition stranded rather than fronted.

*She put in her application* and *He brought the chairs in* show the same particle in two positions. A particle is an intransitive preposition that can sit between a verb and its direct object. Pronouns are stricter about order: *She put it in* is grammatical, *She put in it* is not.

A particle and a PP complement can look alike on the surface. Take *She jumped off the wall*: *off the wall* is a single PP complement. *She took off the label* is different: *off* is a particle and *the label* is the object. Look at the syntax, not only at the meaning.

*Give up the struggle*, *take me to task*, *pull my leg* are lexical units larger than a word, and their meanings cannot be built from their parts. Idioms need not form syntactic constituents. In *take me to task*, *to task* belongs to the idiom but the object separates it from *take*. The syntax still has ordinary constituents; the idiom lives above them.
She put in her application. — In is a particle between the verb and its object.
She put it in. — A pronoun object follows the particle.
She jumped off the wall. — Off the wall is one PP complement, not a particle plus object.
He took me to task. — A verbal idiom whose parts do not form a single syntactic constituent.

Why phrasal verb is not used here: Calling verb and particle a phrasal verb suggests they form a single verb constituent. In this analysis, the verb heads the clause and the particle is a complement. The combination can be idiomatic without becoming one syntactic word.

*She gave him a kiss* says much the same as *She kissed him*, but the work is distributed differently. A light verb contributes relatively little meaning of its own; the noun complement carries the content. *We took a rest* corresponds to *We rested*, and *I made a calculation* to *I calculated*. The noun supplies the predicative content, the light verb the grammatical structure.

Light verbs earn their place by what they let the noun do. Modifiers and determiners attach to it: *She gave him an unusually passionate kiss*, *We took a well-earned rest*. Aspect and quantification can shift too: *He had a drink of my milk* suggests he drank only part of it, while *He drank my milk* suggests he drank it all.

*I had a bath* wobbles between two readings: that I bathed, or that I owned a bath. *He gave me a lick* can describe a dog licking me or a person allowing me a lick of ice cream. With light verbs the ordinary use of the same verb is always nearby, and context together with the noun’s interpretation decides which reading survives.
Light verb alternatives
give someone a kiss | kiss someone | Single event; noun can be modified
take a rest | rest | Activity presented as a bounded event
make a calculation | calculate | Allows quantification of the product
have a drink | drink | Often implies a smaller or bounded amount
She gave him a kiss. — Light give; kiss carries the main meaning.
We took a well-earned rest. — The modifier attaches to the noun rest.
He had a drink of my milk. — Suggests a bounded amount, unlike He drank my milk.
I had a bath. — Ambiguous between bathing and owning a bath.

Most verbs occur in more than one complementation pattern, and *make* moves through several. *They made some cakes* takes a direct object; *They made me a filing cabinet* takes an indirect and a direct object; *They made me impatient* takes an object plus a predicative complement. The meaning stays recognisable while the syntax changes.

Four kinds of transitive/intransitive contrast are worth separating. The intransitive subject may match the transitive subject, as in *They shot him* and *They shot at him*. It may match the object, as in *The sun radiates heat* and *Heat radiates from the sun*. The transitive may simply add an object, as in *She drank some water* and *She drank*. Or the object may become the intransitive subject, as in *He broke the vase* and *The vase broke*.

Ditransitive/monotransitive pairs have their own logic. *I gave her the key* alternates with *I gave the key to her*; *They offered us $100* alternates with *They offered $100*. In *They fined us $100* and *They fined us*, the indirect object alone corresponds to the single object of the monotransitive.

Core/non-core contrasts and combined complements complete the picture. *He supplies arms to the rebels* alternates with *He supplies the rebels with arms*. *She kissed him on the cheek* has two complements, while *She kissed his cheek* folds their content into one. Complementation is a system of related options, not a fixed frame attached to each verb.
Types of complementation contrast
Transitive/intransitive | They shot him / They shot at him | Object versus PP complement
Causative/inchoative | He broke the vase / The vase broke | Object becomes subject
Ditransitive/monotransitive | I gave her the key / I gave the key to her | Indirect object versus PP complement
Core/non-core | He supplies arms to them / He supplies them with arms | Alignment of object and PP
Combined complement | She kissed him on the cheek / She kissed his cheek | Two complements versus one
They shot him. — Transitive: him is the direct object.
They shot at him. — Intransitive with a PP complement; the conative suggests attempted contact.
He broke the vase. — Transitive causative.
The vase broke. — Intransitive inchoative; the object becomes subject.

Complementation shapes what a verb can mean in a sentence. *They gave the key to Pat* and *They gave Pat the key* describe the same transfer, but the second presents Pat as an indirect object and the first puts Pat inside a PP. *They shot him* says he was hit; *They shot at him* does not.

A writer needs the pattern as much as the analyst does. A dictionary entry records the structures a verb permits, not just its meaning. *Refer* requires *to*; *blame* allows *on* or *for*; *supply* permits either *supply arms to the rebels* or *supply the rebels with arms*. You learn the pattern along with the verb.

Ambiguity often turns on complement structure. *Flying planes can be dangerous* can involve planes that fly or the activity of flying them, because one form can realise different functions. *The chicken is ready to eat* can describe the chicken as food or as an eater. Syntax narrows interpretation without always settling it.

Everything in the chapter radiates from the verb. It selects complements, and that selection decides whether the clause is intransitive, monotransitive, ditransitive, complex-intransitive or complex-transitive. The subject sits outside the verb phrase; objects and predicative complements sit inside. Core complements attach directly, non-core complements through a preposition.

Grammatical function and semantic role answer different questions. A subject may be agent, experiencer or patient; an object may be patient, stimulus or theme. Presentational status accounts for the way active, passive, existential and preposing constructions align the same roles differently. The subject is identified by grammatical behaviour, not by meaning.

Objects, predicative complements and obliques each have their own syntax. Prepositional verbs demand specified prepositions; particles sit between verb and object; light verbs lodge the main content in a noun; most verbs appear in several complementation patterns. To read a clause is to identify those choices and watch them shape the meaning.

A complement checklist: Find the verb and its subject. Identify the internal complements. Decide whether each is an object, a predicative complement or a PP complement. Check for a particle or an oblique. Then ask what semantic roles the participants have and whether a different construction would present the same situation differently.

Take *The committee gave the designer an award for the new bridge*. The subject is *the committee*, the predicator is *gave*, and the two internal core complements are *the designer* and *an award*. *The designer* is the indirect object and *an award* is the direct object. *For the new bridge* is a PP complement expressing the reason or basis for the award.

The same situation can be presented as *The committee gave an award to the designer for the new bridge*. Now *an award* is the direct object and *to the designer* is a PP complement, with *the designer* as an oblique. The participants and their roles have not changed, but the syntactic functions have. That contrast is the core of this chapter.

When you analyse a clause, find the verb first. Its subclass tells you which complements to expect. Then identify the subject, objects, predicative complements and any PP complements. Do not assume that every phrase after the verb is an object: *at the paper*, *to Pat* and *in the box* are PP complements, while *the paper*, *Pat* and *the box* can be objects in other patterns.

Next, separate function from role. The subject of a passive is often the patient, not the agent. The object of *hear* is a stimulus, not a patient. A predicative complement ascribes a property rather than naming a participant. Keeping these levels distinct prevents a description from turning into a list of traditional definitions.

Finally, compare alternations. *Give the key to Pat* and *give Pat the key*, *shoot him* and *shoot at him*, *break the vase* and *the vase broke* are related patterns with different syntax and sometimes different meaning. The comparison shows what the verb licenses and what the construction adds.

In *The committee gave the designer an award for the new bridge*, the clause is ditransitive: *the committee* is subject, *the designer* is indirect object, *an award* is direct object, and *for the new bridge* is a PP complement. The related *gave an award to the designer* is monotransitive with a PP complement, and *the designer* is an oblique inside that PP.

Clauses contain a predicator, complements and adjuncts. The subject is the external core complement; objects and predicative complements are internal. Core complements are directly related to the verb, while non-core complements are realised by PPs and contain obliques.

Semantic roles describe participants, while grammatical functions describe syntactic structure. The subject has a cluster of distinctive properties. Objects and predicative complements differ in form, meaning and behaviour. Prepositional verbs, particles, idioms, light verbs and multiple complementation patterns extend the basic system.

key_terms.definition: The clause function realised by the verb phrase.
A dependent closely related to a head and licensed by it.
A modifier or supplement that is not required by the verb.
The external core complement, prototypically an NP, with distinctive syntactic properties.
The internal core complement that in agent-patient clauses expresses the patient.
The internal core complement characteristically associated with the recipient.
A complement that expresses a property predicated of the subject or object.
The element to which a predicative complement applies, usually the subject or object.
A complement directly related to the verb and prototypically realised by an NP or AdjP.
A complement realised by a PP or another oblique structure rather than a direct NP.
An NP related to the verb through a preposition rather than directly as a core complement.
The presence or absence of a direct object in a clause or verb use.
The number of syntactic complements a verb takes in a given use.
The part an entity plays in the situation expressed by a clause, such as agent, patient or goal.
The prototypical conscious causer of an action.
The entity affected by an action.
The entity that feels, perceives or cognises something.
The entity or proposition that arouses a feeling, perception or cognition.
A broad role for an entity involved in a situation without being a prototypical agent or patient.
The endpoint or recipient towards which a situation is directed.
The starting point from which a situation or entity moves.
A complex-intransitive clause whose predicative complement is related to the subject by be or a similar verb.
A use of be that ascribes a property to the subject.
A use of be that identifies the value of a variable, often allowing subject and complement to reverse.
A verb that selects a PP complement headed by a specified preposition.
An intransitive preposition that can occur between a verb and its direct object.
A verb such as give, take or make whose main semantic content comes from its noun complement.
The occurrence of a verb in more than one complementation pattern.
