teaching.text: Ask a room of students what a preposition is and someone will offer *in*, *on*, *under* — little words that say where or when. That list is a reasonable start, and almost everything interesting about the category lies in how quickly it breaks down. *In* in *She stayed in* has no noun after it at all. *Because* in *Because it rained* carries a whole clause. *From behind the curtain* puts one preposition phrase inside another. Small words, yes; simple, no.

The change of perspective is to treat a preposition as a head. It projects a phrase, takes a complement, tolerates modifiers, and can stand alone when nothing needs saying. Once *because* and *outside* and *downstairs* count as heads of phrases, the class grows well beyond the traditional short list, and its membership stops looking arbitrary. What matters is the structure a word builds, not the size of the word itself.

From there the account works outward: membership first, then the complements and modifiers a preposition can carry, then the curious business of stranding — the preposition left behind when its complement moves to the front. Idioms, phrase functions, grammaticised uses, spatial and temporal meaning, and finally the stylistic question of when to strand and when to front.

*Max sent a photograph of his new house to his parents.* Two phrases in that clause are doing work no single word could do: *of his new house* picks out which photograph, *to his parents* says where it went. Each begins with a preposition, and each preposition relates what follows to something already established — *of* ties the house to the photograph, *to* ties the parents to the sending.

*From behind the curtain* puts a PP inside a PP; *on whether we should call the police* puts an interrogative clause after the preposition; *until recently* puts an adverb phrase there. The relation survives when the complement is not a noun phrase at all. This is the same head–complement pattern that links a verb to its object, and it is what makes the preposition a head rather than a mere linker. The filler varies; the structure does not.

Modification follows from the same analysis. In *just inside the penalty area*, *just* narrows a location that *inside* has already fixed; in *two years after their divorce*, the measure phrase sets a distance in time. Neither modifier is selected by the head, so neither is a complement. Drop them and the phrase survives, thinner but intact.
A preposition phrase
Head | in | Preposition
Complement | the drawer | Object of the preposition
Modifier | just | Focus or degree modifier
Nested PP | from behind the curtain | PP complement
Clause complement | on whether we should go | Interrogative clause
the photograph of his new house — Of heads a PP complement inside the NP.
from behind the curtain — One PP is nested inside another.
until recently — Until takes an AdvP complement.
just inside the penalty area — Just modifies the PP inside the penalty area.

*Of*, *to*, *in*, *on*, *at*, *by*, *for*, *with*, *from*, *between*: the familiar core, every one of them taking a noun phrase and building a phrase that slots into a clause as complement or adjunct. Around that core sit words doing the same structural work while looking less like prepositions — *after* with a clause, *outside* with no complement, *provided* with a condition attached. Membership is decided by the work, not the appearance.

*Because it rained* is a phrase headed by *because* whose complement is a finite clause, exactly parallel to *in the garden*. Most of what older grammars call subordinating conjunctions are prepositions here. The traditional label tracks meaning and clause-linking; the analysis tracks heads and complements, and the second test is the one that groups words together. Three items stay outside the class — *whether*, interrogative *if*, and the *that* which introduces clauses — because they mark a clause without heading a phrase.

*She is outside.* Nothing follows the preposition, and the sentence is complete. *I haven’t seen her since* and *put it downstairs* show the same intransitive use. A missing complement does not change the category, any more than a missing object turns a verb into something else; that is why *outside* counts as a preposition in *They are outside* while *locally*, an adverb, cannot take its place.

New prepositions do appear, but English has no productive suffix or compounding pattern that manufactures them, so the list grows slowly and by borrowing rather than by rule. The class is relatively closed. Closure does not mean uniformity: many members have grammaticised uses in which a construction selects the preposition and its spatial or temporal meaning fades. The *by* of the passive, the *of* in *the destruction of the city*, the *to* in *give it to Kim* are chosen by grammar, not by the speaker’s picture of the scene.
Members and near-members
Central prepositions | of, to, in, on, at | Take NP complements; head PPs
Clause-taking prepositions | after, because, provided | Take finite clause complements
Intransitive prepositions | outside, since, downstairs | Occur without complements
Subordinators | whether, interrogative if, that | Mark clauses rather than head PPs
Grammaticised uses | by, of, to, with | Selected by grammatical constructions

*Ahead of the ship, there was a small island* locates the island and says nothing about anyone’s state of mind. Replace the PP with an adjective phrase and the sentence commits itself: *Tired of the ship, the captain saw an island* attributes the tiredness to the captain. A fronted AdjP of that kind is predicative and needs a predicand; a PP in the same slot is a plain adjunct, free of the commitment.

*Go*, *went*, *gone*: verbs mark tense by inflection. *In*, *into*, *inside*: prepositions do not. Complementation is a softer test. Both categories take objects, and a PP can be fronted with its object intact — *the knife with which she cut it* — while a verb cannot drag its object forward the same way.

*I put it in the drawer* cannot shrink to *I put it*; the locative is required, and *Jill is in the office* resists *Jill is* for the same reason. An *-ly* adverb does not fill that slot. *Jill is locally* does not give *be* the complement it needs, which is why adverbs serve as complements only in restricted cases while many prepositions head obligatory ones.

Some words sit on the boundary. *Worth* takes a noun phrase complement like a preposition — *worth the effort* — but predicates and modifies like an adjective, so the label depends on which part of the pattern you weight. *Owing* is a preposition in *owing to the weather* and a participle in *owing money to the bank*. *Opposite* goes both ways. No single resemblance settles these cases; the whole distribution does.
Category contrasts
Function | Ahead of the ship, there was an island. | Tired of the ship, the captain left.
Inflection | in, into, inside | verb: go, went, gone
Complement | I put it in the drawer. | I put it.
Modification | right under the bed | very happy
Fronting | with which she cut it | adjective cannot front with complement
Ahead of the ship, there was a small island. — The PP is an adjunct: it locates the island without predicating anything of a subject.
Tired of the ship, the captain saw an island. — The fronted AdjP is predicative and ascribes tiredness to the captain.

*In the garden*, *to Paris*, *with my sister*. The default shape is a preposition plus a noun phrase, and the noun phrase is the object of the preposition, which makes the preposition transitive in the ordinary sense. *In* is transitive in *She stayed in the house* and intransitive in *She stayed in*, with no change in the word itself.

Beyond the noun phrase the range widens. *From* takes a PP in *from behind the curtain*; *until* takes an adverb phrase in *until recently*. Both are ordinary head–complement structures with unusual fillers, and the complement type belongs to the head’s lexical entry as much as it does for a verb.

*I regard their behaviour as outrageous.* The adjective phrase after *as* describes the behaviour, not the regarding, so it is a predicative complement and *as* is the preposition that licenses it. *For* does similar work after *take* and *pass*: *I took him for harmless*, *He passed for dead*. Most other prepositions take ordinary objects, and the object/predicative line inside a PP is the same line that runs through verb complementation.

*Apart from Jill* and *since before the war* look alike and are not. In the first, *apart* selects *from*; the two form a fixed combination. In the second, *since* does not select *before* — *before* makes its own contribution, which is why *since after the war* contrasts with it. Specified versus unspecified prepositions: that is the distinction at work.
PP complement types
Object NP | in the garden | in
PP | from behind the curtain | from
AdvP | until recently | until
Interrogative clause | on whether we should go | on
Predicative AdjP | for dead | for
Predicative NP | as treasurer | as
She stayed in the house. — The house is the object of in.
The magician emerged from behind the curtain. — Behind the curtain is a PP complement of from.
We can’t agree on whether we should go. — An interrogative clause complement.
I took him for harmless. — For takes a predicative complement related to him.

*Two years after their divorce* and *just inside the penalty area* both place something before the preposition, but the somethings do different work. The measure phrase sets a distance in time; the focus adverb narrows a location. *Very much in control* adds degree, *right under the bed* adds emphasis. Where the modifier sits depends on what it takes scope over.

*Right* and *straight* are unusually choosy. They modify spatial and temporal prepositions — *right under the bed*, *straight upstairs* — and refuse verbs, adjectives and adverbs. The choosiness is a test. If *right* can stand in front of a word, that word is probably heading a PP, which is how *in*, *inside* and *upstairs* separate themselves from adverbs of identical shape.

PPs nest productively. *From behind the curtain*, *out of the box*, *next to her sister*: in each, a PP sits inside a PP, and the inner preposition contributes a relation while the outer one selects or adjusts it. *Out of the box* is not a wordier *outside the box*; it is *out* taking *of the box* as its complement. The recursion is syntactic, not a quirk of individual idioms.

*Notwithstanding the weather* and *the weather notwithstanding* show a preposition that may follow its complement. Head before complement is the norm, so the exceptions stand out. A different pattern appears in *spoonful by spoonful*, *day by day*, *piece by piece*, where a repeated form distributes a situation over time or quantity rather than locating it once.
PP modification
Measure | two years after the divorce | Specifies distance in time
Degree | very much in control | Intensifies the relation
Focus | just inside the area | Narrows the location
Restricted adverb | right under the bed | Spatial emphasis
Reduplicative | day by day | Distributive sequence
She died two years after their divorce. — Two years modifies the PP after their divorce.
They pushed it right under the bed. — Right is a restricted modifier of the spatial PP.
the weather notwithstanding — The complement precedes the head in this construction.
The pain eased day by day. — A reduplicative PP expressing gradual change.

*What was she referring to?* The preposition sits at the end, its complement has moved to the front, and the sentence is unremarkable. English does this constantly — in questions, relatives, exclamatives, comparatives, hollow clauses and passives — leaving the preposition behind and co-indexing the gap with the fronted phrase. Head before complement, as in *with pride*, is the default order, not the only possible one.

In some of those constructions the preposition can travel with its complement instead: *To whom are you speaking?*, *the article to which I referred*. This is pied-piping, and the choice between it and stranding is partly structural, partly a matter of register.

The old prohibition on ending a sentence with a preposition has no basis in the grammar. Stranding has been standard for centuries and is unremarkable in most registers. Fronting often sounds formal, and it sounds pedantic when the stranded version is what any speaker would say. What is at stake is a choice between constructions, not a verdict on correctness.

A handful of prepositions allow the complement before the head: *the weather notwithstanding* alongside *notwithstanding the weather*. The complement is still present, so this is not stranding; it is an alternative order inside the PP. Preposing a whole PP is a third phenomenon: *To your father I’m even more deeply indebted* moves preposition and complement together.
Order and displacement
Stranding | What are you looking at? | Complement fronted; preposition stranded
Pied-piping | At what are you looking? | Preposition fronts with complement
Postposed complement | the weather notwithstanding | Complement precedes head
PP preposing | To your father I’m indebted. | Whole PP moves to the front
What was she referring to? — The complement what is fronted; to is stranded.
To whom are you speaking? — The preposition fronts with its complement in formal style.
the article she was referring to — A relative clause with a stranded preposition.
the weather notwithstanding — The complement precedes the head; not a stranded preposition.

*For the sake of the children* has a recognisable shape and a meaning you cannot compute from its parts. *At odds with the evidence*, *on the grounds that the evidence is unreliable*, *up against a deadline*, *in brief*: each is headed by a preposition, each is more or less fixed, and none is fully predictable from the words inside it.

Fixed does not mean unstructured. *For the sake of* still takes a noun phrase complement; *on the grounds that* still takes a content clause; *at odds with* still takes a PP. The idiom is a lexical unit built out of ordinary syntax, which is why a complement can appear inside it and why a modifier can sometimes squeeze in without breaking it.

*In brief* and *of old* have petrified further. The element after the preposition looks adjectival, but there is no predicand for it and no reason to call it predicative; the phrase has hardened into a single unit. *What with* behaves differently again, introducing a reason adjunct and taking a coordination of PPs or clauses after it.
for the sake of the children — For the sake of takes an NP complement.
at odds with the evidence — At odds with takes a PP complement.
on the grounds that the evidence is unreliable — On the grounds that takes a content clause.
in brief — A fossilised PP with an adjective-like complement.

*Rely on the evidence* and *before breakfast* both contain a PP, and only the first is required by the word it attaches to. Complements are licensed — by a verb, noun, adjective or preposition, as in *rely on*, *a reliance on*, *keen on*, *inside of*. Adjuncts such as *in the garden* or *with great care* attach to the clause and add information. One PP can be a complement in one clause and an adjunct in another.

Phrases also take PP modifiers: *proud of her* modifies an adjective, *independently of the result* an adverb, *the woman in the garden* a noun, *from behind the curtain* another PP. Some PPs stand outside the clause as supplements, as *In short, the plan failed* shows. A few can even be subjects — *From here to London is over fifty miles*.

Meaning does not settle the function. *On the table* is a complement in *The report is on the table* and an adjunct in *She read it on the table*, with the same preposition and the same kind of complement. What changes is what the verb requires: *be* needs the locative, *read* does not. Clause structure then decides whether the phrase counts as complement or adjunct.
PP functions
Complement of verb | rely on the evidence | rely
Complement of noun | a reliance on the evidence | reliance
Complement of adjective | keen on opera | keen
Adjunct | before breakfast | Clause
Modifier | the woman in the garden | woman
Supplement | In short, the plan failed. | Clause
Subject | From here to London is fifty miles. | Clause
She relied on the report. — On the report is a complement of relied.
She read it on the train. — On the train is a locative adjunct.
the woman in the garden — In the garden modifies the nominal woman.
From here to London is fifty miles. — A PP functioning as subject.

*The plan was approved by the boss.* Nothing in *by* means “agent”; the passive puts it there. This is what it means for a preposition to be grammaticised: the construction selects it, and its contribution is relational rather than spatial or temporal. *Of* in *the destruction of the city*, *to* in *give it to Kim*, *with* in *pleased with the result* work the same way, as required markers rather than free lexical choices.

The passive *by* is the clearest case because the correspondence with the active is so tight. *By the boss* is the internalised version of the active subject, and the same *by* marks an agent inside a noun phrase — *the approval of the plan by the boss* — although the NP construction is not a passive clause with its pieces rearranged.

*Of* is the default linker between a noun or adjective and its complement: *the destruction of the city*, *proud of her achievements*. Where the head prefers something else, the preference is a lexical fact — *marriage to Pat*, *a ban on smoking*, *keen on opera*. There is no route from meaning to preposition here; the pattern has to be learned with the word.

Comparison grammaticises *as* and *than*, and *as* also heads predicative complements — *I regard her as my best friend*. *At*, *for*, *from*, *in*, *on* and *with* each carry clusters of grammaticised uses beside their spatial and temporal ones. The same preposition can be a free choice in one construction and a required marker in another.
Common grammaticised uses
by | Passive agent | approved by the boss
of | Noun complement | the destruction of the city
to | Recipient | gave it to Kim
with | Adjective complement | pleased with the result
as | Predicative complement | regard her as a friend
than | Comparison | taller than Pat
on | Selected complement | rely on the evidence
The plan was approved by the boss. — By marks the agent in the passive construction.
the destruction of the city — Of relates the city to the noun destruction.
I gave the key to Kim. — To marks the recipient.
I left the parcel by the door. — By has its ordinary locative meaning here.

*The pen is on the table.* Two entities, one relation: the pen is located, the table locates it. Cognitive semantics calls the located entity the trajector and the reference point the landmark, and the labels earn their keep once the relation stops being static, since a trajector can move from a source, along a path, to a goal.

English divides the basic spatial work among a small set of contrasts. *At* locates, *to* marks a goal, *from* marks a source; *on* pairs with *off* and *in* with *out*; *into* and *onto* mark goals while *off* and *out of* mark sources. *Away* can mark source with or without *from*, which is one reason the system is better handled as a set of oppositions than as a list of translations.

Time borrows the spatial vocabulary almost wholesale. *At three o’clock* marks a point, *on Monday* a day, *in July* a month, each with the preposition that suits its granularity. *Before the meeting* and *after lunch* use path relations; *since 2020* marks a source; *for two hours* marks extent. The mapping holds because time is construed as a line and situations as points or regions along it.

*Between* and *among* are not divided by number. *Between* treats the members individually, as boundary points; *among* treats them as a collective. Both *between the trees* and *among the trees* are grammatical, but *between my toes* is normal and *among my toes* is not, because toes present themselves as individual boundaries rather than as a mass.
Spatial and temporal relations
Location | at the station | at six o’clock
Location | on the table | on Monday
Location | in the box | in July
Goal | to Paris | until Friday
Source | from London | since 2020
Duration | for two miles | for two hours
The pen is on the table. — Static location: on contrasts with off.
She walked from the station to the hotel. — Source and goal in one path.
We met at six o’clock on Monday. — At marks a point in time; on marks a day.
I have lived here since 2020. — Since marks a temporal source.

*Who did you speak to?* or *To whom did you speak?* Both are grammatical; they belong to different registers. A writer who avoids stranding everywhere produces prose that feels stiff, and a writer who fronts without control sounds archaic. Choose according to the occasion, not according to a blanket rule.

Idioms need more care, because their meaning is not compositional. *For the sake of* is not a paraphrase of “for the reason of”; *at odds with* is not a spatial relation; *on the grounds that* carries a fixed evidential force. Change the preposition and the idiom changes, or collapses.

Preposition choice also encodes lexical patterns that a dictionary has to record. *Depend on*, *rely on*, *keen on*, *a reliance on* share a preposition because each head selects it. *Different from*, *different to* and *different than* vary by dialect and register. Meaning alone will not tell you which form a head takes.

Everything here follows from one move: a preposition heads a phrase. It takes complements of several categories, accepts modifiers, and can occur without one. The class includes many traditional subordinating conjunctions and a subset of traditional adverbs, and it is closed without being small.

PPs serve as complements, adjuncts, modifiers, supplements and, occasionally, subjects. Their complements range over NPs, PPs, AdvPs, AdjPs and clauses, and the object/predicative distinction applies inside the phrase. Stranding, pied-piping and the rare complement-before-head order are structural options, not errors.

Grammaticised prepositions — *by*, *of*, *to*, *with* — are selected by constructions and often behave like case markers. Spatial meanings extend into time and abstraction. Style is a matter of choosing the construction that fits the register, not of applying a blanket prohibition.

A PP checklist: Find the preposition and its complement. Decide whether the complement is an object, predicative, PP, AdvP or clause. Check for modifiers and nesting. Then identify the PP’s function in the larger construction: complement, adjunct, modifier or supplement.

Take *The keys were left just inside the drawer, behind a pile of old photographs*. The main PP *just inside the drawer* is headed by *inside*, modified by *just* and complemented by *the drawer*. The second PP *behind a pile of old photographs* is an adjunct locating the keys relative to another landmark.

The example shows the layered structure of PPs: a head, a modifier, a complement and a nested NP. It also shows that a PP can function as an adjunct in clause structure without being predicated of the subject. The keys are not “behind” in any inherent sense; the PP merely locates them.

When you analyse a PP, find its head and complement first. Then decide whether any other expression is a modifier or a second complement. A nested PP such as from behind the curtain has its own head and complement inside the larger phrase.

Next, identify the PP’s function. Is it required by a verb, noun, adjective or preposition? Is it an adjunct, a modifier, a supplement or a subject? The same PP can have different functions in different clauses, and the function determines whether it is a complement or an adjunct.

Finally, consider order and register. Stranding is normal, fronting is often formal, and a few prepositions allow their complement to precede them. Idiomatic PPs have fixed internal patterns, and grammaticised prepositions are selected by the construction rather than chosen freely.

In *The keys were left just inside the drawer, behind a pile of old photographs*, *inside* heads the PP *just inside the drawer* and takes *the drawer* as its object. *Just* modifies that PP. *Behind a pile of old photographs* is a separate PP adjunct with *a pile of old photographs* as its complement.

Prepositions are phrase heads and take a wide range of complements. The category includes clause-taking and intransitive prepositions, and excludes whether, interrogative if and clause-introducing that. PPs can be nested, modified and used in all major syntactic functions.

Stranding and pied-piping are both grammatical. Grammaticised prepositions mark grammatical relations, while spatial meanings extend into time and other domains. The main analytical task is to identify the head, complement and function of each PP.

key_terms.definition: A word that heads a preposition phrase and typically takes a complement.
A phrase headed by a preposition, with an optional complement and optional modifiers.
A dependent licensed by the head, such as the drawer in inside the drawer.
A dependent that adds information without being required by the head.
A preposition used without a complement, such as outside in She is outside.
The use of a preposition without its complement in the normal post-head position, as in What are you looking at?
Fronting a preposition together with its complement, as in To whom are you speaking?
A preposition selected by a grammatical construction rather than chosen for its independent meaning.
An NP related to a head through a preposition rather than directly.
The NP complement of a transitive preposition, as in the garden in in the garden.
A complement related to a predicand, as in as treasurer.
A modifier in clause structure, often realised by a PP.
The entity whose location or movement is specified in a spatial relation.
The reference point or area relative to which a trajector is located.
The starting point of a path or change of location, often marked by from or off.
The endpoint of a path or change of location, often marked by to or into.
A static spatial relation, often marked by at, on or in.
An expression whose meaning is not fully predictable from its parts.
A fixed expression with limited internal variation, often headed by a preposition.
A clause functioning as the complement of a preposition or other head.
A marker introducing a subordinate clause, such as whether, if or that.
A preposition that takes an object NP complement.
Movement of a constituent to a position before the nucleus clause.
A detached element related to an anchor without being a syntactic dependent.

lessons.title: The clause: adjuncts

outcomes.text: Explain the main ideas in The clause: adjuncts.
Recognise the patterns in real sentences.
Use the ideas when you read and write.

key_terms.definition: A modifier in clause or VP structure, together with related supplements.
A dependent licensed by a head and closely integrated into its structure.
The way in which a process is carried out, as in She spoke quietly.
The method by which something is achieved, as in by breaking the door down.
An entity used to carry out an action, as in with a hammer.
An adjunct that evaluates or qualifies the act performed rather than its manner.
A static spatial or temporal relation, as in in the garden or at six.
The starting point of a path or change, as in from the station.
The endpoint of a path or change, as in to the station.
An intermediate route between source and goal, as in through the tunnel.
The orientation of movement, as in towards the door.
The measured size or reach of a situation, as in five miles or two hours.
The temporal extent of a situation, as in for two hours.
Presenting a situation as having a terminal point or complete extent.
How often a situation occurs, as in twice or every day.
The intensity or extent of a property or process, as in very much.
The intended result of an action, as in in order to help.
The explanation for a situation, as in because of the strike.
The outcome of a situation, as in so that the hills glowed.
A contrast in which a circumstance might lead one to expect the opposite of the main clause.
A construction in which one situation is presented as dependent on another.
The subordinate clause expressing the condition in a conditional construction.
The matrix clause expressing the consequence in a conditional construction.
A conditional that leaves the fulfilment of the condition open.
A conditional using modal preterite or irrealis marking to present the condition as remote.
The sphere or field within which a clause is claimed to hold, as in politically.
The qualification of a proposition for possibility, probability or necessity.
A comment on the value or fortunate status of a situation.
The act performed in speaking, such as asserting, asking or conceding.
An adjunct that links a clause to the surrounding discourse.
A prosodically detached element related to an anchor without being a modifier.

teaching.text: *They left.* Grammatical, complete, and almost empty. Add *quietly*, *at noon*, *because the train was cancelled*, *fortunately*, *according to Kim*, and the same three words become a situated event, a reported cause, an evaluation and a hedge. Everything added is an adjunct: optional from the verb’s point of view, and doing very different work from one another.

This chapter sorts that work. It starts with the complement/adjunct boundary, then moves through manner and instrument, space, time and duration, frequency and degree, cause and result, concession and condition. The later sections take up the categories that sit further out — domain, modality, evaluation, speech act, discourse connection — and the positions that help tell them apart.

Two questions recur. How tightly is the dependent bound into the clause? And what kind of meaning does it contribute? The answers are related but not identical. A manner phrase is usually bound tight; an evaluation usually floats free as a supplement. A reason can belong to the proposition or comment on why the speaker is asserting it — same words, different scope.

*She presented her case very eloquently.* Remove the adverb and the clause still works: something is lost, nothing is missing. *She put the file in the drawer* behaves differently. Take out *in the drawer* and *She put the file* leaves a hole the verb itself has opened. The first dependent is an adjunct, the second a complement, and the predicator — the verb phrase — licenses only the second.

Manner, means, instrument, act-related evaluation, place, time, extent, duration, aspect, frequency, serial order, degree, purpose, reason, result, concession, condition, domain, modality, evaluation, speech act, discourse connection: that is a wide range. A list that long is a reminder that “adjunct” names a structural position, not one semantic job.

Categories overlap in practice. *If you must know* has the form of a condition and the function of a speech-act comment. *Because her light is off* can give the reason she went home or the reason I can assert that she did. Same string, two scopes, two categories — which is why the analysis keeps asking what a dependent takes scope over rather than what it looks like.
A semantic map of adjuncts
Manner | She spoke quietly. | How?
Instrument | She cut it with a knife. | With what?
Location | They met in the garden. | Where?
Duration | They stayed for two hours. | How long?
Frequency | She visits every week. | How often?
Reason | They left because of the strike. | Why?
Condition | We’ll go if it’s fine. | Under what condition?
Evaluation | Fortunately, nobody was hurt. | What is the speaker’s attitude?
She presented her case very eloquently. — Adjunct: the clause survives without it.
She put the file in the drawer. — Complement: put requires a locative.
She put the file. — The required locative is missing; the clause is incomplete.

*It was yesterday that he returned* sounds fine; *It was fortunately that he returned* does not. Both are adverbs in the same position, so the difference is not positional. *Yesterday* can be the focus of a cleft, an alternative question or contrastive negation — *Did he return yesterday or on Tuesday?* — and *fortunately* cannot. Focus potential is the first of six parameters.

*Yesterday* restricts truth: if he returned the day before, the sentence is false. *Fortunately* does not — the return can have happened and the sentence still be true when it was not fortunate at all. Restrictiveness is the second parameter. Evaluations are typically non-restrictive.

*When* and *where* question temporal and locative adjuncts, *why* questions purpose and reason. The remaining four parameters are questioning, scope, bounding and realisation. Scope decides whether an adjunct applies inside or outside negation, or inside or outside another adjunct. Bounding explains why *She ran to the station* goes with *in twenty minutes* rather than *for twenty minutes*. Realisation is the internal form: AdvP, PP, NP, clause.
Parameters of analysis
Focus | Can it be clefted or contrastively questioned? | It was yesterday that he left.
Restrictiveness | Does it affect truth conditions? | yesterday vs fortunately
Questioning | Which interrogative word fits? | When? Where? Why?
Scope | What does it take scope over? | not ... because
Bounding | Does it bound the situation? | to the station, two miles
Realisation | What is its internal form? | AdvP, PP, NP, clause
It was yesterday that he returned. — A temporal adjunct can be focused in a cleft.
Fortunately, he returned. — An evaluation is a non-restrictive supplement.
I didn’t buy it because it was too expensive. — The reason adjunct has scope over the negation.
I didn’t appoint him just because he was my son. — The negation has scope over the reason adjunct.

*She walked slowly away*, *He got in by breaking the door down*, *I broke the nut with a hammer*. Each answers *how*, and each answers differently. The first describes how the walking was done; the second names the method that achieved the entry; the third names the thing used. Manner, means, instrument, in that order.

*Carefully*, *hastily*, *raucously* are gradable *-ly* adverbs, but the category is functional, not morphological. PPs do the same job in *with great care*, *without much consideration*, *in a studiously nonchalant manner*. AdvP and PP manner expressions coordinate freely, as in *She handled the situation skilfully and with great tact*, which is one sign that they share a function.

*She behaved outrageously* and *They treated her shabbily* need the manner expression for the intended sense, and *word* and *dress* pattern the same way. Some manner dependents are complements. With most verbs the manner phrase is optional and qualifies a predicate that is already complete.

Manner can reach into the result. *He sealed the window hermetically* describes how the sealing was done and implies that the window ended up sealed that way. *They painted the house badly* can describe the process, the finished appearance, or both at once.
She departed very hastily. — Manner: the departure was hasty.
He got in by breaking the door down. — Means: the method used to get in.
I broke the nut with a hammer. — Instrument: the hammer was used.
She behaved outrageously. — A manner complement required by the verb’s sense.

*He spoke to them rudely* and *Rudely, he spoke only to her husband* are not the same claim. The first says the speaking was rude. The second says the act of speaking only to the husband was rude — he might have been perfectly polite to the husband while cutting everyone else. Position turns a manner adverb into an act-related one.

Act-related adjuncts come in subjective and volitional kinds. Subjective ones give the speaker’s evaluation of the act: *foolishly*, *wisely*, *tactfully*, *carelessly*. Volitional ones give the agent’s intention or willingness: *deliberately*, *reluctantly*, *accidentally*, *voluntarily*. PPs join in, as in *with his usual tact*, *on purpose*, *under duress*.

*Foolishly, he answered two questions* evaluates the act; *He answered the question foolishly* describes the answer. Position is the usual clue: front position favours the act-related reading, end position the manner reading. Central position can be genuinely ambiguous, or it can lean one way or the other depending on the adverb.
Rudely, he spoke only to her husband. — The act of speaking only to the husband was rude.
He spoke to them rudely. — The manner of speaking was rude.
Foolishly, he answered two questions. — The act of answering two questions was foolish.
He answered the question foolishly. — The answer itself was foolish.

*We met under the station clock* locates the meeting; *The key is on the table* locates the key. Both are spatial, but only the second is a complement of *be*. Location can be either complement or adjunct — *put* and *be* select it, *have breakfast* does not — and the same phrase can change role with the verb.

Motion adds structure. *John ran from the attic to the kitchen* gives source and goal in one path. *She took her passport out of the drawer* gives only the source; *Kim put the key under the mat* only the goal. *We drove through the tunnel* traces an intermediate path, and *She ran towards the house* gives direction without arrival.

Locatives attach to different things. *I saw your father in London* locates the event; *I saw your father at the window* locates your father. *She carried the child on her shoulders* locates the object carried. English does not mark these readings with different forms, so context and the choice of landmark do the work.

*She poked him in the ribs*; *He patted her on the shoulder*: these relate to *She poked his ribs* and *He patted her shoulder*, but they are not simple locatives — the person is affected, not merely positioned. A special case is the affected body part. Locatives also extend metaphorically into *in Smith’s class*, *in our family*, *in medicine*, where the “place” is social or conceptual rather than physical.
Spatial categories
Location | under the clock | Static position
Source | from the attic | Starting point
Goal | to the kitchen | Endpoint
Path | through the tunnel | Intermediate route
Direction | towards the house | Orientation of movement
Theme location | at the window | Location of a participant
Affected body part | in the ribs | Part of the patient affected

*Yesterday* is read off the moment of utterance, *on 3 May* off the calendar, *after the meeting* off another situation. Deictic, calendar-based, anaphoric: three ways of locating a situation in time. Temporal location is usually an adjunct, though some verbs take it as a complement — *The meeting is tomorrow*, *I’ve scheduled it for Tuesday*.

*For two hours*, *all week*, *from Monday until Thursday*, *since 2020*: these measure duration either overall or by terminal points. Duration is extent in time. The preposition matters: *for* marks overall duration, *in* marks the time taken to reach a terminus. *She wrote it in two days* and *She studied for two days* differ in aspect, not in the calendar.

*She ran for ten minutes* presents an unbounded activity; add a goal and the situation closes — *She ran to the station in ten minutes* supports the accomplishment reading. Bounding is where the aspectual difference shows. Some clauses allow either construal, because the same situation can be viewed perfectively or imperfectively.

Aspectual adjuncts — *already*, *still*, *yet*, *any more*, *no longer* — are polarity-sensitive. They say where a situation stands in its own history: beginning, continuing, ending. Which of them can appear depends on the clause’s polarity and viewpoint, not simply on when the event happened.
Temporal categories
Temporal location | I read it last week. | When?
Duration | She stayed for two hours. | How long?
Starting point | She has been here since Monday. | Since when?
Endpoint | She stayed until Friday. | Until when?
Bounding duration | She wrote it in two days. | How long did it take?
Aspectuality | She has already left. | What is the situation’s phase?

Frequency adjuncts quantify situations much as determiners quantify entities. *She lectured twice* is the verbal counterpart of *two lectures*, *She always wins* of *every match*, *People sometimes misunderstand this* of *some people*. The parallel is not decorative. Both kinds of expression make a predicate or a noun countable, universal or partial.

Frequency splits into bounding and non-bounding. *She lectured ten times* gives a total, and the situation becomes perfective. *She lectured regularly*, *every day*, *quite frequently* give a rate rather than a total, and the situation stays imperfective. *Three times a week* belongs with the rates: it says how often, not how many.

Serial order — *first*, *next*, *finally*, *for the third time* — places a situation in a sequence. Degree — *very much*, *greatly*, *somewhat*, *a lot* — measures intensity or extent. The two interact with frequency, and the interaction shows in scope: *I always proofread an article three times* has a non-bounding *always* over a bounding *three times*.
She lectured ten times. — Bounding frequency: a total count.
She lectured every day. — Non-bounding frequency: a recurring pattern.
I always proofread an article three times. — Non-bounding always has scope over bounding three times.
I enjoyed it very much. — A degree adjunct modifying the verb phrase.

*They had to walk because of the bus strike*, *He left the door open in order to let the cat in*, *She spoke so softly that nobody could hear her*, *He died of pneumonia*. Reason, purpose, result, cause. The labels are close enough to blur in ordinary talk and distinct enough to matter in analysis.

Purpose looks forward, presenting an intended outcome. Reason looks back, explaining why a situation occurred or why the speaker says it did. Result is the outcome itself, often signalled by *so that* or *such that*. The same marker can shift category with scope — *because her light is off* can be an ordinary reason or a reason for asserting that she has gone home.

Negation exposes the difference. *I didn’t buy it because it was too expensive* normally means the expense explains the not buying. *I didn’t appoint him just because he was my son* means he was appointed, but not for that reason. Same negative, different scope, and the two readings are not interchangeable.
Cause and result categories
Cause | He died of pneumonia. | Source of the situation
Reason | They walked because of the strike. | Explanation
Purpose | She left to catch the train. | Intended future outcome
Result | She spoke so softly that no one heard. | Consequence
Speech-act reason | She’s gone home, because her light is off. | Reason for the assertion
I didn’t buy it because it was too expensive. — The reason adjunct has scope over the negation.
I didn’t appoint him just because he was my son. — The negation has scope over the reason adjunct.
She left early to catch the train. — Purpose: the intended outcome.
She spoke so softly that nobody heard. — Result: the consequence of the manner.

*Sonia doesn’t speak French although she grew up in Paris.* The subordinate clause is conceded as true. It also raises an expectation — that someone raised in Paris would speak French — and the main clause denies it. That expectation is an implicature, not an entailment, which is why the sentence stays true when the expectation is unreasonable.

Reverse the clauses and the truth conditions hold while the packaging changes: *Sonia grew up in Paris although she doesn’t speak French*. Split the same content into coordinated clauses — *Sonia doesn’t speak French; nevertheless, she grew up in Paris* — and the concession becomes a separate act of assertion.

The markers differ in what they take. *Although* and *though* take finite or reduced clauses; *despite* takes an NP or a gerund-participial; *notwithstanding* can follow its complement; *for all* is informal; *albeit* is formal and compressed. Concessives resist direct questioning and usually fall outside the scope of matrix negation, which is part of why they sit with the less integrated adjuncts.
Although Sam was extremely rude to her, Beth defended him. — The subordinate clause is entailed; the expectation is cancelled.
Despite the recession, travel agents are doing well. — Despite takes an NP complement.
Notwithstanding Ed’s reservations, the agreement was accepted. — Notwithstanding takes an NP complement.
Sonia grew up in Paris although she doesn’t speak French. — Reversed concession: information packaging changes.

*If you touch that wire, you will get a shock.* Two clauses, one conditional: *you touch that wire* states the condition — the protasis — and *you will get a shock* states the consequence, the apodosis. The conditional adjunct is the *if* together with its complement clause.

An open conditional leaves the condition genuinely open. Its invariant meaning is narrow: it excludes the combination of a true protasis with a false apodosis. Everything else the sentence suggests is implicature — that the apodosis follows from the protasis, that it fails when the protasis fails, that the speaker does not know either way. None of the three is an entailment, and the last two can be cancelled outright.

The consequence can be causal or inferential. Touch the wire and the shock is caused; *If the key is not in my pocket, I left it in the door* reasons from absence to a conclusion. The only-if implicature can be cancelled outright — *If it’s fine I’m going to the beach, and in fact I’ll probably go even if it’s wet* — and the don’t-know implicature disappears when the condition is already established.

*Only* and *even* focus the condition rather than creating new conditional types. *Only if you apologise will I help* makes the condition necessary; *Even if it rains, I’m going* presents the apodosis as holding across a range of conditions that includes rain. What changes is the set of conditions quantified over, not the if-then structure.
Components of an open conditional
Protasis | if it rains | Condition
Apodosis | we’ll cancel the match | Consequence
Invariant meaning | P true and Q false is excluded | Entailment
Consequence | Q follows from P | Implicature
Only-if | if not P, then not Q | Cancellable implicature
Don’t-know | speaker does not know whether P | Cancellable implicature
If you touch that wire, you will get a shock. — Causal consequence.
If the key is not in my pocket, I left it in the door. — Inferential consequence.
If it’s fine, I’m going to the beach, and I’ll probably go even if it’s wet. — The only-if implicature is explicitly cancelled.
If you need help, Helen is willing to lend a hand. — A relevance protasis: the help is available regardless.

*If you got it right, you’d win $100.* The past tense does not put the winning in the past. It puts the condition at a distance — remote, unlikely, contrary to fact. *If Ed were here, he could come too* uses irrealis *were* for the same effect, with a modal in the apodosis to match.

*Unless* introduces a negative condition: *Unless you hurry, we’ll be late* is roughly *If you do not hurry, we’ll be late*. It is not a general synonym for *if not*, because it is restricted to conditions whose non-fulfilment would lead to the apodosis. *Even if* and *only if* shift the focus and the range of conditions without touching the underlying structure.

Exhaustive conditionals quantify over a set. *Whether you like it or not, we’re going* covers both alternatives; *Whoever comes, the door will be locked* quantifies over people. In the governed construction the conditional contains an interrogative clause; in the ungoverned one it contains a free relative or a conditional phrase.

Conditionals stack, focus and take scope. *If it rains, we’ll stay in, but if it clears, we’ll go out* sets two conditions in contrast. *Only* and *even* can select one condition over another. Prosody and word order help the reader recover which relation is intended.
If you got it right, you’d win $100. — Remote: modal preterite in the protasis and would in the apodosis.
If Ed were here, he could come too. — Irrealis were marks the remote condition.
Unless you hurry, we’ll be late. — A negative condition.
Whether you like it or not, we’re going. — An exhaustive conditional covering both alternatives.

*Technically, he did not commit an offence.* The claim is not that he acted in a technical manner; *technically* restricts the domain in which the claim holds. *Politically, the decision was a disaster* and *In medicine, mistakes can be fatal* do the same: they say where the proposition applies, not how anything was done.

Modal adjuncts qualify commitment: *probably*, *certainly*, *perhaps*, *possibly*, *necessarily*. They overlap in meaning with modal auxiliaries while differing in syntax. *He probably left* comes close to *He may have left* in epistemic effect, but the adverb and the auxiliary occupy different positions and carry different force.

They favour front or central position and typically outscope frequency and manner adjuncts. Both kinds are clause-oriented. *He probably sees them regularly* means it is probable that he sees them regularly, not that his seeing them is regularly probable.
Technically, he did not commit an offence. — Domain: the claim holds within a technical classification.
Politically, the decision was a disaster. — Domain: the judgement is political, not necessarily personal.
He probably sees them regularly. — Probably has scope over the frequency adjunct.
Perhaps she misunderstood. — A modal adjunct qualifying the proposition.

*Fortunately, we got there on time.* Reply *That’s not true* and you are denying that we got there on time, not disputing that it was fortunate. Evaluative adjuncts comment on the value or fortunate status of a situation, and they sit outside the proposition they comment on. *Sadly, the plan failed* works the same way.

Speech-act adjuncts comment on the saying rather than on the situation. *Frankly, I’m disappointed* does not describe a frank manner of being disappointed; it qualifies the assertion. *Honestly, I don’t know* and *If you must know, I’ve already left* qualify an admission or a refusal in the same way.

Connective adjuncts work between clauses: *Moreover*, *However*, *Therefore*, *Nevertheless*, *Then*. They organise an argument or a narrative rather than modifying an event. Like evaluations, they are normally supplements, and they resist focusing and questioning.
Fortunately, we got there on time. — Evaluation of the situation as fortunate.
Frankly, I’m disappointed. — Speech-act comment: I am speaking frankly.
Moreover, nobody had warned us. — Connective: adds a further point to the argument.
However, the plan still failed. — Connective of contrast.

*Happily, they watched TV* and *They watched TV happily* contain the same words in a different order and make different claims. The first evaluates the situation; the second describes the manner. Front, central and end positions map onto orientations well enough to be a useful first test.

VP-oriented adjuncts — manner, means, degree, frequency, duration, temporal location — modify the predicate and prefer central or end position. Clause-oriented ones — domain, modality, evaluation, speech act, connective — modify the applicability of the clause and prefer front position. The correlation is strong, not absolute.

Detachment turns an adjunct into a supplement. A fronted evaluation is normally set off prosodically; a central interpolation is detached from the clause around it; an end-position manner adjunct is normally integrated. Writing signals the difference with commas, though usage is not uniform, and the same string can shift reading when the intonation changes.
Position and orientation
Front | Evaluation, modality, domain, connective | Fortunately, they left.
Central | Frequency, modality, act-related | They often leave early.
End | Manner, place, time, purpose | They left quietly at noon.
Detached | Evaluation, speech act, supplement | They left, fortunately.
Happily, they watched TV. — Evaluation in front position.
They happily watched TV. — Manner in central position.
They watched TV happily. — Manner in end position.
They watched TV, happily. — Detached supplement, often evaluative.

The same repertoire of meanings keeps returning: manner, means, instrument, place, time, duration, frequency, degree, cause, purpose, reason, result, concession, condition, domain, modality, evaluation, speech act, discourse connection. What varies is how tightly each is bound into the clause.

The licensing test separates complements from adjuncts, and six parameters sharpen the boundary: focus, restrictiveness, questioning, scope, bounding, realisation. Adjuncts can be AdvPs, PPs, NPs, finite clauses, non-finite clauses or verbless clauses, and position often tracks orientation.

The later categories sit further out. Domain, modality, evaluation, speech act and connective adjuncts take scope over the proposition or over the act of speaking rather than over the verb alone. Conditionals and concessives add layered relations between situations, expectations and alternatives.

An adjunct checklist: Identify the dependent and ask whether the verb licenses it. Classify its meaning. Check focus, truth-restrictiveness, questioning and scope. Then locate it in front, central or end position and decide whether it is integrated or detached.

Take *Fortunately, the train left on time, although the platform was crowded*. *Fortunately* is an evaluative supplement: it comments on the situation but does not restrict its truth. *On time* is a temporal adjunct locating the departure. *Although the platform was crowded* is a concessive adjunct: it entails that the platform was crowded and presents that fact as contrary to the expectation that the train might be delayed.

The example shows three levels of integration. The temporal adjunct is a modifier inside the clause; the concessive is a subordinate clause in a PP; the evaluation is a detached supplement. All three are adjuncts, but they do not have the same scope, focus potential or position.

When you meet an adjunct, first ask what the verb licenses. If the dependent is required by the verb’s sense, it is a complement. If it merely adds information, it is an adjunct. Then classify the meaning: manner, place, time, reason, condition and so on.

Next, test its integration. Can it be focused in a cleft? Does it affect the truth of the clause? Can it be questioned? What does it take scope over? These tests separate integrated modifiers from supplements and clause-level comments.

Finally, consider position and prosody. A fronted evaluation is not the same construction as an end-position manner adverb, even when the form is identical. The position signals orientation, scope and information structure.

In *Fortunately, the train left on time, although the platform was crowded*, *fortunately* is an evaluative supplement, *on time* is a temporal adjunct, and *although the platform was crowded* is a concessive adjunct. The concessive clause is entailed and creates a contrary-to-expectation contrast with the main clause.

Adjuncts cover a wide range of semantic categories, from manner and space to condition and speech acts. They differ in focus potential, restrictiveness, scope, bounding effect and syntactic realisation.

Position correlates with orientation: VP-oriented adjuncts favour central or end position, while clause-oriented adjuncts favour front position. Supplements are detached and typically non-restrictive.
