lessons.title: Negation

outcomes.text: Explain the main ideas in Negation.
Recognise the patterns in real sentences.
Use the ideas when you read and write.

key_terms.definition: The contrast between positive and negative clauses.
Negation that makes the whole clause negative.
Negation that affects a constituent without making the whole clause negative.
Negation marked in association with the verb, often with not or n’t.
Negation marked on a dependent rather than on the verb.
Negation marked by a dedicated negative word such as not or no.
Negation marked by a word or affix with another function as well, such as never or un-.
A negator meaning zero or none, such as no, none, never, neither or nor.
A word located towards the negative end of a scale, such as few, hardly or rarely.
Negation marked by a prefix or suffix, such as un-, non- or -less.
Negation used to reject a formulation, implicature or pronunciation rather than the truth of a proposition.
The part of the meaning that is negated.
The part of the scope that is most prominently negated.
An expression such as any, ever or at all that is favoured in negative or non-affirmative contexts.
An expression such as some or already that is favoured in positive contexts.
A question, conditional, comparative or other context that is not a positive assertion.
An idiom with a negative meaning that is not simply a polarity-sensitive item, such as not lift a finger.
The marking of a single semantic negation more than once, as in non-standard I didn’t say nothing.
A negative marker that adds no separate semantic negation.
Negation understood in an embedded clause even when marked in the matrix.
A tag whose polarity is opposite to that of the clause it follows.
A reduced negative response that rejects a proposition or proposal.
Not used as a pro-form for a negative clause, as in I think not.
A negative expression used to convey a positive meaning indirectly, as in not uncommon.

teaching.text: *He didn’t read the report, not even the summary.* Take the second half away and the sentence still stands; keep it, and the denial reaches down to the smallest item. That one small word can do more than deny a proposition. It can cancel an implication, reject a pronunciation, or stand in for a whole clause that nobody wants to repeat.

The description begins with the tests that separate a negative clause from a positive one, then sorts negation along four contrasts: verbal and non-verbal, analytic and synthetic, clausal and subclausal, ordinary and metalinguistic. From there it turns to approximate and affixal negators, to the items that live only in negative or non-affirmative company, and to the questions of scope and focus that decide what a negative actually denies. Multiple negation, negative concord, metalinguistic correction, responses with *so* and *not*, and the rhetorical use of negation bring the chapter to a close.
The question worth asking is not whether a word is negative. It is how far the negative reaches, which element it throws into relief, and whether it turns the whole clause or only a phrase inside it.

Set *It is raining* beside *It isn’t raining* and the difference looks like one word. The two clauses then part company in ways that have nothing to do with weather: they accept different continuations, different tags, different connectives. Positive is the simpler case, the one a description can take for granted; almost everything interesting happens on the negative side.

Four continuations expose the difference. A negative clause tolerates a *not even* supplement and takes *neither* or *nor* where a positive clause wants *so*. Its tag reverses polarity, and a negative constituent moved to the front drags the auxiliary with it. The table below sets the four side by side, each row pairing a negative clause with its positive counterpart.

No single test settles the matter. Inversion also follows *so* and *only*, and same-polarity tags turn up with their own pragmatic point. The tests are strongest as a set, and strongest of all when a clause is placed next to its positive counterpart and the two are made to behave differently.
Tests for clause polarity
Not even continuation | He didn’t read it, not even the abstract. | He read it, not even the abstract.
Connective | He didn’t read it; neither did I. | He read it; so did I.
Reversed tag | He didn’t read it, did he? | He read it, didn’t he?
Inversion | Not once did he read it. | After lunch he read it.

*He doesn’t dine out* and *He never dines out* deny the same habit, but the negative has moved: in the first it hangs on the auxiliary, in the second on the adverb. That is one contrast among several. A description of negation needs more than one axis; the one used here has four.

*He doesn’t dine out* puts the negative on the auxiliary; *He never dines out* puts it on a dependent. Two of the axes concern form. Verbal negation attaches *not* or *n’t* to the verb or its auxiliary and calls on *do* when no auxiliary is there; non-verbal negation puts the negative on a dependent, as *never* and *nothing* do. Analytic negation uses a marker whose only job is negation, while synthetic negation uses a word or affix that does something else as well — *never* carries time, *un-* builds an adjective. The axes cross: *He never dines out* is non-verbal and synthetic at once.

*We were friends at no time* denies a friendship and behaves like any negative clause. *We were friends in no time* says the friendship formed quickly, and the clause itself is positive, because the negative is walled up inside a phrase. The other two axes concern meaning. Ordinary negation denies that something is so. Metalinguistic negation objects to how something was put: *Max hasn’t got four children, he’s got five* does not deny the four so much as the suggestion that four is the end of the count.
Four contrasts
Form | Verbal: He doesn’t dine out. | Non-verbal: He never dines out.
Form | Analytic: The report is not complete. | Synthetic: The report isn’t complete.
Meaning | Clausal: We were friends at no time. | Subclausal: We were friends in no time.
Meaning | Ordinary: Max hasn’t got four children; he’s got three. | Metalinguistic: Max hasn’t got four children; he’s got five.
He doesn’t dine out. — Verbal negation with supportive do.
He never dines out. — Non-verbal synthetic negation with never.
The report isn’t complete. — Synthetic verbal negation marked by n’t.
We were friends in no time. — Subclausal negation: the clause itself is positive.

English verbs do not inflect for negation. There is no form *readn’t*, no negative ending on *read*. What the grammar does instead is attach *not* to the first auxiliary, and when a clause has no auxiliary it presses *do* into service to carry tense and agreement: *He is not ready*, *They have not finished*, *He didn’t read it*.

The imperative makes its own arrangements. *Be late* has no auxiliary, yet its negative is *Don’t be late*; *Be not late* survives only as archaism or literary flourish. Negative imperatives are a construction in their own right, not declaratives with the subject deleted.

Non-finite clauses take *not* without *do*. In a *to*-infinitival the marker normally comes before *to*, though a split infinitive puts it after; gerund-participials and subjunctives place it before the verb. None of these constructions accepts dummy *do*, and the examples below show the three shapes.
It seemed unwise not to answer. — Not precedes the to-infinitival.
Not having read the report, she said nothing. — Gerund-participial with initial not.
It is essential that he not be told. — Subjunctive with not before the plain verb.
Three kinds of verbal negation
Primary | He didn’t read it. | Finite auxiliary or dummy do
Imperative | Don’t be late. | Do even with be
Secondary | Not to bend it is important. | Not before a non-finite verb
She isn’t ready. — Primary negation marked on the auxiliary.
She did not read the report. — Dummy do supplies the finite auxiliary.
Don’t be late. — Imperative negation with do.
It is important not to bend it. — Secondary negation in a to-infinitival.

*Not happy* is the clearest case: the negative sits on an adjective, and the clause around it can stay positive. The same marker can be aimed at a quantifier, at an adverb, or at a preposition phrase, leaving the rest of the clause untouched. *No* works differently, doing negation and determination at once, which is why *no money* and *no excuses* need no separate *not*.

The absolute negators mean zero or none, and they differ more in grammar than in meaning. *No* is a determinative. *None* stands alone, often as a fused head, as in *None of them came*. *Nobody*, *nothing* and *nowhere* are compounds. *Never* belongs here too, though its meaning leans on time and frequency as much as on absence.

Some of these forms negate a clause and some only a phrase, and the surface does not show which. *I saw nothing* denies that any seeing took place, exactly as *I didn’t see anything* does. *We were friends in no time* contains the same negative word but describes a quick friendship; the clause passes the tests for a positive, because the negative is sealed inside the phrase.

Between the two lies the idiom. *He is no fool* can deny foolishness outright or offer a wry compliment, and only context and intonation decide which. Here the negator is doing lexical work, not clause-level work.
Absolute negators
no | no money | Determiner
none | None of them came. | Fused head
never | She never calls. | Temporal or frequency negator
neither | Neither answer was correct. | Disjunctive determiner
nor | Nor did I. | Connective or coordinator
nobody / nothing | Nobody came; nothing happened. | Compound pronoun
Not many people came. — Not negates the quantifier many.
I saw nothing. — Non-verbal clausal negation with nothing.
None of them came. — None is a fused head.
We were friends in no time. — Subclausal: no time means a very short time.

Not every negative sits at zero. *Few*, *little*, *barely*, *hardly*, *scarcely*, *rarely* and *seldom* place a situation near the bottom of a scale and leave the possibility of some. *Few of them supported her* suggests that a handful did, yet the clause still behaves as negative in the polarity tests; approximation and polarity are separate matters.
The indefinite article makes the difference plain. *A few people came* reports that some came; *Few people came* reports that not many did. The same reversal separates *a little* from *little*.

Affixal negation works inside a word: *unhappy*, *intolerant*, *non-negotiable*, *careless*. Because the negative never reaches clause level, the clause itself counts as positive and takes a negative tag. *These terms are non-negotiable, aren’t they?* is therefore normal, while *These terms aren’t negotiable, are they?* belongs to the verbal pattern.

*Unhappy* is a lexical item with its own degree and colour, not simply the syntactic negation of *happy*; *not common* and *uncommon* differ in strength and register. Treating an affix as a compressed *not* misses the point. *Not unattractive* shows what happens when a negative is allowed to stand in front of a positive adjective: the result is litotes, an indirect and usually weaker positive.
Approximate and affixal forms
Approximate quantity | few, little | Small amount, not zero
Approximate degree | barely, hardly, scarcely | Only just
Approximate frequency | rarely, seldom | Not often
Affixal | un-, in-, non-, -less | Negative lexical item
Litotes | not uncommon | Indirect positive
Few people came. — Negative orientation: not many came.
A few people came. — Positive orientation: some people came.
These terms are non-negotiable, aren’t they? — Affixal negation is subclausal; the clause is positive.
The result was not uncommon. — Litotes: a negative form conveys a positive assessment.

*I didn’t see anything* is unremarkable. *I saw anything* is not English. The word *any* seems to need a negative or a question somewhere near it, and the same holds for *ever*, *yet*, *at all*, *any longer* and idioms such as *lift a finger* and *sleep a wink*. These are negative polarity items, and they are not equally strong: *any* is the weakest, *at all* adds emphasis, and the idioms are more emphatic still.

*Any* turns up in questions, conditionals, comparatives, *before* clauses, *only*, *few*, and the complements of *doubt*, *deny* and *surprise*, not just under negation. Negation is only the most conspicuous licensor. What unites these contexts is not a single negative word but a shared failure to assert: each leaves a proposition open, denied, or merely supposed. The examples below arrange several of them side by side.

*Not lift a finger* has a fixed negative meaning and very little internal variation; *any* is a quantifier with a wide distribution across contexts. An idiom is not just a strong NPI. One is a lexical item with a negative cast, the other a polarity-sensitive word that the grammar licenses.
Polarity-sensitive items
some / any | I bought some bread. | I didn’t buy any bread.
already / yet | She has already left. | She hasn’t left yet.
somewhat | It was somewhat useful. | It wasn’t any use at all.
ever | She is happier than ever. | She hardly ever calls.
at all | I liked it a lot. | I didn’t like it at all.
I didn’t see anything. — Any is licensed by clausal negation.
Did you see anything? — A question is a non-affirmative context.
If you need any help, call me. — A conditional licenses any.
Few people said anything. — Few has negative orientation.
She didn’t lift a finger. — A negative idiom with a fixed negative meaning.

*I have already eaten* passes without comment. *I haven’t already eaten* does not; it wants a contrast, a correction, or a very specific tone. *Already* is a positive polarity item, and it keeps company with *some*, *still*, *somewhat*, *rather* and *pretty*. The restriction is a strong tendency, not an absolute law, and a cooperative context can override it.

Put a PPI under negation and it usually needs a special reading. *I don’t have some money* is odd unless *some* is contrastive: not money in general, but some particular sum. *She isn’t still here* is easier, because *still* can fall under the scope of the negative and yield the reading ‘she is no longer here’. The label matters less than the scope relation.

Questions, conditionals, comparatives, *before* clauses, *only*, *few*, and the complements of *doubt*, *deny* and *surprise* all qualify as non-affirmative. The wider environment is easier to list than to define. These contexts resemble one another family by family rather than sharing a single semantic feature.
PPIs and their alternatives
some | I bought some bread. | I didn’t buy any bread.
already | She has already left. | She hasn’t left yet.
still | She is still here. | She isn’t here any more.
somewhat | It was somewhat useful. | It wasn’t at all useful.
rather | It was rather good. | It wasn’t very good.
I have already eaten. — Already favours a positive context.
I haven’t eaten yet. — Yet is the negative-context counterpart.
She is still here. — Still is positive-oriented.
She isn’t here any more. — Any more supplies the negative-context counterpart.

*Liz didn’t delete the backup file* denies a whole event: no deletion of that file by Liz took place. The scope of the negative is the proposition, and the focus is the part the denial lands on hardest. Stress can move that focus without changing the syntax: *Liz* didn’t delete the file, or she didn’t delete *the backup file*.

Removing the negative gives a rough test. The positive counterpart of the sentence is *Liz deleted the backup file*, and the negative denies exactly that. Apply the same procedure to *Not many people came* and the result differs: what is denied is the size of the crowd, not the arrival of any people at all. Two negatives, two scopes.

Scope also shifts under quantifiers, modals and reason clauses. *Not all the students passed* denies a universal; *All the students didn’t pass* can deny the universal or report a universal failure, depending on where the negative is understood. A *because* clause is just as slippery: *I didn’t buy it because it was expensive* can give the reason for not buying or deny that the price was the reason.
Liz didn’t delete the backup file. — The negative denies the whole proposition.
Not many people came. — The negative applies to the quantifier many.
I didn’t buy it because it was expensive. — Ambiguous: reason for not buying or scope over the reason.
I didn’t buy it because it was cheap. — The reason reading is strongly favoured.

*Mary doesn’t like you* usually means something stronger than its literal content: that Mary dislikes you. Strictly, it is true if she has no feelings either way, and a flat denial can cancel the inference. *He doesn’t have many friends* works the same way, implicating a small circle without quite saying so. Negative clauses tend to be read towards the more specific, more informative end of what they allow.

Medium-strength predicates produce a related effect. *I don’t want to hear about it* is normally heard as *I want not to hear about it*, with the negative transplanted into the subordinate clause. *I don’t think she’s coming* leans towards *I think she isn’t coming*. In both, the negative is written in the matrix and understood in the complement.

The effect depends on strength. *I’m not willing to be included* entails *I’m willing not to be included*, so no implicature is needed. *I don’t insist on being included* does not suggest *I insist on not being included*; *insist* is too strong to let the negative slide downward. *Want*, *advise*, *likely*, *think*, *believe* and *seem* occupy the middle ground, while *know* and *insist* sit outside it.

Modals can build subordinate negation into their meaning rather than leaving it to inference. *You mustn’t tell anyone* says that you are obliged not to tell, with the negative inside the complement of *must*. *You needn’t tell anyone* says that no obligation applies, with the negative outside. Scope explains the contrast, and it survives even when the two forms sound equally forbidding.
Mary doesn’t like you. — Implicates that Mary dislikes you, but does not entail it.
I don’t want to hear about it. — Implicates that I want not to hear about it.
You mustn’t tell anyone. — Internal negation: obligated not to tell.
You needn’t tell anyone. — External negation: not obligated to tell.

Two negative words in one clause can mean two denials or one. *I didn’t say I didn’t want it* contains two separate negations, one in the matrix and one in the complement, and they do not cancel. Non-standard *He didn’t say nothing* contains two negative markers but a single denial: he said nothing. The first pattern is multiple semantic negation; the second is negative concord.

Standard English has small pockets of concord of its own. *Neither illegal nor immoral* marks both coordinates and negates once. A negative parenthetical can double the marking without doubling the meaning, as in *They aren’t here, I don’t think*. And a subordinate clause after *I wouldn’t be surprised if* may carry a negative that adds nothing at all, a pleonastic marker rather than a second denial.

Cockney and African American Vernacular English regularly use *He didn’t say nothing* for a single negation. Concord is regular in many non-standard varieties, and it is not a lapse in logic. The rule that two negatives cancel belongs to semantic negation, not to the number of negative words a grammar allows. Italian and Spanish mark a single negation more than once in much the same way.
Multiple negation and concord
Multiple semantic negation | I didn’t say I didn’t want it. | Two
Standard concord | Neither illegal nor immoral. | One
Parenthetical concord | They aren’t here, I don’t think. | One
Pleonastic negation | I wouldn’t be surprised if it didn’t rain. | One in the relevant reading
Non-standard concord | He didn’t say nothing. | One
I didn’t say I didn’t want it. — Two semantic negations: I didn’t say that I didn’t want it.
Neither illegal nor immoral. — One semantic negation marked on both coordinates.
He didn’t say nothing. — Non-standard negative concord: one semantic negation.
I wouldn’t be surprised if it didn’t rain. — Can contain a pleonastic subordinate negative.

*She didn’t have lunch with my old man: she had lunch with my father.* The denial is not aimed at the lunch. It objects to the phrase *my old man*, and the correction supplies a more acceptable wording. This is metalinguistic negation: a negative that rejects a formulation, an implicature or a pronunciation rather than the truth of a proposition.

The classic case targets an implicature. *Max hasn’t got four children: he’s got five* would contradict itself if *not* denied the proposition outright, because a man with five children has four as well. What is rejected is the suggestion that four is the upper limit. *Max hasn’t got four children: he’s got three* is ordinary negation by comparison, denying the count itself.

Metalinguistic negatives tend to sound different. They carry a marked intonation, often a fall-rise on the offending item, and they invite a correction. The target can be a word, a pronunciation, a register or a presupposition, and the negative is doing corrective work rather than descriptive work.
Max hasn’t got four children: he’s got three. — Ordinary negation of the proposition.
Max hasn’t got four children: he’s got five. — Metalinguistic denial of the implicature “no more than four”.
She didn’t have lunch with your ‘old man’: she had lunch with your father. — Rejection of a formulation, not the truth of the meeting.
She doesn’t live in a /kæsl/; she lives in a /kɑːsl/. — Rejection of a pronunciation.

*Isn’t it ready?* can be answered with *Yes* to confirm readiness or *No* to deny it, and the same words can confirm or reject depending on which proposition the speaker takes as the anchor. Answers to polar questions are shaped by the polarity of the question and by what the answerer wants to do with it. Agreement and disagreement are not the same as yes and no.

*So* and *not* work as pro-forms for whole clauses. *I think so* stands in for a positive complement; *I think not* stands in for a negative one. *I was told so* and *I was told not* show the same division. In these uses *not* is a complement, not a modifier hovering near the verb.

Preposed adverbs and preposition phrases can accompany the pro-form, but not symmetrically. *Apparently so* and *Apparently not* both work. *On the whole not* is possible; *On the whole so* is not. The difference follows from the different syntactic status of the two pro-forms in reduced clauses.
Are they reliable? I think so. — So stands for the positive proposition.
Are they reliable? I think not. — Not stands for the negative proposition.
Apparently so. — An adverb can accompany so.
On the whole not. — A PP can accompany not, but not so in the same way.

*I didn’t buy it because it was expensive* can give the price as the reason for not buying, or deny that the price was the reason. Negation is a reliable source of ambiguity in writing because its scope is often invisible. *All that glitters is not gold* can mean that nothing glittering is gold or that not everything glittering is. Word order alone does not settle either case; scope and focus do.

Negative concord attracts social judgement out of proportion to its linguistic interest. It is a regular feature of many dialects and follows its own rules. Formal Standard English can use multiple semantic negation for emphasis or contradiction, but the result needs a context strong enough to keep the two denials apart.

Litotes turns negation into indirect praise or criticism: *not uncommon*, *not unattractive*, *not a little worried*. The figure softens a claim or shades it with irony, and its effect depends on the scale and on what the reader expects. Pushed too far, the negative goes vague, and the reader stops being able to measure the positive behind it.
All that glitters is not gold. — Ambiguous between universal and non-universal scope.
I didn’t buy it because it was expensive. — The reason clause can fall inside or outside the scope of negation.
The result was not uncommon. — Litotes: an indirect way of saying it was fairly common.
He didn’t say nothing. — Non-standard negative concord; standard English has He didn’t say anything.

The four contrasts — verbal and non-verbal, analytic and synthetic, clausal and subclausal, ordinary and metalinguistic — give the description its axes. Nothing about negation is settled by a single word. The polarity tests decide whether a clause as a whole is negative.

Verbal negation puts *not* or *n’t* on a primary verb and uses *do*-support where no auxiliary exists. Non-verbal negation covers *not* with a constituent, absolute negators such as *no* and *never*, approximate negators such as *few* and *hardly*, and affixes. Polarity-sensitive items distribute across positive, negative and non-affirmative contexts, and those contexts form a family rather than a single class.

Scope and focus explain how one negative form can deny different things, and multiple negation divides into separate denials and concord. Metalinguistic negation corrects formulations and implicatures rather than facts. *So* and *not* supply pro-forms for the clauses that would otherwise have to be repeated.

A negation checklist: Identify the negative marker. Decide whether it is verbal or non-verbal, analytic or synthetic. Test whether the clause is negative or only a constituent. Then identify the scope and focus, and check whether the negation is ordinary or metalinguistic.

Take *He didn’t read the report, not even the summary*. The finite clause is negative: it takes the *not even* continuation, would take *neither* rather than *so*, and takes the reversed tag *did he?*. The negative is verbal, marked on the auxiliary *did*, and it has scope over the proposition that he read the report.

The phrase *not even the summary* is a detached supplement, not part of the core clause. It identifies a more specific focus for the negation: the report was not read, and even the summary was not read. The example shows how a negative clause can combine clause-level polarity with a focused supplement.

Start with the negative marker and identify what it is attached to. If it is on the verb or an auxiliary, the negation is verbal. If it is on an NP, AdjP, AdvP or PP, it may be non-verbal and possibly subclausal.
Next, test the clause. Does it allow not even? Does it take neither or so? Which tag does it take? Does a prenuclear negative trigger inversion? These tests separate clausal from subclausal negation.

Then identify scope and focus. Remove the negative and compare the positive counterpart. Decide which part of the proposition is denied and which element is most prominent. Finally, check whether the negation is ordinary or metalinguistic, and whether multiple negative markers express one semantic negation or several.

In *He didn’t read the report, not even the summary*, the negative is verbal and clausal: it is marked on the auxiliary *did* and denies the proposition that he read the report. *Not even the summary* is a focused supplement that strengthens the negation by extending it to a minimal case.

Polarity is a clause-level property with syntactic tests. Negation can be verbal or non-verbal, analytic or synthetic, clausal or subclausal, ordinary or metalinguistic. Scope and focus determine what the negative actually denies.

NPIs and PPIs are licensed by positive, negative and non-affirmative contexts. Multiple negative markers can express several negations or a single negation with concord. Metalinguistic negation rejects formulations and implicatures rather than truth.

teaching.text: *Would you mind closing the window?* has the shape of a question and the force of a request. Nothing in its grammar says ‘request’; the interrogative form asks about willingness, and the situation does the rest. English is full of clauses whose grammatical type and practical job pull apart, and the space between them is what this chapter maps.

It begins with the five major clause types and the syntax that distinguishes them. It then separates illocutionary force from grammatical form, examines indirect speech acts and the main kinds of question, and follows the layers that adjust force: bias, echo questions, tags, parentheticals and presuppositions. Interrogative words, exclamatives, imperatives and the minor clause-like expressions close the account.
Two questions are worth asking of every clause: what type is it, and what is the speaker doing with it? Often the answers match. The cases where they diverge are the ones that repay attention.

Change *You are generous* into a question and the auxiliary jumps in front of the subject. Recast it with an initial *how* and it becomes an exclamation: *How generous you are!* English sorts clauses into five major types, and the differences between them are syntactic, not decorative: each type has its own order, its own markers, its own restrictions.

*You are generous*, *Are you generous?*, *How generous are you?*, *How generous you are!* and *Be generous* show the five types in action: declarative, closed interrogative, open interrogative, exclamative and imperative. The table below gives the paradigm. Each type has a characteristic use — statement, closed question, open question, exclamatory statement, directive — but characteristic is not definitional. *Passengers are requested to remain seated* is declarative in form and directive in effect. *Would you mind opening the door?* is a closed interrogative doing polite directive work. The form is stable; the use bends.

Types belong to clauses, not to sentences. *Come around six, or is that too early for you?* puts an imperative and a closed interrogative in one sentence, and the sentence as a whole is neither. Any description that assigns a single type to the sentence will have to distort one of its clauses.
The five major clause types
Declarative | You are generous. | Statement
Closed interrogative | Are you generous? | Closed question
Open interrogative | How generous are you? | Open question
Exclamative | How generous you are! | Exclamatory statement
Imperative | Be generous. | Directive

Say *I apologise for the delay* and the words do not report an apology; they perform one. Stating, asking, ordering, promising, apologising and conceding are acts of the same kind, and the act an utterance performs is its illocutionary force. Clause type is a grammatical classification; force is what the speaker is doing. The two are linked by convention, not by identity.

An indirect speech act exploits that link. *Would you like to close the window?* is a closed interrogative about willingness, but in a cold room it is a request. *I promise to be home by six* is declarative in form and a promise in force. The literal meaning is not cancelled; it is the route by which the hearer reaches the act.

Context, intonation and institutional role do the rest. *You’re leaving?* can be a question, an expression of surprise or a challenge. *Sleep well* is imperative in form and often a wish rather than an order. Form, meaning and use have to be kept apart if any of these descriptions is to be accurate.
Form and force
Declarative | Statement | Promise, request, warning
Closed interrogative | Polar question | Directive, offer, challenge
Open interrogative | Variable question | Exclamation, rhetorical question
Exclamative | Exclamatory statement | Evaluation, emphasis
Imperative | Directive | Wish, permission, advice
Passengers are requested to remain seated. — Declarative form, directive force.
Would you mind opening the door? — Closed interrogative form, polite directive force.
Sleep well. — Imperative form, wish force.
You’re leaving? — Declarative form, question or challenge force.

*You are generous* has subject before predicator, no interrogative or exclamative phrase, and no imperative verb. The declarative is the shape a clause takes when nothing special is demanded of it. That negative definition is the standard one, and it is useful: the other types are recognised by the special properties the declarative lacks.

*Are you generous?* and *Did they see her?* show the two markers of a closed interrogative: subject-auxiliary inversion and tensed verb. When no auxiliary is present, *do* carries the inversion. Inversion is not unique to interrogatives — a fronted negative, *only*, or connective *so* can trigger it too — so the type has to be identified from the whole bundle of properties, not from inversion alone.

Open interrogatives contain an interrogative phrase built on *who*, *what*, *which*, *when*, *where*, *how* or a related word. A non-subject phrase is normally fronted, and in a main clause it brings the auxiliary with it: *Which one did he choose?* The phrase can also stay where it belongs: *So you told him what, exactly?* Fronting is the norm, not a requirement.

The type also appears in reduced and embedded forms. *Why make such a fuss?* is infinitival; *Which one?* is no more than the interrogative phrase. Embed one and the inversion usually disappears: *I know which one he chose*. Subordinate interrogatives keep the phrase and lose the main-clause order.
Declarative and interrogative properties
Declarative | Subject before predicator | No special auxiliary | Usually
Closed interrogative | Auxiliary before subject | Do-support if needed | Always
Open interrogative | Interrogative phrase fronted or in situ | Inversion in main clauses | Usually, but can be infinitival
Is it true? — Closed interrogative with auxiliary inversion.
Did they see her? — Do-support supplies the inverted auxiliary.
Which one did he choose? — Non-subject interrogative phrase fronted and inverted.
Who broke the window? — Interrogative phrase is subject; no inversion.
Why make such a fuss? — Infinitival open interrogative.

Exclamatives begin with a *what* or *how* phrase and put it first: *What a disaster it was!*, *How generous you are!* The normal order keeps the subject before the predicator, but the type tolerates subject postposing and inversion, as in *How great would be their embarrassment!* At its thinnest, the clause is just the exclamative phrase: *What a disaster!*

*Sit down*, *Be careful* and *Don’t be late* share a plain-form verb and an omissible second-person subject. Imperatives are built that way and are normally main-clause constructions. Negation and emphatic polarity call for supportive *do*, even with *be*. With an overt subject, the usual negative order is *don’t* before *you*: *Don’t you forget it*.

*You sit down* has an overt subject; *Kim, sit down* has a vocative. The subject can be omitted, and in *Kim, sit down* it is. Overt subjects appear for emphasis or contrast, which is why they sound pointed.
What a disaster it was! — Exclamative with an initial what phrase.
How happy would he be! — Exclamative with subject-auxiliary inversion.
Don’t be late. — Imperative negation with do even with be.
You sit down. — Overt imperative subject for emphasis.
Kim, sit down. — Kim is a vocative, not the subject.

An indirect speech act uses one clause type to do the work of another. *Can you pass the salt?* asks about ability and functions as a request. *I was wondering whether you could help* is declarative and equally a request. In each case the literal act is available and the practical act is inferred from it.

*Would you mind closing the window?* is a recognised polite request; *Is the window capable of being closed?* is not, even though it describes the same situation. These acts are conventional, not arbitrary. What makes the first work is a shared habit of interpretation, not the logical content alone.

Tags, parentheticals and intonation adjust the force further. *You’re coming, aren’t you?* seeks confirmation. *You’re coming, are you?* can express surprise or challenge, and the same words with a different contour can sound like a threat. The clause type stays constant while the act shifts.
Can you pass the salt? — Closed interrogative form, request force.
I was wondering whether you could help. — Declarative form, polite request force.
You’re coming, aren’t you? — Tag seeks confirmation.
You’re coming, are you? — Same-polarity tag can express surprise or challenge.

*The door is open?* with a rising contour asks a question, and it contains none of the syntax of an interrogative. Question is a category of meaning and use; interrogative is a clause type. They overlap often enough to hide the difference, but they are not the same thing.

*Is the door open?* expects yes or no; *Would you like tea or coffee?* offers a choice; *Which door is open?* asks for a value; *Which way did they go?* asks for a route. These are the main semantic kinds: polar, alternative, variable and direction. The table below sets them beside the answers they invite.

Questions can also be biased, carrying an expectation or preference about the answer. *Isn’t it already finished?* expects agreement; *Is it really finished?* voices doubt. Negative interrogative form, declarative form, polarity-sensitive words and context can all supply the bias.
Kinds of question
Polar | Is the door open? | Yes or no
Alternative | Is the door open or closed? | One of the stated alternatives
Variable | Which door is open? | A value for which
Direction | Which way did they go? | A direction or route
Biased | Isn’t the door open? | Expectation of yes
Echo | They went which way? | Repetition or clarification

Polar questions have a closed answer set, prototypically yes and no. They are usually closed interrogatives — *Is the door open?* — but a declarative with a rising contour can do the same job: *The door is open?* What makes the question polar is the answer system it sets up, not the clause type alone.

Alternative questions present the answers rather than leaving them open: *Is the door open or closed?*, *Would you like tea or coffee?* The alternatives are often coordinated noun phrases or clauses, and the hearer is asked to select one. This is not a polar question with an extra option; the set itself is the content.

Prosody separates the readings. *Would you like tea or coffee?* with a final fall offers a choice between two drinks; with a final rise it can ask whether the hearer wants either. The words are identical, and the contour does the disambiguating.
Is the door open? — Polar: yes or no.
Is the door open or closed? — Alternative: choose one of the stated options.
Would you like tea or coffee? — Can be alternative or polar depending on prosody and context.
The door is open? — Declarative form used as a polar question.

Variable questions ask for the value of a missing element. They usually carry an interrogative phrase — *Who broke the window?*, *Which one did he choose?* — and the missing element can be subject, object, adjunct, complement or predicative. The phrase names the role; the answer fills it.

Direction questions ask for a route or orientation: *Which way did they go?*, *How do I get to the station?* They are a subtype of variable question, but the answer is specifically a path rather than any value. The interrogative phrase is spatial, and the answer is expected to be spatial too.

*Who did she say he thought had won?* links the fronted phrase to a gap several clauses deep. Variable questions are unbounded dependency constructions. The interrogative phrase sits in the prenucleus and is co-indexed with that gap; wherever it falls, it carries the function the fronted phrase would have had in a declarative.
Who broke the window? — Variable question with the interrogative phrase as subject.
Which one did he choose? — Variable question with a fronted object phrase.
Which way did they go? — Direction question asking for a route.
Who did she say he thought had won? — The gap is several clauses deep.

A biased question does more than request information; it leans. *Isn’t it already finished?* expects a positive answer. *Is it really finished?* suggests that the evidence is doubtful. *You do want to come with us, don’t you?* makes agreement the easy response and disagreement the marked one.

The bias can be epistemic, evidential or deontic. Epistemic bias concerns what the speaker believes about the likelihood of an answer; evidential bias concerns what the evidence points to; deontic bias concerns what the speaker wants or thinks appropriate. Negative interrogatives often carry a positive epistemic bias, which is why *Isn’t it finished?* sounds like a prediction.

Polarity-sensitive items carry bias too. *Did someone call?* leans towards yes, while *Did anyone call?* is neutral or leans towards no. The choice between *some* and *any* is grammatical, but it is also a signal of the speaker’s orientation.
Isn’t it already finished? — Negative interrogative with a positive expectation.
Is it really finished? — Evidential bias: the evidence seems doubtful.
Did someone call? — Some suggests a positive answer.
Did anyone call? — Any is more neutral or negative-oriented.

If someone says *Give it to Angela* and the name does not land, the natural reply is *Give it to who?* The clause repeats the shape of the original and turns the doubtful part into a question. Echo questions are not a sixth clause type; the echo feature is laid over an imperative, an interrogative, a declarative or a fragment.

Variable echo questions usually leave the interrogative phrase where the doubtful material was: *You saw who?*, *She bought what?* They tend to rise, and they sound surprised or incredulous. Polar echo questions repeat the proposition with a high rise: *You’re leaving?*

An echo can ask for repetition or for clarification. *You saw who?* may mean ‘I didn’t catch the name’ or ‘I can’t believe you saw that person’. The same form does both jobs, and context decides which. Echoes can also challenge a presupposition, which is why they are useful in argument.
Give it to who? — Echo question superimposed on an imperative.
Did I use a what? — Echo question superimposed on a closed interrogative.
You saw who? — Variable echo with the interrogative phrase in situ.
You’re leaving? — Polar echo with declarative form and high rise.

*You’re coming, aren’t you?* and *You’re not coming, are you?* show the usual pattern: a short auxiliary-plus-pronoun tag hung on the end, reversing the polarity of its anchor. A positive clause takes a negative tag; a negative clause takes a positive one.

Reversed tags seek confirmation. Same-polarity tags do something else: *You’re coming, are you?* can express surprise, challenge or disapproval. The words are nearly the same as the confirmation tag, and the intonation and context carry the difference.

*I think*, *I suppose*, *you know* and *she said* comment on the clause from a detached position. Parentheticals are detached expressions. They can carry negation of their own: *They aren’t here, I don’t think* marks the negative twice and means it once, which makes the construction a small lesson in the difference between form and meaning.
You’re coming, aren’t you? — Positive anchor with negative tag seeking confirmation.
You’re not coming, are you? — Negative anchor with positive tag.
You’re coming, are you? — Same-polarity tag with a marked pragmatic effect.
They aren’t here, I don’t think. — Parenthetical concord with one semantic negation.

*Who broke the window?* takes for granted that someone broke it. That assumption is not asserted; it is presupposed, and it survives in the background of the question. An alternative question presupposes that one of its alternatives holds, or at least that the alternatives are the relevant set.

Questions also carry Q–A presuppositions: the form of the question constrains the form of its answers. A negative polar question can presuppose or implicate a particular orientation, which is one reason *Isn’t she coming?* is not a neutral request for information. Such presuppositions can be rejected or cancelled, especially by an echo or a metalinguistic comment.

*If anyone broke the window, who did it?* treats a breaker as a live possibility without claiming that one exists. Presupposition is not entailment. A question does not assert what it presupposes, and the assumption can survive under negation or inside a conditional.
Who broke the window? — Presupposes that someone broke the window.
Which one did he choose? — Presupposes a set of candidates and a choice.
Is the door open or closed? — Presents two alternatives as the relevant set.
Who broke the window? Nobody did! — The presupposition can be rejected in context.

*Who*, *whom*, *whose*, *which*, *what*, *when*, *where*, *why* and *how* each head a phrase that can serve as subject, object, complement, adjunct or predicative. These are the interrogative words. *Which* selects from a set, *whose* asks about possession, and *who* and *whom* preserve a case distinction in formal style.

*Which one did he choose?* has a gap in object position; *Who broke it?* has the interrogative phrase in subject position and no gap at all. Interrogative phrases are unbounded dependency constructions. The phrase occupies the prenucleus and is co-indexed with a gap in the nucleus, and the gap preserves the function of the questioned element.

The words can be modified and combined: *how much*, *how many*, *which one*, *whose car*, *what on earth*. The interrogative feature passes from the word to the phrase, which is why the whole phrase fronts as a unit and why the gap is interpreted as a phrase rather than a bare word.
Interrogative words
who / whom | Who called? / Whom did you see? | Person; subject or object
whose | Whose car is this? | Possessor
which | Which one do you want? | Selection from a set
what | What happened? | Thing or proposition
when | When did they leave? | Time
where | Where are they? | Place
why | Why did they leave? | Reason
how | How did they do it? | Manner, degree or means

*What a disaster it was!* and *How generous you are!* begin with an exclamative phrase. Exclamatives are a clause type with an initial *what* or *how* phrase. *What* usually modifies a nominal; *how* modifies an adjective, adverb or determiner. The exclamative phrase is fronted, and the clause may show subject postposing or inversion.

The type also appears in reduced form. *What a disaster!* and *How wonderful!* are verbless exclamatives understood predicatively, and their meaning is an exclamatory statement: surprise, admiration or dismay delivered as a whole.

*Get the hell out of here!* is imperative in form; *What on earth are you doing?* is an open interrogative. Not every exclamation is an exclamative. Exclamatory meaning can be added to almost any clause type, so the grammatical category has to be identified by the *what*/*how* syntax rather than by the punctuation.
What a disaster it was! — What modifies a nominal; exclamative phrase fronted.
How generous you are! — How modifies an adjective.
How great would be their embarrassment! — Subject postposing in an exclamative.
What a disaster! — Reduced verbless exclamative.

*Sit down*, *Be careful*, *Don’t be late* and *Let’s go* all have a plain-form verb and an omissible second-person subject. Imperatives are plain in form and characteristically directive. They differ in how much structure they carry.

*You sit down* and *You be careful* use an overt subject for emphasis or contrast. It is not the same as a vocative. *Kim, sit down* addresses Kim without making Kim the subject, and the ordinary imperative still has no subject at all.

*Let*-imperatives are first-person inclusive: *Let’s go*, *Let us consider the evidence*. They negate in two ways — *Don’t let’s go* and *Let’s not go* — and they take their own tags, as in *Let’s go, shall we?* Open *let*-imperatives such as *Let them eat cake* are a different matter; they are not first-person inclusive, and they are not suggestions.

An imperative can express a wish, grant permission, offer advice or set up a condition, as well as issue a command. The directive use is characteristic, not exhaustive. The examples below separate those uses from the plain command.
Have a nice day. — A wish rather than a directive.
Help yourself. — Permission.
Take the train. — Advice.
Take one more step and I’ll shoot. — Conditional interpretation.
Imperative subtypes and uses
Ordinary imperative | Sit down. | Directive
Overt subject | You sit down. | Emphasis or contrast
Negative imperative | Don’t be late. | Prohibition
Let-imperative | Let’s go. | First-person inclusive suggestion
Conditional use | Take one more step and I’ll shoot. | Condition and consequence
Wish | Have a nice day. | Well-wishing

Some clause-like expressions do not fit the five types at all. *What about the others?* has interrogative force without interrogative syntax. *Out with it!* issues a directive without an imperative verb. Expressions of this kind — *Thanks*, *The sooner the better* — are conventionalised fragments, and forcing them into the major system would obscure what they do.

Verbless clauses can still be classified when they keep a clear interrogative or exclamative meaning. *What about the others?* is an open interrogative fragment; *What a disaster!* is an exclamative fragment. Others are better described as formulae, learnt as units and interpreted against the major patterns.

Minor types do not weaken the major system. The five types remain mutually exclusive for full clauses, and fragments are understood by reference to them. The grammar’s job is to describe the conventionalised forms and their uses, not to force every expression into one of five boxes.
What about the others? — Open interrogative fragment.
What a disaster! — Exclamative fragment.
Out with it! — Conventionalised minor clause with directive force.
Thanks. — Formulaic fragment, not a major clause type.

The five types — declarative, closed interrogative, open interrogative, exclamative and imperative — each have their own syntax and their own characteristic use. The classification applies to clauses rather than sentences, and for full clauses the five are mutually exclusive.

A declarative can request; an interrogative can direct; an imperative can wish. A clause’s type does not fix what its speaker is doing. Illocutionary force, the act the utterance performs, is related to type by characteristic use but not determined by it. Indirect speech acts use one form to do another act, and tags, parentheticals, intonation and context keep shifting the force without touching the grammar.

Questions form a semantic and pragmatic category with polar, alternative, variable, direction, biased and echo varieties. Presuppositions and Q–A constraints add another layer. Exclamatives and imperatives have their own syntax and ranges of use, and the minor types cover the conventionalised fragments that the five-term system leaves over.

A clause-type checklist: Identify the clause boundaries. Determine the type from its syntax. Then ask what act the speaker is performing. Check for fronting, inversion, tags, bias and presupposition. Keep form, meaning and use separate.

Take *Would you mind opening the door?* It is a closed interrogative in form: the auxiliary *would* precedes the subject *you*. Its literal meaning asks about willingness, but its characteristic use is a polite directive. The embedded gerund-participial *opening the door* names the requested action.

The example shows why form and force must be kept apart. The clause is not imperative, yet it performs a directive. A reply such as *No, not at all* addresses the literal question, while opening the door addresses the intended request. Both responses are coherent because both layers of meaning are available.

Begin with the clause boundaries and the verb. Check whether the subject precedes the predicator, whether an auxiliary is inverted, whether an interrogative or exclamative phrase is fronted, and whether the verb is imperative. These features identify the clause type.

Then ask what act the speaker is performing. Is the clause making a statement, asking a question, issuing a directive, expressing a wish or performing a promise? The answer may differ from the characteristic use of the type.

Finally, examine the layers that modify force: tags, parentheticals, intonation, bias, presupposition and context. A question can be neutral or biased; a tag can seek confirmation or challenge; an exclamative can express surprise or evaluation.

In *Would you mind opening the door?*, the clause is a closed interrogative with subject-auxiliary inversion. Its literal content asks whether the hearer would mind opening the door, but its conventional force is a polite request. The gerund-participial clause *opening the door* is the complement of *mind*.

Clause type is a five-term grammatical system applying to clauses. Declarative is the default; closed interrogatives invert; open interrogatives contain an interrogative phrase; exclamatives begin with what or how; imperatives have a plain verb and an omissible subject.

Illocutionary force is the act performed, not the clause type. Questions form a semantic and pragmatic category with polar, alternative, variable, direction, biased and echo subtypes. Tags, parentheticals and presuppositions add further structure.

key_terms.definition: The grammatical system whose major terms are declarative, closed interrogative, open interrogative, exclamative and imperative.
The default clause type, lacking the special properties of the other major types.
An interrogative clause with a closed set of answers, typically yes or no.
An interrogative clause containing an interrogative phrase that asks for a missing value.
A clause type with an initial what or how phrase, characteristically used for exclamatory statements.
A clause type with a plain-form verb and an omissible second-person subject, characteristically used for directives.
The speech act performed by an utterance, such as stating, asking or directing.
A speech act performed by a clause whose literal form is characteristic of another act.
A cover term for requests, commands, instructions and similar acts.
A semantic or pragmatic category concerned with seeking information, not a clause type.
A question with a closed set of answers, typically yes and no.
A question offering a stated set of alternatives.
A question asking for the value of a variable, typically with a wh-phrase.
A question asking for a direction or route.
A question that conveys an expectation or preference about the answer.
A question that repeats part of a preceding utterance in order to question or clarify it.
A short interrogative clause attached to a preceding clause, typically seeking confirmation.
A detached expression commenting on or qualifying the clause, such as I think.
A proposition treated as already assumed in an utterance.
A presupposition carried by a question and reflected in the form of its answers.
A phrase based on an interrogative word, such as which one or how much.
Placement of a constituent in prenuclear position.
In the position normally occupied by the corresponding element in a declarative clause.
A relation in which a fronted phrase is co-indexed with a gap that may be deeply embedded.
The characteristic use of an exclamative clause, distinct from exclamation as a general meaning.
An imperative beginning with let, often used for first-person inclusive suggestions.
An NP used to address someone directly, distinct from an imperative subject.
A conventionalised clause-like expression that does not fit the major type system neatly.
