lessons.title: Content clauses and reported speech

outcomes.text: Explain the main ideas in Content clauses and reported speech.
Recognise the patterns in real sentences.
Use the ideas when you read and write.

key_terms.definition: A clause that characteristically functions as dependent within a larger construction.
A clause that functions as head of the construction containing it.
A clause headed by a primary verb form, including subjunctive clauses.
A clause headed by a gerund-participle, past participle or infinitival plain form.
The default class of finite subordinate clause, lacking the special properties of relative and comparative clauses.
A content clause with declarative clause type.
A content clause with closed or open interrogative type.
A content clause with exclamative type, based on what or how.
A marker such as that, whether or if that introduces a subordinate clause.
A declarative content clause introduced by that.
A declarative content clause without that.
A declarative content clause whose governing item excludes that.
Placement of a clause after dummy it rather than in subject position.
A construction expressing requirement or recommendation, often with a subjunctive or should.
A finite clause construction using the plain form, as in that he be told.
A past-tense form used to mark modal remoteness rather than past time.
The residual mood form were used in hypothetical or counterfactual clauses.
The property of a predicate that treats its complement as factive, presupposing its truth.
A construction expressing doubt about a question or its answer.
A subordinator introducing closed interrogative content clauses.
A conditional preposition or subordinator; in content clauses it introduces interrogatives only under restricted conditions.
A conditional construction quantifying over a set of alternatives, such as whether he comes or not.
The reporting of another utterance, either directly or indirectly.
A report of what was said using a content clause, often with backshift and deixis shifts.
A report that quotes the original utterance.
A blend of indirect report and the original speaker’s perspective or wording.
The use of past tense in reported speech to mark anteriority relative to the report.
The adjustment of pronouns, time and place expressions in indirect report.

teaching.text: Start with *She said that the committee would announce its decision*, then drop the *that*: *She said the committee would announce its decision*. The words are almost the same, the meaning is the same, and the grammar has quietly changed shape. In both versions the clause after *said* does the work of a single complement: it names what was said, and it cannot stand on its own.

The clause is not tied to reporting. The same shape appears as the subject of *That they were lying is obvious* and, with a change of host, as the complement of an adjective in *I’m glad that she is right*. What holds these together is not a shared meaning but a shared job: each clause fills a slot that the surrounding construction has opened for it.

This chapter treats the content clause as one construction with several faces: declarative, interrogative and exclamative; subject, object and adjunct; mandative, factive and hypothetical. Once those distinctions are in place, reported speech stops looking like a separate topic. It is what happens when the same clause carries someone else’s words into a new time and a new speaker’s mouth.

Begin with *He knows that she is right*, then try to say *that she is right* on its own. It will not stand: the clause needs a host to lean on. The same dependence shows up when the clause modifies a noun, as in *the report she recommended*, or leans on a connective, as in *Although the paper is poorly written*.
He knows that she is right. — The content clause is complement of knows.
the report she recommended — The relative clause modifies report.
Although the paper is poorly written — The concessive clause is complement of although.

Containment alone tells you nothing. In *Although the paper is poorly written, it contains some good ideas*, the second clause sits inside the sentence but heads the construction. Status is a job, not a location.

Subordinate clauses often advertise themselves. *That* opens a declarative content clause, a missing object opens a relative, and a fronted interrogative phrase with subject-predicator order opens an open interrogative. But the advertisement is optional. *He knows she is right* contains a subordinate clause with the internal shape of a main clause, and only the matrix tells you which is which.

Finite subordinates fall into three classes. Relative clauses carry a gap tied to a nominal, comparatives carry a reduced measure tied to *than* or *as*, and content clauses carry neither special feature. That makes content the default class, the one whose internal grammar most closely resembles a main clause. Non-finite subordinates form a separate system and wait for another chapter.
Main and subordinate
Main | Head of the containing construction | It contains some good ideas.
Subordinate | Dependent complement | He knows that she is right.
Subordinate | Relative modifier | the report she recommended
Subordinate | Comparative complement | more copies than I wanted
Subordinate form | Elliptical answer or supplement | That the workers be reinstated.

*He insists that she be here* looks like a piece of a sentence that has lost its tense. There is no *-s*, no past marker, nothing to agree with *she*. Yet the clause is finite, because the plain form here is the subjunctive, and subjunctives count as primary verb forms. *He thinks that she is here* is finite for the ordinary reason; the two belong to the same class. Non-finite clauses, by contrast, are headed by a gerund-participle, past participle or infinitival plain form, and they lie outside this system.

What separates the three finite subordinate classes is not meaning but what the clause is missing. A relative clause has a gap that takes its interpretation from a nominal. A comparative clause has a reduced measure that takes its interpretation from *than* or *as*. A content clause has neither: it arrives with the full complement structure of a main clause, or with a marker such as *that* or *whether* doing the subordinating.

Content clauses are therefore the ones that look least subordinate. In *I know she is right* nothing inside the clause announces its dependent status; the matrix verb *know* does all the work. Calling the clause subordinate is a statement about its function, not about its shape.
Three classes of finite subordinate clause
Relative | Modifies a nominal; contains a gap | the report she recommended
Comparative | Complement of than or as; reduced measure | more copies than I wanted
Content | Default; no relative or comparative feature | that she is right; whether she is right
the report she recommended — Relative clause modifying report.
more copies than I wanted — Comparative clause complement of than.
I know she is right. — Bare declarative content clause.
I wonder whether she is right. — Closed interrogative content clause.

Try to report an order with a content clause and the construction resists. *He said be quiet* does not work as a subordinate construction; an imperative cannot be subordinated that way. Declarative, closed interrogative, open interrogative and exclamative clauses all can. The missing type is a fact about the system, not an accident of vocabulary.

The declarative is the unmarked option, and it comes in two guises: with *that* and without. Closed interrogatives take *whether* or *if*, open interrogatives front a wh-phrase, and exclamatives front *what* or *how*. The clause type is visible in the clause itself, which is why the matrix verb can select for it.

One consequence is easy to miss. Subordinate interrogatives keep subject-predicator order: *I wonder what he does*, never *I wonder what does he do*. A main-clause question inverts; an embedded one does not.
He says that they are in Paris. — Declarative content clause.
He asked whether she was ill. — Closed interrogative content clause.
I wonder what he does. — Open interrogative content clause with subject-predicator order.
You know what a liar he is. — Exclamative content clause.
*He knows that you are here* and *He knows you are here* say the same thing. With *that*, the boundary between matrix and subordinate clause is marked; without it, the listener infers it.

Some hosts will not tolerate the marker at all. *If* and *before* take bare declaratives, as in *I’ll do it if you pay me* and *He left before she died*. These are non-expandable. Others are more permissive: *provided* allows both *provided that you pay me* and *provided you pay me*.

Where both forms exist, the choice carries information about register and processing. *That* is likelier in formal prose, after longer or rarer verbs, when the clause is separated from its verb, and when the clause has been moved to the front. Omission is likelier after everyday verbs of thinking and saying, especially in speech.
That and bare declaratives
Common verb of cognition | Optional | I think (that) it’s a good idea.
Subject position | Obligatory | That they were lying is obvious.
Adjunct | Obligatory | He appealed to us that justice might be done.
After if or before | Excluded | if you pay me; before she died
After provided | Optional | provided (that) you pay me
He knows that you are here. — Expanded declarative.
He knows you are here. — Bare declarative.
I’ll do it if you pay me. — If excludes that.
I’ll do it provided that you pay me. — Provided allows that.

Move a content clause to the front and the marker stops being optional. *That he really intended to cheat us I still can’t believe* is grammatical; drop *that* and the opening becomes unparseable until the reader reaches *I*. The same demand arises when the clause is an adjunct, and when it follows comparative *than* or *as* and would otherwise be mistaken for a comparative clause.

At the other extreme, *that* can be impossible. *Who does she think is the ringleader?* is fine; *Who does she think that is the ringleader?* is not. The subject of the content clause is a gap, and the fronted *who* must reach it. *That* would sit between the two halves of a single dependency, and the dependency cannot survive the interruption.

Elsewhere the marker comes and goes. Common verbs such as *think*, *say* and *know*, short matrix clauses and casual style all favour omission. Complex vocabulary, distance between verb and clause, and coordination where a second *that* prevents a main-clause reading all favour retention. Nothing in the grammar forces the choice; usage, rhythm and clarity do.
That he really intended to cheat us I still can’t believe. — The clause is preposed; that is obligatory.
He appealed to us that justice might be done. — The content clause is an adjunct; that is obligatory.
Who does she think is the ringleader? — The subject of the content clause is a gap; that must be omitted.
I think it’s a good idea. — Common verb and informal style favour omission.

*That they were lying is obvious* is grammatical, and almost nobody says it. English prefers to park a dummy *it* in subject position and send the clause to the end: *It is obvious that they were lying*. The preference grows stronger as the clause gets longer or the predicate gets shorter.
The moved clause is still the subject in meaning. *It* is an empty placeholder, and the clause supplies what the predicate is about.

The same dummy can appear in object position. *They made it clear that the meeting was cancelled* has *it* as object and the clause as an extraposed object; *made* takes *it* as its object, and the clause is related to that object rather than selected directly by the verb.
That they were lying is obvious. — Content clause as subject.
It is obvious that they were lying. — Extraposed subject with dummy it.
They made it clear that the meeting was cancelled. — Extraposed object with dummy it.
It seems that nobody was informed. — Extraposed subject with seem.

*He knows that she is right* is the easy case: a verb taking a clause complement. Change the host and the same clause keeps its shape while its label changes. A noun can take it in *the belief that she is right*, an adjective in *I’m glad that she is right*. A preposition can take an interrogative version, as in *We agreed on whether to go*. The clause does not care; the host decides what the function is.

Not every content clause is selected. *He appealed to us that justice might be done* contains a clause expressing a desired outcome, and here *that* is obligatory. The *so ... that* construction is a different special case: *It was so cold that the lake froze* pairs a degree expression with a clause stating its consequence.

“Object clause” survives in older descriptions, but it fits only a minority of the examples. A content clause can be subject, complement of a noun, adjective or preposition, extraposed, or an adjunct. The function has to be read off the matrix construction; the label cannot be carried over from Latin grammar and applied wholesale.
Functions of content clauses
Subject | That she was right is clear. | Matrix predicate
Extraposed subject | It is clear that she was right. | Dummy it
Verb complement | He knows that she is right. | know
Noun complement | the belief that she is right | belief
Adjective complement | I’m glad that she is right. | glad
Preposition complement | We agreed on whether to go. | on
Adjunct | He appealed to us that justice might be done. | Matrix clause

*He asked whether she was ill* and *He asked if she was ill* are both closed interrogative content clauses. The difference is the marker, not the clause type. Open interrogatives work differently: they front a wh-phrase and leave the rest of the clause in declarative order.

*Whether* and *if* overlap, but only one of them travels well. *Whether* survives after a preposition (*We discussed whether to go*), in subject position (*Whether he comes is uncertain*), and in exhaustive conditionals (*whether you like it or not*). *If* is barred from those positions in Standard English. The restriction is grammatical, not a matter of tone.

Beyond complements, interrogative clauses appear as supplements, as complements of adjectives such as *uncertain*, and in infinitival form after verbs like *know* and *decide* (*I don’t know what to do*). They also occur ungoverned, as in *Whether you like it or not, we’re going*, where the clause quantifies over alternatives and the matrix holds whichever one obtains. Dubitatives such as *I doubt whether he will come* put the same clause to work expressing doubt.
He asked whether she was ill. — Closed interrogative content clause.
He asked if she was ill. — If is possible as a complement of ask.
We discussed whether to go. — Whether after a preposition; if is not possible here.
Whether he comes is uncertain. — Whether as subject; if is excluded.
Whether you like it or not, we’re going. — Exhaustive conditional adjunct.

The same interrogative clause can point in two directions. *I asked whether she was coming* leaves the issue open; *I know whether she is coming* closes it, naming an answer the speaker already has. Verbs of asking and wondering tend one way, verbs of knowing the other.

Doubt has its own construction. *I doubt whether he will come* and *It’s doubtful whether they can finish* present the embedded question as unresolved, and the doubt attaches to the clause rather than to a negative answer. Infinitival interrogatives are common after *know*, *decide*, *wonder* and *ask*, as in *She asked how to apply*.

*Whether you like it or not, we’re going* has no governing predicate at all. The clause is an adjunct, and it quantifies over two alternatives: the matrix clause is presented as holding under either. This is a conditional use of an interrogative clause, not a complement, and it is why the construction can stand at the front of the sentence with nothing to license it.
I asked whether she was coming. — Question-oriented: the issue is open.
I know whether she is coming. — Answer-oriented: the speaker knows the answer.
I doubt whether he will come. — Dubitative: the issue is doubtful.
I don’t know what to do. — Infinitival interrogative complement.

*You know what a liar he is* contains a *what*, but nothing is being asked. The clause reports an exclamation, and the matrix verb *know* presents it as something the addressee already appreciates. Verbs of realizing, remembering and reporting license the same pattern, and the clause stays close to an open interrogative in form while differing from it in meaning and distribution.

Inside the clause the exclamative phrase moves to the front. In *You know what a liar he is*, *what a liar* occupies the prenuclear position and *he is* follows as the nucleus. The clause is subordinate, but its exclamative type is intact.

Exclamative content clauses tend to appear after factive or semi-factive predicates. *I know how difficult it was* presupposes that it was difficult; *I wonder how difficult it was* does not. The predicate decides whether the exclamation is offered as shared knowledge or left as an open question.
You know what a liar he is. — What a liar is fronted in an exclamative content clause.
I realize how difficult this must be. — How difficult is fronted in an exclamative content clause.
She told me what a mess the office was in. — Exclamative content clause as object of told.

Mandative constructions take a requirement and put it in a clause. *It is important that she be told* uses the subjunctive; *It is important that she should be told* uses *should*; *It is important that she is told* uses the indicative. Verbs such as *insist*, *demand* and *recommend* behave the same way, and the choice among the three forms is partly regional and partly stylistic.

The subjunctive is easy to misclassify because the verb looks bare. *She be told* has no agreement and no tense ending, but the clause is finite: the plain form is the subjunctive marker, and subjunctive clauses belong with finite clauses, not with infinitivals. The absence of inflection is the signal, not the absence of finiteness.

Tense can also be used for distance rather than time. *I wish she were here* puts *were* in a clause about the present, and *If he knew, he would tell us* uses a past form to mark a hypothesis. Present tense can point to the future in a content clause, as in *I hope she arrives tomorrow*. Factivity is a separate dimension: *I know that she left* presupposes that she left, while *I believe that she left* leaves the question open.
Mood and factivity
Mandative subjunctive | It is important that she be told. | Requirement
Mandative should | It is important that she should be told. | Requirement with should
Modal preterite | I wish she were here. | Remote or hypothetical
Present for future | I hope she arrives tomorrow. | Future time with present form
Factive | I know that she left. | Presupposes the complement

*She said that the committee would announce its decision* reports words without reproducing them. There is a reporting verb, a content clause, and a set of adjustments: the tense, the pronouns, and the time and place words all shift to fit the reporter’s position. Nothing is quoted.

Backshift is the most conspicuous adjustment. *She said she was tired* uses a past tense even if the tiredness was present when she spoke; the past marks the report’s perspective, not necessarily past time. Deixis shifts with it: *now* becomes *then*, *today* becomes *that day*, *here* becomes *there*, and *I* becomes *she*.
Backshift is not a mechanical rule. *She said she is tired* is fine when the state still holds; the choice depends on how the speaker frames the report.
She said, ‘I am tired.’ — Direct report: the original words are quoted.
She said that she was tired. — Indirect report with backshift and pronoun shift.
She said she is tired. — Present tense can be retained when the state is still current.
She said she would arrive the next day. — Future-in-the-past and deictic shift.

*She said, ‘I am tired.’* keeps the original words and the original deictic centre. *I* still means the person who spoke, *now* still means the time of speaking, and *here* still means the place. Quotation marks are the visible sign of that retention, but the pronouns and adverbs are what do the work.

Free indirect speech drops the reporting clause and lets the character’s perspective leak into third-person past narration. *She was tired. Tomorrow she would leave.* The pronouns and tense are the narrator’s; the evaluation and the deictic orientation are the character’s. The effect is a voice that belongs to neither fully.

Free direct speech keeps more of the original wording, often without quotation marks. The boundary between it and free indirect style is a matter of degree, and the choice controls how close the reader stands to the character.
She said, ‘I am tired.’ — Direct report with the original deictic centre.
She said that she was tired. — Indirect report with backshift and third person.
She was tired. Tomorrow she would leave. — Free indirect style: third-person narration with the character’s perspective.

By now the content clause should look less like a single construction than like a family. Its members can be declarative, interrogative or exclamative, but never imperative; they can be marked by *that*, *whether*, *if*, a fronted phrase, or nothing at all; and they can serve as subject, complement, adjunct or supplement.

*That* is required when the clause is subject, preposed or an adjunct, impossible when a subject gap is linked to a fronted phrase, and optional elsewhere. Interrogatives divide into question-oriented, answer-oriented and dubitative uses; exclamatives follow factive or semi-factive predicates.

Mood and factivity decide how the content is presented. Mandatives choose among subjunctive, *should* and indicative; modal preterite and irrealis mark distance; factive predicates presuppose their complements. Reported speech then adds a further layer, since indirect report shifts deixis and tense, direct report preserves them, and free indirect style holds both in suspension.

A content-clause checklist: Identify the clause boundaries and its function in the matrix. Decide whether it is declarative, interrogative or exclamative. Check whether that is present, optional or excluded. Then examine mood, factivity and the deictic shifts of reported speech.

Take *She said that the committee would announce its decision after the report had been published*. The matrix clause is *She said that ...*; its complement is the declarative content clause *that the committee would announce its decision after the report had been published*. The clause is expanded with that and functions as the object of said.

Inside the content clause, the past-tense *would* is a future-in-the-past form, and *had been published* is a past perfect locating the publication before the announcement. The report is indirect: the original speaker’s words are not quoted, and the deictic centre has shifted to the narrator’s past perspective.

Find the subordinate clause and identify its function in the matrix. Then classify its type: declarative, closed interrogative, open interrogative or exclamative. Check whether it is finite or non-finite and whether it is marked by that, whether, if or a fronted phrase.

Next, examine the marker. Is that obligatory, optional or excluded? Does the clause function as subject, extraposed subject, complement of a verb, noun, adjective or preposition, or adjunct? The position and the governing item determine the possibilities.

Finally, interpret mood and report. Is the clause mandative, modal, factive or hypothetical? If it reports speech, identify the deictic shifts and whether the report is direct, indirect or free indirect. The same content can be presented from different perspectives.

In *She said that the committee would announce its decision after the report had been published*, the content clause is declarative and functions as the object of said. It is expanded with that. Would is a future-in-the-past modal, and had been published is a past perfect marking anteriority to the announcement.

Content clauses are the default finite subordinate class. They carry declarative, interrogative or exclamative type and function as subjects, complements, adjuncts or supplements. That is obligatory in some positions, excluded in others, and optional in the default case.

Interrogative content clauses use whether or if and occur in question-oriented, answer-oriented and dubitative constructions. Exclamative content clauses use what or how. Mood, factivity and reported speech shape how the content is interpreted and attributed.

lessons.title: Relative constructions and unbounded dependencies

outcomes.text: Explain the main ideas in Relative constructions and unbounded dependencies.
Recognise the patterns in real sentences.
Use the ideas when you read and write.

key_terms.definition: A cover term for relative clauses and fused relatives, including NP and PP types.
A clause containing an overt or covert element interpreted through an antecedent.
The expression that supplies the interpretation of a relative word or gap.
The element in a relative clause that is linked anaphorically to the antecedent.
An abstract empty position in a relative clause, co-indexed with the antecedent or relative phrase.
A relative clause containing a relative word such as who, which or whose.
A non-wh relative introduced by the subordinator that.
A non-wh relative with no relative word or that.
A relative clause integrated into the nominal it modifies, prototypically restricting its denotation.
A prosodically detached relative clause adding information about an antecedent.
The relative clause following the foregrounded element in an it-cleft.
A relative construction in which antecedent and relative clause are fused into one phrase.
The initial phrase in a wh relative, containing the relative word and any material that percolates with it.
A word such as who, whom, whose, which, where or when used in a relative construction.
The spread of a relative feature from a word to the larger phrase containing it.
A relative phrase containing more than the relative word itself, such as whose house or with which.
A relative use that delimits the set denoted by the head nominal.
A relative use that adds information without restricting the antecedent’s denotation.
A detached element related to an anchor without being a syntactic dependent.
A relative clause with an infinitival verb, such as a place to watch the procession from.
A non-finite clause with an understood non-subject element supplied by context.
A fused relative phrase headed by what, whoever or whichever and functioning as an NP.
A fused relative phrase based on where or when and functioning as a PP.
An interrogative clause asking for a value, contrasting with a fused relative.
A relation in which a gap can be embedded arbitrarily deeply inside the clause.
A gap that is licensed by another gap in the same construction.
A construction in which an elided VP is interpreted through an antecedent containing the elided material.

teaching.text: *The things that your father was saying* and *what your father was saying* pick out the same set of remarks. One is a noun phrase with a clause attached; the other is a single phrase in which the antecedent and the clause have fused. The pair is a good place to begin, because the difference between them is the difference between a relative clause and a relative construction.

Relative constructions come in several shapes. A relative word can carry the link, a subordinator can accompany a gap, or the gap can stand alone. The clause can be integrated into a nominal, detached as a supplement, or built into a cleft.

Behind all the variety is one question: how does the missing or anaphoric element get interpreted? A wh relative links a relative word to an antecedent and leaves a gap to mark the original function. A bare relative leaves only the gap. A fused relative folds antecedent and relativised element into one phrase. The rest of the chapter works through the consequences.

*I agree with most of the things that your father was saying* contains a relative clause modifying *things*. Replace the noun phrase and the clause with *what your father was saying* and the meaning survives, but the grammar changes: *what* now does the work of both the antecedent and the relativised element. That is a fused relative.

The traditional term *relative clause* is too narrow for the whole family. *What your father was saying* is a noun phrase, not a clause, and the corresponding forms based on *where* and *when* are prepositional phrases. *Relative construction* is the cover term that lets the clause and phrase types sit together.

The syntactic difference matters. A relative clause can be separated from its antecedent, which is what makes *the things [that your father was saying]* analyzable as two pieces. A fused relative cannot be split that way, because *what* is holding both pieces at once. That is why the fused type needs its own analysis rather than a footnote under relatives.
Clause and phrase relatives
Relative clause | the things that your father was saying | Clause modifying an NP
Fused relative | what your father was saying | NP
Fused relative | where you found it | PP
Cleft relative | who wanted Pat as treasurer | Clause in a cleft

Take *the toys you don’t want*. Nothing in the clause marks it as relative: no wh-word, no *that*, just a gap where *toys* would be understood. Add *that* and the clause has a subordinator; add *which* and it has a relative pronoun. English offers three formal routes to the same relation, and they are not interchangeable in every position.

*Which* in *the toys which you don’t want* is a pronoun linked to *toys*. Replace it with *that* and the word is no longer a pronoun: it is the subordinator familiar from content clauses, and the object position is a gap. Remove both and the gap has no company at all.
Position constrains the choice. A subject relative in the non-wh form needs *that*; an object relative tolerates all three forms, which is why *the advice my neighbour gave me* sounds unremarkable.
Formal types of relative clause
Wh relative | the toys which you don’t want | Overt relative pronoun which
That relative | the toys that you don’t want | Subordinator that plus gap
Bare relative | the toys you don’t want | Gap only
Subject wh relative | the letter which drew our attention | Relative pronoun as subject
Subject that relative | the letter that drew our attention | That plus subject gap
the toys which you don’t want — Wh relative with which as object.
the toys that you don’t want — That relative with a gap in object position.
the toys you don’t want — Bare relative with a gap in object position.
the letter that drew our attention — Subject relativisation; that is required in the non-wh form.

Begin with two sentences that look alike but behave differently. *The boys who defaced the statue were expelled* uses its clause to narrow the set of boys; *My father, who retired last year, now lives in Florida* uses its clause to add a fact about a man already identified. The first is integrated, the second supplementary. Two further relational types complete the set: the cleft relative, which follows the foregrounded element in an *it*-cleft, and the fused relative, which combines antecedent and clause in a single phrase.

Integration is primarily a matter of information structure. The boys who defaced the statue are a subset of the boys, and the clause is what tells you which subset. A supplementary relative does not narrow anything: *my father* already picks out one person, and *who retired last year* adds a fact about him. The clause adds; it does not select.

Cleft relatives belong to the cleft construction rather than to the nominal system, and their internal structure differs in ways that are easy to overlook. Fused relatives are further removed again: they are phrases, not clauses, and their antecedent is not a separate word at all but part of the same phrase.
Relational types
Integrated | The boys who defaced the statue were expelled. | Modifier inside the NP
Supplementary | My father, who retired last year, now lives in Florida. | Detached supplement
Cleft | It was Kim who wanted Pat as treasurer. | Relative in a cleft
Fused | What you say is quite right. | Phrase combining antecedent and relative

In *the letter that drew our attention*, nothing sits in the subject position after *that*. The clause has a hole, and the antecedent *letter* supplies what belongs there. That hole is the gap, and the element it stands for is the relativised element. In a wh relative a relative word makes that element visible; in a non-wh relative the gap does all the pointing. Either way the gap keeps the grammatical function the element would have had: subject, object, complement of a preposition, adjunct or predicative.

In *I accepted the advice which my neighbour gave me*, *which* sits at the front and the gap sits after *gave*, where the object belongs. The pronoun is interpreted as object because the gap is an object. Put the gap in subject position, as in *the letter that drew our attention*, and the clause has no overt subject at all.

The gap is what separates a relative clause from a content clause. *The suggestion that Kim made* has one; *the suggestion that Kim cheated* does not. The words *that Kim* appear in both, which is why the gap has to be diagnosed rather than heard.
the advice which my neighbour gave me — Which is linked to the object gap after gave.
the letter that drew our attention — The gap is in subject position.
the suggestion that Kim made — Relative: a gap follows made.
the suggestion that Kim cheated — Content clause: no gap; that introduces the clause.

In *the people whose house we are renting*, the relative word does not arrive alone: it brings *house* with it. A wh relative begins with a phrase, and that phrase may be a single word such as *which* or a longer one such as *whose house* or *the result of which*. The extra material travels with the relative word to the front of the clause, even though only the word itself is linked to the antecedent.

The relative feature percolates upward from the word to the phrase that contains it. *Whose* lends its relative status to the noun phrase *whose house*; *which* lends it to the prepositional phrase *with which*. The whole phrase is fronted, but the antecedent relation runs through the word, not through the phrase as a whole.

The patterns are systematic rather than arbitrary: a prepositional complement can pass the feature to a PP, a PP complement of a noun can pass it to an NP, and genitive *whose* or determinative *which* can pass it to a larger NP. Infinitival and gerund-participial clauses provide two more routes. The table sets out all seven; percolation, not fronting alone, explains why such long phrases can open a relative clause.
Percolation patterns
Complement of preposition | PP | behind which
PP complement of noun | NP | the result of which
PP | AdjP | prominent among which
NP | Infinitival | to refute which
NP | Gerund-participial | passing which
Genitive whose | NP | whose essay
Determinative which | NP | which suggestion
the article which he recommended — Simple relative phrase which.
the people whose house we are renting — Complex phrase whose house; whose is linked to people.
the skill with which she handled the situation — Complex phrase with which; the gap is a PP.
the result of which we expect next week — Complex phrase the result of which.

Relativisation reaches most grammatical functions. Subjects relativise in *the letter that drew our attention* and objects in *the advice which my neighbour gave me*; genitive determiners relativise too, though the relative word has to change to *whose*. Complements of prepositions, adjuncts and predicatives are also available, with more constraints.

The dependency can cross clause boundaries. In *the man who she said had won*, the gap is the subject of *had won*, inside the content clause that *said* takes as complement. *Who* is linked to a position several clauses down, and nothing in the grammar sets a limit on how far down it can go.

Some functions are harder to reach than others. Adjunct relativisation usually wants a wh-phrase or a preposition, as in *the day when we met* or *the place where they stayed*. Manner and reason relatives are more restricted still. What licenses the gap depends on the relative word, the antecedent and the function the gap fills.
the letter that drew our attention — Subject relativisation.
the advice which my neighbour gave me — Object relativisation.
the people whose house we are renting — Genitive determiner relativisation.
the man who she said had won — The gap is the subject of an embedded clause.

*The boys were expelled* says something about all the boys. Add *who defaced the statue* and the claim narrows to a subset. That narrowing is the characteristic work of an integrated relative: it sits inside the nominal, shares its prosody, and helps fix what the nominal refers to.

The clause usually sits right against its head: *the boys who defaced the statue*, not *the boys were expelled who defaced the statue*. That adjacency is part of how the antecedent is identified. The pattern has extensions: a relative can modify a superlative, as in *the fattest he has ever been*, or an interrogative pronoun, as in *Where can we eat that isn’t too expensive?* These are peripheral, but they show that nominal head plus clause is a prototype rather than a rule.

*Restrictive* is the traditional label, and it is close to *integrated* without being identical. An integrated relative can fail to restrict when the head is already unique or when the clause only adds a comment. Integration is structural; restrictiveness is interpretive, and the two can come apart.
The boys who defaced the statue were expelled. — The relative restricts the set of boys.
the fattest he has ever been — Integrated relative modifying a superlative.
Where can we eat that isn’t too expensive? — Relative clause modifying an interrogative preposition.

*My father, who retired last year, now lives in Florida* says two things at once, and the commas mark the seam. The clause is detached, its antecedent is already identified, and what it contributes is information rather than a restriction. Remove it and the sentence still makes a complete claim.

Detachment widens the range of possible antecedents. A supplementary relative can attach to an adjective phrase, as in *Pat is afraid of snakes, which I’m sure Kim is too*, or to a whole clause, as in *Pat is afraid of snakes, which doesn’t surprise me*. It comments on its anchor instead of narrowing it, which is why such loose attachment is possible.

*Non-restrictive* is the usual contrast term, but it names an interpretation rather than a structure. Supplementary relatives are detached and informationally secondary; they are not always non-restrictive in meaning, and integrated relatives are not always restrictive. The two distinctions overlap without coinciding.
My father, who retired last year, now lives in Florida. — Detached relative adding information about my father.
Pat is afraid of snakes, which I’m sure Kim is too. — The antecedent is an AdjP.
Pat is afraid of snakes, which doesn’t surprise me. — The antecedent is a clause.

Move a relative away from its head and the listener has to work harder to find the antecedent. That is why an integrated relative normally follows its head nominal immediately: adjacency is one of the cues that identifies what the clause modifies. Postposing for emphasis or ease of processing is possible, but the relation stays with the head nominal rather than wandering to whatever noun happens to precede.

Supplementary relatives have more freedom and less tolerance. *My father, who retired last year, now lives in Florida* interrupts the main clause cleanly. Move the same clause to the end, as in *My father now lives in Florida, who retired last year*, and the result is awkward: the relative is separated from its antecedent and lands where a new predication is expected.

Coordination creates genuine ambiguity. *The students and the teachers who attended the meeting* can mean the teachers who attended, or the students and teachers who both attended; the clause can attach to the second coordinate or to the whole coordination.
the report that the committee published — Integrated relative immediately after the head.
My father, who retired last year, now lives in Florida. — Interpolated supplementary relative.
The students and the teachers who attended the meeting — Attachment ambiguous between the teachers and the whole coordination.

*A good place from which to watch the procession* and *a good place to watch the procession from* describe the same spot. In the first, the preposition is fronted with *which*; in the second it is stranded at the end and the relative phrase is missing altogether. Both are infinitival relatives, and both leave something understood.

Infinitival relatives are hollow clauses: a non-subject element is missing and gets its interpretation from the head nominal. In *a place to watch the procession from*, the complement of *from* is understood as the place. The head supplies the content; the clause supplies the frame.

The construction is more restricted than its finite counterparts. It clusters after nouns such as *place*, *time*, *way* and *thing*, and it often carries a purpose-like or availability-like meaning: a place to sit, work to do, a way to escape. The interpretation is predictable enough that the missing element rarely needs to be spelled out.
a good place from which to watch the procession — Wh infinitival relative.
a good place to watch the procession from — Bare infinitival relative with a stranded preposition.
She has a lot of work to do. — Hollow infinitival relative modifying work.

*What he did was outrageous* contains no separate antecedent for *what*. The word does two jobs at once: it stands for the thing, and it marks the relativised element inside the clause. *Whoever devised this plan* and *whichever car appeals to you* work the same way, each fusing antecedent and clause into a single noun phrase.

*Where* and *when* produce fused relatives of a different category. *Put it back where you found it* and *He calls his parents whenever he is in trouble* function as prepositional phrases, not noun phrases, even though their meaning is relative in the ordinary sense. The category follows the word, not the meaning.

A fused relative can look exactly like an open interrogative, and the difference is not always visible in the string. *What he did was outrageous* asserts something about a deed; *What did he do?* asks for the deed. The fused relative has no separate antecedent and functions as a noun phrase, while the interrogative asks for a value. The surrounding predicate usually decides which reading is available.
Fused relatives
Fused NP | what he did | NP
Fused NP | whoever devised this plan | NP
Fused NP | whichever car appeals to you | NP
Fused PP | where you found it | PP
Fused PP | whenever he is in trouble | PP
What he did was outrageous. — Fused relative NP functioning as subject.
What did he do? — Open interrogative asking for a value.
Put it back where you found it. — Fused relative PP functioning as an adjunct.
Whoever devised this plan must be naive. — Fused relative NP with whoever.

*The man who she said had won* puts *who* at the front and its gap inside a clause that is itself inside another clause. The link crosses two boundaries without difficulty, and another layer could be added without breaking it. That is what *unbounded* means: the distance between the fronted phrase and its gap is not fixed by the grammar.

The gap keeps its own function. In *the man who she said had won*, it is the subject of *had won*; in *the report which he claimed she had written*, it is the object of *written*. The relative phrase is interpreted through the gap, not through the matrix verb, which is why *said* and *claimed* contribute nothing to the relativised role.

The same machinery operates outside relatives. *Who did she say had won?* has the same long-distance relation as its relative counterpart, and exclamatives and comparatives use it too. Parasitic gaps and antecedent-contained deletion are further cases where one gap depends on another, or where an elided verb phrase is recovered from material that contains it.
the man who she said had won — The gap is subject of had won, inside the content clause.
the report which he claimed she had written — The gap is object of written, two clauses down.
Who did she say had won? — The interrogative phrase has the same long-distance relation.

The family of relative constructions is wider than the name *relative clause* suggests. It includes wh, that and bare clauses, fused noun phrases and prepositional phrases, and the relatives that appear in clefts. What unites them is a link between a clause-internal position and an antecedent, whether that antecedent is a separate phrase or folded into the relative word itself.

Relational labels describe where the clause sits and what it does there. Integrated relatives modify a nominal and typically restrict it; supplementary relatives are detached and add information about a wider range of anchors; cleft relatives belong to the cleft construction; fused relatives combine antecedent and clause in a single phrase. Infinitival relatives are hollow clauses whose missing element comes from the head.

The mechanics are consistent across the types. A relative phrase can be simple or complex, with the relative feature percolating upward from the word to the larger phrase; relativisation can target subjects, objects, genitives, adjuncts and deeply embedded positions; and the gap always preserves the grammatical function of the element the antecedent interprets.

A relative-construction checklist: Find the antecedent and the relative phrase. Identify the gap and its function. Decide whether the relative is integrated or supplementary, and whether it is wh, that or bare. Then check for fused, cleft or infinitival structure.

Take *The report that the committee finally published confirmed what everyone had suspected*. The subject NP is *The report that the committee finally published*. Its head is *report* and the that relative clause modifies it; the gap is the object of published, co-indexed with report.

The object of confirmed is the fused relative NP *what everyone had suspected*. What combines the antecedent and relative word, and the gap after suspected is its object. The example shows an integrated relative inside the subject and a fused relative inside the object, both relying on a gap for interpretation.

Start with the antecedent. Identify the relative phrase or gap and the function it has inside the relative clause. Then decide whether the relative is wh, that or bare, and whether it is integrated, supplementary, cleft or fused.

For a complex relative phrase, trace the percolation from the relative word to the larger phrase. In whose house, whose is linked to the antecedent and the whole NP is fronted. In with which, which is linked to the antecedent and the PP is fronted.

For a fused relative, do not look for a separate antecedent. The phrase itself functions as an NP or PP, and the relative word combines the antecedent and the relativised function. Check whether the form is a fused relative or an open interrogative from the syntax and the surrounding predicate.

In *The report that the committee finally published confirmed what everyone had suspected*, the that clause is an integrated relative modifying report; its gap is the object of published. The fused relative what everyone had suspected is the object of confirmed, and its gap is the object of suspected.

Relative constructions include wh, that and bare clauses, plus fused NP and PP relatives. Integrated relatives modify nominals; supplementary relatives are detached; cleft relatives occur in clefts; fused relatives combine antecedent and relative.

Relativisation involves a gap or relative word linked to an antecedent. Complex relative phrases arise by upward percolation, and the dependency can be unbounded. Infinitival relatives are hollow clauses, and fused relatives must be distinguished from open interrogatives.

lessons.title: Comparative constructions

outcomes.text: Explain the main ideas in Comparative constructions.
Recognise the patterns in real sentences.
Use the ideas when you read and write.

teaching.text: *The new bridge is slightly longer than the old one* does one kind of work; *it is not as beautiful as the stone bridge upstream* does another. Both are comparisons, and both draw on the same small set of markers, yet one ranks two values on a scale while the other says the new bridge falls short on a different scale. English also compares for identity (*the same bus as last time*) and for likeness (*similar to the old one*), where no scale is involved at all.

The chapter follows two distinctions that cut across each other: scalar versus non-scalar, and equality versus inequality. From there it moves to term and set comparison, to the governors that license comparative clauses, and to the *than*/*as* phrases that carry the secondary term. Later sections take up *as*, *like* and *unlike*, and the comparative and superlative forms that rank a member within a set.

A question worth asking of every example: what is being compared, and on what dimension? A degree, an identity, a likeness, a rank within a group — the syntax can look alike while the interpretation shifts. The sections that follow keep returning to that question.

Take *She is much bigger than she was then*. The word *bigger* carries a grade inflection, and the clause *than she was then* is a comparative clause — one of the three major kinds of finite subordinate clause in English. *She went to the same school as I went to* contains the same kind of subordinate clause, though nothing is being graded.

*Very big*, *quite big* and *rather big* turn the volume up on a property, but they do not bring a second term along. *Bigger than* does: it sets two values against each other on a scale. The two systems overlap in the adjectives they use, and that overlap is exactly what makes them easy to confuse.

*I took the same bus as last time* compares two buses for identity, and *I took a different bus from last time* compares them for difference. Neither ranks anything. They borrow *as* and *than* from the scalar system — *different than* turns up in some varieties — but the question they answer is whether the terms are the same, not how much they differ.
Comparison and adjacent systems
Degree grading | very big; rather useful | Grades a property without a second term
Scalar comparison | bigger than; as big as | Compares values on a scale
Non-scalar equality | the same bus as | Compares for identity or likeness
Non-scalar inequality | different from | Compares for difference
Set comparison | the biggest of the three | Ranks a member within a set

*Kim is as old as Pat* and *Kim is older than Pat* both ask us to place two ages on a scale. The first puts them at the same point or above it; the second puts Kim higher. What makes the comparison scalar is the gradable expression — *old*, *heavy*, *careful* — and the marker says where the terms sit.
*I took the same bus as last time* asks whether the bus is the same one; *I took a different bus from last time* asks whether it is not. Nothing gradable is at stake, and no ranking follows.

*As* marks equality in both types, which is why the parallel is tempting. *Than* marks scalar inequality and some non-scalar inequality, as in *other than* or, in some varieties, *different than*. Sharing a marker is not sharing a meaning: the scalar use locates values, the non-scalar use sorts entities.
Four types of comparison
Scalar | Kim is as old as Pat. | Kim is older than Pat.
Non-scalar | I took the same bus as last time. | I took a different bus from last time.
Kim is as old as Pat. — Scalar equality: at least equal on the age scale.
Kim is older than Pat. — Scalar superiority.
I took the same bus as last time. — Non-scalar equality: identity of bus.
I took a different bus from last time. — Non-scalar inequality: difference of bus.

In *Ed is more tolerant than he used to be*, two degrees of tolerance are held up against each other: Ed now, Ed then. Call the one in the matrix clause the primary term and the one in the comparative clause the secondary term. The labels matter less than the split, since each term belongs to a different clause layer.

*Ed made the most mistakes of them all* works differently. There is no second term to pair with Ed; instead a set — *them all* — provides the field, and Ed is placed at the top of it. *It sold for the highest price ever paid for a Cézanne* does the same with a set of prices.

The secondary term can go unsaid when context supplies it: *Ed was difficult then, but now he’s more tolerant* leaves *than he was then* to be recovered. Set comparisons often rewrite as term comparisons — *Ed made more mistakes than all the others* — which is a useful check on what the set actually contains.
Term and set comparison
Term | Ed is more tolerant than he used to be. | Present Ed vs past Ed
Term | Kim’s version is superior to Pat’s. | Kim’s version vs Pat’s
Set | Ed made the most mistakes of them all. | All members of the group
Set | the highest price ever paid | All prices in the relevant set

Something in the matrix has to license the comparison. *More*, *less*, *as*, *so*, *such*, *than*, *superior*, *inferior*, *prefer* and *rather* all do that work; call them comparative governors. What separates them is the complement each one allows: a clause, an NP or a phrase.

The governor and its complement form a comparative phrase. In *much bigger than she was*, *much* modifies *bigger* and *than she was* completes it; in *as careful as her sister*, the phrase is *as careful* and the complement is *as her sister*. The modifier sits inside the phrase, the complement outside the head.

Treating *than* and *as* as prepositions rather than subordinating conjunctions changes where the clause sits: it becomes the complement of the preposition. That analysis survives reduction. *Bob is as generous as Sue* has a one-word complement, and the missing material — *as Sue is generous* — is recovered from the matrix rather than spelled out.
Governors and complements
more | than clause or phrase | more careful than before
less | than clause or phrase | less careful than before
as | as clause or phrase | as careful as before
so | as clause | so careful as to check twice
superior | to phrase | superior to the old model
prefer | to phrase or clause | prefer tea to coffee
much bigger than she was — Much modifies bigger; than she was is the complement.
as careful as her sister — As careful is the comparative phrase; as her sister is the complement.
superior to the old model — Superior takes a to phrase.
prefer tea to coffee — Prefer takes a to phrase.

*She is much bigger than she was then* leaves us to supply the complement of *was*: we hear it as *big*. That gap is not sloppiness. The clause borrows structure from the matrix, which is why the comparison can be reduced and still understood.

Reduction has limits. *She wrote more plays than he wrote novels* is fine with the measure after *more* left empty. Put the measure in — *She wrote more plays than he wrote five novels* — and the sentence collapses. The comparative clause cannot spell out the very quantity that the comparison is measuring.

Reduction can go further, down to one remnant: *Bob is as generous as Sue*, *She is taller than him*. That remnant identifies the secondary term, and everything else comes from the matrix. Which element survives is decided by what the comparison needs to pick out.
She is much bigger than she was then. — The comparative clause lacks the repeated adjective big.
She wrote more plays than he wrote novels. — The measure after more is left empty.
Bob is as generous as Sue. — The comparative clause is reduced to Sue.
She is taller than him. — The secondary term is a single pronoun.

The remnant after *than* or *as* is usually an NP or a pronoun. *Bob is as generous as Sue* and *She is taller than him* each supply just enough to identify the second term, while the rest of the clause is understood.

*She is taller than I* and *She is taller than me* identify the same secondary term, but they wear their clause structure differently. Formal writing favours the nominative when a subject is understood; informal speech uses the accusative. The nominative makes the clausal source more visible.

The remnant can also be a phrase: *more quickly than before*, *as often as ever*. *Than before* is read as *than she was before*, *as ever* as *as she ever was*. The governor and the matrix decide what the fragment is understood to contain.
Bob is as generous as Sue. — Sue is the secondary term.
She is taller than I. — Formal nominative in the reduced clause.
She is taller than me. — Informal accusative in the reduced clause.
more quickly than before — The complement is a temporal phrase.

Comparison does not always set values against each other. *She looks like her mother* asserts likeness; *She looks different from her mother* asserts contrast. The complement can be an NP, a PP or a clause depending on the governor — *like her mother*, *different from her mother*, *the same as her mother*.

*More apparent than real* is stranger than it looks. Nothing is more apparent than something else; the sentence measures how well the description *apparent* fits against the description *real*. The syntax is comparative, but the comparison is between labels, not between degrees of a property.

*More apparent than real* sounds fine; *more apparent than the surface* does not. The reduced clause has to match the matrix category by category and function by function. A poor match leaves the comparison odd or ambiguous, which is why a sentence can be grammatical and still hard to read.
She looks like her mother. — Likeness between two people.
She looks different from her mother. — Contrast between two people.
The recovery is more apparent than real. — Metalinguistic comparison of descriptions.
He is more lucky than skilful. — Comparison of two descriptions of the same person.

Scalar inequality comes in two directions. *Bigger than* and *more careful than* mark superiority; *less big than* and *less careful than* mark inferiority. Only superiority has an inflectional form. Equality and inferiority are built with separate words.

*Older than* and *younger than* are both superiority comparatives: each says the primary term is further along its scale. The scales run opposite ways, so *younger* moves towards zero while *older* moves away from it. Superiority is a grammatical relation, not a compass direction.

*More* and *less* also quantify nouns and combine with degree determinatives: *more mistakes*, *fewer mistakes*, *less money*, *much more useful*. *Rather*, *prefer*, *superior* and *inferior* are peripheral governors with their own complements — *prefer tea to coffee*, *superior to the old model* — and they select *to* rather than *than*.
Scalar inequality
Superiority | -er or more | bigger than; more careful than
Inferiority | less | less big than; less careful than
Superiority with nouns | more / fewer | more mistakes; fewer mistakes
Inferiority with nouns | less / fewer | less money; fewer coins
Less central governor | prefer / superior | prefer tea to coffee; superior to
She is taller than her brother. — Superiority on the height scale.
She is less tall than her brother. — Inferiority on the same scale.
He made more mistakes than I did. — More with a count noun.
He made fewer mistakes than I did. — Fewer with a count noun.

*Kim is as old as Pat* is true if Kim is older; it only rules out Kim being younger. Equality is usually a floor, not an exact match. Negate it — *Kim isn’t as old as Pat* — and the floor disappears, leaving inferiority.

Why the lower-bound reading? Most scales resist precise measurement, so exact equality is rarely the issue. *He made as many as eighteen mistakes* leans towards exactness because the number is explicit; *He made as many mistakes as I did* does not.

*So* and *such* handle neighbouring jobs: *so careful as to check twice*, *such a careful worker as Pat*. *As* is the general equality marker across scalar and non-scalar comparison, while *so* is more restricted and usually pulls a result or degree clause along with it.
Scalar equality
as ... as | Kim is as old as Pat. | At least equal
Negative as ... as | Kim isn’t as old as Pat. | Inferior
so ... as | so careful as to check twice | Degree and result
such ... as | such a worker as Pat | Equality of kind or degree
as many as | as many as eighteen | At least or exact, context-dependent
Jill is as clever as Liz. — Compatible with Jill being cleverer.
Jill isn’t as clever as Liz. — Entails that Jill is less clever.
He made as many as eighteen mistakes. — Strongly suggests exact equality.

Degree modifiers adjust the gap between the two terms: *much bigger*, *far more useful*, *slightly less expensive*, *rather better*. *Very* is the odd one out — *very bigger* fails, though *very much bigger* works, because *very* modifies the adjective rather than the comparative.

*The* can attach to a comparative and turn it into a selector: *the bigger of the two*, *the more useful option*. It picks one alternative out of two, or one member out of a small set. That is close to superlative work but stops short of ranking an entire set.

The correlative comparative pairs two of these phrases: *The more you practise, the better you become*. The first sets a degree or condition, the second reports what varies with it. *The sooner, the better* is the same construction with both halves trimmed.
much bigger than before — Much modifies the comparative degree.
the bigger of the two — The article selects one of two alternatives.
The more you practise, the better you become. — Correlative comparative: degree correlates with result.
The sooner, the better. — Reduced correlative comparative.

The non-scalar family sorts into three relations. *Same* claims identity, or at least exact correspondence; *similar* claims likeness without identity; *different* claims non-identity. The examples below show how little the nouns matter: a bus, a design, a person. None of these comparisons ranks anything.

Each governor brings its own complement pattern: *same as*, *similar to*, *different from*, *different than* in some varieties, *other than*, *else*. *Like* takes an NP and expresses likeness; *unlike* expresses contrast. None of these ranks two values, even when *as* or *than* appears.

*Such* compares kind or quality — *such a report as this*, *such reports as these*. *Other* and *else* mark difference or exclusion — *someone other than Kim*, *nothing else*. The governor dictates what can follow it, and the relation follows the governor.
Non-scalar comparison
Identity | same ... as | the same bus as last time
Likeness | similar to; like | similar to the old one; like her mother
Difference | different from; other than; else | different from the old one; someone else
Kind or quality | such ... as | such a report as this
Contrast | unlike | unlike her mother
I took the same bus as last time. — Identity of bus.
This design is similar to the old one. — Likeness, not identity.
This design is different from the old one. — Difference.
She looks like her mother. — Likeness with like.

*As* is the busiest of the markers. It carries scalar equality in *as old as*, non-scalar identity in *the same as*, and exemplification in *such as*. Its complement may be a clause or a reduced phrase, which is one reason it spreads across so many constructions.

*Like* is a preposition of likeness — *She looks like her mother* — but it also takes finite clauses in some constructions: *It looks like it’s going to rain*. *As* can introduce a comparison or a supplement: *As you know, the deadline is Friday*. Its territory is wider than equality alone.

*Unlike* is not merely *not like*. It sets the subject against the complement, often in a detached supplement: *Unlike her sister, she stayed calm*. The relation is contrast between entities, not a position on a scale.
She is as tall as her brother. — As marks scalar equality.
She looks like her mother. — Like marks likeness.
Unlike her mother, she enjoys publicity. — Unlike marks contrast.
It looks like it’s going to rain. — Like with a finite clause complement.

Set comparison needs a set. With two members, the comparative does the work: *the bigger of the two*. With more, the superlative picks out the extreme: *the biggest of the three*, *the most useful option*.

*Biggest* and *most useful* both mark the extreme of a set, but they do it by different means: one inflects, the other uses *most*. And *most* has a second life meaning “very” in *a most interesting article*. Context separates the absolute reading, which intensifies, from the relative reading, which ranks.

The set can be spelled out with *of* or *in* — *the best of the three*, *the tallest in the class* — or left to context, as in *She is the tallest*. Relative superlatives normally take *the*, the definite article anchoring the ranking.
Grade in set comparison
Plain | big | No comparison
Comparative | bigger | Two members or a restricted set
Superlative | biggest | Extreme of a set
Analytic superlative | most useful | Longer adjectives
Absolute most | a most interesting article | Very, not superlative ranking
the bigger of the two — Comparative with a two-member set.
the biggest of the three — Superlative with an explicit set.
the most useful option — Analytic superlative.
a most interesting article — Absolute most: very interesting.

Two distinctions organise everything in this chapter: scalar versus non-scalar, and equality versus inequality. Scalar comparison places values on a scale; non-scalar comparison asks about identity, likeness or difference. Cutting across them is the difference between term comparison, which pairs a primary and a secondary term, and set comparison, which ranks a member within a group.

Comparative governors decide what kind of complement appears. *Than* and *as* take clauses or reduced phrases, and those clauses are incomplete by design. Superiority may be inflectional or analytic; inferiority and equality are analytic. Scalar equality sets a lower bound rather than an exact value.

*Same*, *similar*, *different*, *other*, *else*, *as*, *like* and *unlike* cover the non-scalar ground, while comparative and superlative forms handle sets, with *most* split between absolute and relative readings. Because the markers recur across types, the construction and the context have to settle what is being compared.

A comparison checklist: Identify the primary term and the secondary term or set. Decide whether the comparison is scalar or non-scalar, equality or inequality. Find the governor and its complement. Then check whether the clause is reduced and whether the reading is metalinguistic, absolute or relative.

Take *The new bridge is slightly longer than the old one, but it is not as beautiful as the stone bridge upstream*. The first comparison is scalar inequality: *longer than* expresses superiority on the length scale, modified by *slightly*. The secondary term is *the old one*.

The second comparison is scalar equality under negation: *not as beautiful as the stone bridge upstream* entails that the new bridge is less beautiful. The comparison set is the two bridges, and the scale is beauty. The example contrasts superiority and inferiority using the same comparative system.

Find the governor: more, less, as, than, same, similar, different, like or a superlative. Identify the primary term and the secondary term or set. Then decide whether the comparison is scalar or non-scalar and whether it expresses equality or inequality.

For a comparative clause, reconstruct the omitted material from the matrix. Check whether the reduction is to a single element, a phrase or a full clause. Then identify the function of the gap or remnant inside the comparative clause.

For a superlative, identify the comparison set and decide whether the reading is relative or absolute. For non-scalar comparison, decide whether the relation is identity, likeness, difference or exclusion. The markers overlap, but the interpretations do not.

In *The new bridge is slightly longer than the old one, but it is not as beautiful as the stone bridge upstream*, *longer than* is a scalar superiority comparison and *not as beautiful as* is a negated scalar equality entailing inferiority. The secondary terms are *the old one* and *the stone bridge upstream*.

Scalar comparison ranks values on a scale; non-scalar comparison concerns identity, likeness and difference. Term comparison relates two terms; set comparison ranks a member within a set. Comparative clauses are reduced and interpreted through the matrix.

More, less, as, than, same, similar, different, like and unlike are comparative governors with different complement patterns. Scalar equality gives a lower bound, and superlatives can be relative or absolute.

key_terms.definition: A construction relating two or more things or quantities on a scale or by identity and likeness.
Comparison of relative position on a gradable scale, as in older than or as old as.
Comparison concerned with identity, likeness or difference rather than degree.
A comparison presenting two values as equal or at least equal, typically with as.
A comparison presenting values as unequal, typically with than or less.
Scalar inequality in which the primary term is higher on the scale.
Scalar inequality in which the primary term is lower on the scale.
The direction of a scale determined by lexical meaning, as with old versus young.
Comparison between a primary term and a secondary term.
Comparison among members of a set, often with a superlative.
The term expressed in the matrix clause of a term comparison.
The term expressed in the subordinate comparative clause or phrase.
A subordinate clause complement of than or as, with part of its interpretation supplied by the matrix.
The expression that licenses a comparative complement, such as more, less, as or than.
The phrase containing the comparative marker and its complement or modifier.
The inflectional or analytic form marking scalar superiority, as in bigger or more useful.
The form marking the extreme of a scale within a set, as in biggest or most useful.
A comparison that measures how well a description fits rather than comparing the things themselves.
A comparative formed with more or less rather than an inflection.
A comparative formed with the suffix -er.
Identity or likeness expressed with same, similar or as.
Difference or unlikeness expressed with different, other, else or unlike.
A relation of similarity rather than identity, often expressed by like or similar.
The relation of being the same entity or set, often expressed by same.
The construction the more ..., the merrier, with paired comparative phrases.
A superlative use expressing a very high degree without comparison to a set.
A superlative use locating the extreme within a comparison set.
The set of entities over which a superlative or set comparison ranges.

lessons.title: Non-finite and verbless clauses

outcomes.text: Explain the main ideas in Non-finite and verbless clauses.
Recognise the patterns in real sentences.
Use the ideas when you read and write.
