teaching.text: Take *She wanted to arrange for the committee to review the proposal before the deadline*. One sentence, several verbs, and only the first is finite. *Wanted* carries tense; *to arrange* and *to review* do not, and the subject of *review* is never spelled out. The rest of the sentence is built from clauses that have subjects, objects and complements but no primary tense.

This chapter starts with that finite/non-finite divide and with the three non-finite form-types. It then follows *to* and *for*, the auxiliaries that non-finites do and do not admit, subjectless and hollow clauses, and the catenative construction in its simple and complex shapes. Later sections turn to non-catenative complements, complements of adjectives, nouns and prepositions, modifiers, supplements and verbless clauses.

The catenative chain is the thread to hold on to. A catenative verb takes a non-finite complement, and the pattern can nest: *She intends to try to persuade him to help her redecorate*. Each verb heads a layer, and every intervening NP has to be attached to the right one.

Compare *She left* with *She wanted to leave*. The first has a verb with primary tense; the second has one too, but its complement does not. *I remember locking the door* and *He got charged* likewise contain clauses with verbs, subjects and objects but no primary tense. The plain form is the tricky case, because it appears on both sides of the line.

A plain form can be imperative (*Be patient*), subjunctive (*It is essential that he be careful*) or infinitival (*It is important for him to be careful*), yet only the last is non-finite. *To*, the absence of *do*-support, the embedding and the subject form separate the three.

Infinitivals normally carry *to*, except after modals and supportive *do*. Negation goes before *to*, not through *do*: *It’s important not to be late*, never *to don’t be late*. They are typically embedded, and when a subject appears it is accusative or plain, often behind *for*.
Finite and non-finite plain forms
Imperative | Be patient. | Finite
Subjunctive | It is essential that he be careful. | Finite
To-infinitival | It is important for him to be careful. | Non-finite
Bare infinitival | They helped him move. | Non-finite
Gerund-participial | I remember locking the door. | Non-finite
Past-participial | He got charged. | Non-finite

The verb form sorts non-finite clauses into three types. *Max wanted to change his name* is infinitival; *I remember locking the door* is gerund-participial; *His father got charged with manslaughter* is past-participial. The label comes from the verb, not from the function the clause performs.

Infinitivals split again. *They forced me to sign* has *to*; *They helped me move the furniture* does not. The to-infinitival appears across a wide range of constructions, while the bare form is largely confined to complements of a small verb class, modals and supportive *do* included.

The old gerund/present participle split does not survive inspection. The gerund-participle is one verb form, whether it appears in a progressive construction or heads a non-finite clause. Two labels for one form hide the syntax they share.
Non-finite form-types
To-infinitival | Plain form with to | to change his name
Bare infinitival | Plain form without to | help me move
Gerund-participial | Gerund-participle | locking the door
Past-participial | Past participle | charged with manslaughter
Max wanted to change his name. — To-infinitival complement.
They helped me move the furniture. — Bare infinitival complement.
I remember locking the door. — Gerund-participial complement.
His father got charged with manslaughter. — Past-participial complement.

*To* is the default marker of the infinitival, and *for* is what lets it have an overt subject: *For them to take the children could endanger the mission*. *For* cannot appear without a subject, and that subject is accusative or plain — *for him to go*, not *for he to go*.

Bare infinitivals drop *to*. They follow modals (*can go*), supportive *do* (*did go*), and lexical verbs such as *help*, *make*, *let* and *see*: *They made him apologise*, *We saw her leave*. A few idiomatic constructions use the bare form too.

Whether *to* appears is not free variation. Some verbs take only to-infinitivals, some only bare ones, and some take both with a meaning difference. *I helped him move* and *I helped him to move* are near synonyms; *I made him move* and *I made him to move* are not.
For them to take the children could endanger the mission. — For introduces the subject of the to-infinitival.
They forced me to sign the petition. — To-infinitival complement of forced.
They helped me move the furniture. — Bare infinitival complement.
We saw her leave. — Bare infinitival after a perception verb.

Modals and supportive *do* are shut out of non-finite clauses. The other auxiliaries are not. *I expect to have finished*, *I expect to be working* and *I expect to be interviewed* show perfect *have*, progressive *be* and passive *be* inside an infinitival.

Gerund-participials admit perfect *have* and passive *be* — *I regret having told them*, *I resent being given so little notice* — but not productive progressive *be*. *I remember being working* is not an established construction; the progressive meaning is carried by the simple *-ing* form itself.

Past participles do two jobs in non-finite clauses. The perfect participle follows auxiliary *have* and can stack with progressive or passive *be*: *has seen*, *has been seeing*, *has been seen*. The passive participle heads a clause that takes no auxiliaries at all: *He had it checked by the manager*.
Auxiliaries in non-finite form-types
To-infinitival | to have finished | to be working | to be interviewed
Gerund-participial | having told | not productive | being given
Past-participial (perfect) | has seen | has been seeing | has been seen
Past-participial (passive) | no | no | checked by the manager
I expect to have finished soon. — Perfect have in a to-infinitival.
I expect to be working all weekend. — Progressive be in a to-infinitival.
I expect to be interviewed by the police. — Passive be in a to-infinitival.
I resent being given so little notice. — Passive be in a gerund-participial.

Most non-finite clauses say nothing about their subject. *Kim was glad to reach home*, *It has been a pleasure meeting you*, *Anyone living nearby will be evacuated* and *The sum spent on gambling was extraordinary* all leave the subject to context. That absence is normal, not a defect.

*Kim was glad to reach home* and *Anyone living nearby will be evacuated* both contain clauses without an overt subject. They are still clauses: a VP heads each one, and the missing subject is supplied by interpretation. The exception is the attributive VP inside an NP — *our rapidly approaching deadline*, *a poorly drafted report* — which allows far less structure.

*The letter isn’t legible enough for you to read* is missing the object of *read*, understood as *the letter*. *I don’t think they are worth spending much time on* is missing the complement of *on*, understood as *they*. Hollow clauses lack an internal element rather than a subject.
Kim was glad to reach home. — Subjectless infinitival; Kim is understood as the one reaching home.
Anyone living nearby will be evacuated. — Subjectless gerund-participial modifying anyone.
The letter isn’t legible enough for you to read. — Hollow infinitival; the object of read is the letter.
They are worth spending much time on. — Hollow infinitival; the complement of on is they.

Watch what happens when one verb takes another as its complement: *I wanted to arrange for Kim to do it*, *She intends to try to persuade him to help her redecorate*. The verbs stack, each heading its own layer, and the stack can keep growing. That stacking is the catenative construction.

In the simple pattern no NP comes between the verbs. *I hope to finish soon*, *I helped wash up*, *I stopped worrying about it* and *I got arrested* all attach the non-finite complement directly to the matrix verb.

*She wants a holiday* and *She wants to leave* look like the same verb with different fillers, but the second complement is a clause, not an object. The test is the verb’s range: *want* takes both, and neither reduces to the other. That is the catenative relation.
I hope to finish soon. — Simple to-infinitival catenative.
I helped wash up. — Simple bare infinitival catenative.
I stopped worrying about it. — Simple gerund-participial catenative.
I got arrested. — Simple past-participial catenative.

Add an NP between the verbs and the construction becomes complex. *I advised you to sell it* and *I made them apologise* both have an intervening NP, and that NP may lean semantically towards the matrix verb or towards the subordinate one. Which way it leans changes the reading.

The plain-complex pattern leaves the NP bare: *I persuaded Liz to go*, *I intended Liz to go*. The for-complex pattern introduces it with *for*: *I arranged for her to go by bus*. The oblique-complex pattern makes it the complement of a preposition: *I signalled to her to move off the road*.

Gerund-participial complexes show the same tension. *I caught him doing it* and *I resented him doing it* differ in where *him* belongs semantically, and *I saw him doing it* adds the perception verb’s own interpretive pattern. The surface shape is identical; the argument structure is not.
Complex catenative subtypes
Plain-complex | I persuaded Liz to go. | Bare NP
Plain-complex | I intended Liz to go. | Bare NP; semantically with go
For-complex | I arranged for her to go by bus. | Subject introduced by for
Oblique-complex | I signalled to her to move off. | Complement of to
Gerund complex | I caught him doing it. | Bare NP with gerund-participial
Perception complex | I saw him doing it. | Bare NP with perception verb
I persuaded Liz to go. — Plain-complex: Liz is object of persuaded and understood subject of go.
I intended Liz to go. — Plain-complex: Liz is semantically the one who goes.
I arranged for her to go by bus. — For-complex: for introduces the subject of the infinitival.
I signalled to her to move off the road. — Oblique-complex: her is the complement of to.

Why not call the non-finite complement an object? Because the same verb takes ordinary objects elsewhere without the two behaving alike. *She wants a holiday* has an object; *She wants to leave* has a clause. The clause has its own auxiliaries and its own internal structure, none of which an NP object brings.

Auxiliaries fit the same analysis. In *She may like it*, *may* takes the non-finite complement *like it*, which makes it a catenative verb. Treating auxiliaries this way — the catenative-auxiliary analysis — explains the layering in *may have been seen*, where each auxiliary heads its own layer.

The traditional gerund/participle distinction plays no role here. *Gerund-participle* names the form; *gerund-participial* names the clause type. The same form appears in progressive constructions and in non-finite complements, and one description covers both more economically than two.
She wants a holiday. — Object complement.
She wants to leave. — Catenative complement.
She may like it. — Modal auxiliary as a catenative verb.
She is working. — Progressive auxiliary with a gerund-participial complement.

Catenative verbs sort into three classes by where they occur. Class 1 is simple only: *hope*, *seem*, *stop*, *get*. Class 2 is both: *want*, *help*, *see*. Class 3 is complex only: *persuade*, *advise*, *arrange*.

*Hope* occurs only in the simple construction, *persuade* only in the complex one, and *want* in both. These are complement patterns, not semantic essences. A verb can shift class with its sense, and the classification describes what it licenses, not what kind of verb it is.

Form-type cuts across the classes. Some verbs take to-infinitivals, some gerund-participials, some bare infinitivals, and some take more than one with a difference. *Remember locking* looks back; *remember to lock* looks forward. *Stop smoking* and *stop to smoke* differ in how the complement relates to the matrix event.
I hope to finish. — Class 1: simple only.
I want to finish. — Class 2: simple; also I want you to finish.
I persuaded Liz to go. — Class 3: complex only.
I remember locking the door. — Gerund-participial complement with past orientation.
Remember to lock the door. — To-infinitival complement with future orientation.

The gap in *John is easy to please* is easy to miss. Nothing is missing from the subject position; what is missing is the object of *please*, and the sentence supplies John. Compare *They are worth spending time on*, where the complement of *on* is the gap and the matrix subject fills it. The gap is internal; the subject is not what is missing.

*John is easy to please* has no overt object of *please*; *The letter isn’t legible enough to read* has no overt object of *read*. A subjectless clause has no overt subject, while a hollow clause has no overt object or other internal dependent. The missing element can be an object, a prepositional complement or another internal dependent.

The pattern clusters around adjectives such as *easy*, *difficult*, *ready* and *worth*, and around *enough* and *too*. What fills the gap depends on the matrix subject or object, and the relation is not always a simple copy of an NP.
John is easy to please. — Missing object of please understood as John.
The letter isn’t legible enough to read. — Missing object of read understood as the letter.
They are worth spending much time on. — Missing complement of on understood as they.

*Kim wants to go* and *Kim persuaded Pat to go* both leave the goer unspoken, but they point to different people: Kim in the first, Pat in the second. *Kim seems to like them* adds a third relation, where Kim is the subject of *seems* and the liker at once.

When another expression supplies that subject, the relation is control. *Want* is a subject-control verb: the matrix subject controls. *Persuade* is object-control: the matrix object controls. *Promise* is subject control despite a prominent object — *Kim promised Pat to go* means Kim goes.

*Kim seems to like them* and *Kim wants to like them* look alike, but Kim has a different relation to each verb. In the first, Kim is the subject of *seems* and is not a semantic argument of *seem*; the paraphrase *It seems that Kim likes them* shows the split. In the second, Kim supplies the subject of *like*. Surface similarity hides the difference between sharing a subject and supplying one.

Some subjectless clauses take a generic subject instead: *To err is human*, *It is important to be careful*. Nobody in the matrix supplies the missing subject; people in general do. Context and the matrix predicate decide whether the subject is controlled, raised, arbitrary or recovered from discourse.

*To underestimate her would be foolish* shows an infinitival in subject position, and *I call that taking liberties* shows a gerund-participial clause as a predicative complement. Objects are open too: *I found talking to her quite helpful*. Non-finite clauses take the ordinary clause functions, not only the catenative one.

They extrapose as well. *It was natural to be worried* has an extraposed subject, and *I found it distressing to see her so ill* has an extraposed object. Dummy *it* holds the core position while the clause sits after the predicate.
So the catenative/non-catenative line is functional, not formal. The same clause can be a catenative complement with one verb and a subject or object with another. The matrix construction decides.
Non-finite complements in clause structure
Subject | To underestimate her would be foolish. | would be
Object | I found talking to her quite helpful. | found
Predicative complement | I call that taking liberties. | call
Extraposed subject | It was natural to be worried. | be
Extraposed object | I found it distressing to see her so ill. | found
Catenative complement | She hopes to hear from them. | hopes

Non-finite complements attach to more than verbs. Adjectives take them (*keen to regain control*), nouns take them (*the opportunity to have my say*), and prepositions take them (*in order to catch the train*). Some are licensed by the adjacent word, others indirectly by the larger matrix.

Interrogative and relative infinitivals extend the range: *I can’t decide whether to go*, *He doesn’t know how to placate her*, *funds with which to conduct a survey*, *a place to stay*. Non-finite syntax here meets interrogative or relative syntax.

Function depends on the governing construction, not on meaning alone. *She left at six to catch the train* has a purpose modifier in clause structure; *in order to catch the train* has a complement inside a PP. Both express purpose; they do not occupy the same slot.
She is keen to regain control. — Complement of the adjective keen.
I’ve missed the opportunity to have my say. — Complement of the noun opportunity.
She left in order to catch the train. — Complement in PP structure.
I can’t decide whether to go. — Interrogative to-infinitival complement.

*I’ve found a box to keep the tapes in* embeds an infinitival inside the NP; *She left at six to catch the early train* attaches one to the clause. Both modify rather than complement. Non-finite clauses can hang from a nominal or from a whole clause, and the two relations are not interchangeable.
*He’s a charlatan, to put it bluntly* adds a supplement. It comments on the clause or on the act of speaking rather than filling a slot, and it is prosodically detached — usually set off by a comma.

*She left at six to catch the early train* and *He’s a charlatan, to put it bluntly* both use a non-finite clause, but one modifies the event and the other comments on the act of speaking. The range of meanings is wider than finite content clauses allow in the same positions: purpose, result, condition, concession or comment. Syntax identifies the relation; semantics has to say which one.
I’ve found a box to keep the tapes in. — Infinitival modifier inside the NP.
She left at six to catch the early train. — Purpose modifier in clause structure.
He’s a charlatan, to put it bluntly. — Supplement commenting on the clause.

Some clauses have no verb at all: *With the windows open, the room stayed cool*, *Although tired, she kept working*, *The meeting over, everyone left*. The missing verb is understood, and the construction still has internal structure and a relation to the matrix.

*With the windows open* describes a circumstance; *The meeting over* gives a temporal relation. Neither contains a verb, which is why verbless clauses are not a fourth non-finite type: the three non-finite types are defined by verb form. A verbless clause usually contains a subject and a predicative complement or a PP.
*With the windows open* and *The meeting over* show how common the pattern is with *with* and *without* and in supplement-like absolutes.
With the windows open, the room stayed cool. — Verbless clause expressing circumstance.
Although tired, she kept working. — Verbless concessive clause.
The meeting over, everyone left. — Verbless absolute with a temporal relation.

*To leave*, *having left* and *left* show the three non-finite verb forms in action: infinitival, gerund-participial and past-participial. *For* and *to* mark subjects and infinitival status, and modals and supportive *do* are excluded from the non-finite system.

Non-finite clauses can be subjectless, hollow or catenative. Hollow clauses lack a non-subject element recovered from context; catenative constructions chain verbs through non-finite complements, either directly or across an intervening NP.

Beyond catenative use, non-finite clauses serve as subjects, objects, predicative complements, complements of adjectives, nouns and prepositions, modifiers and supplements. Verbless clauses form a separate construction, identified by the absence of a verb rather than by a verb inflection.

A non-finite checklist: Identify the verb form and the clause boundaries. Decide whether the clause is infinitival, gerund-participial or past-participial. Check for for and to, an overt or understood subject, and any missing non-subject element. Then identify its function in the matrix.

Take *She wanted to arrange for the committee to review the proposal before the deadline*. The matrix clause is *She wanted ...*; its catenative complement is *to arrange for the committee to review the proposal before the deadline*. The verb *arrange* then takes the for-complex complement *for the committee to review the proposal*.

Inside that complement, *for* introduces the subject *the committee* of the to-infinitival *to review the proposal*. The example contains a catenative chain of three verbs, a for-complex construction, and a subjectless infinitival inside the for-clause. Each layer has its own head and complement structure.

Find each verb and the non-finite clause it licenses. Identify the form-type: to-infinitival, bare infinitival, gerund-participial or past-participial. Check whether there is an overt subject, a for phrase, or an intervening NP.

Decide whether the construction is simple or complex catenative. In a simple construction the non-finite complement follows the matrix verb directly. In a complex construction an NP intervenes and may belong with either verb.

Then identify the clause’s function in the larger structure: catenative complement, subject, object, predicative complement, adjective/noun/PP complement, modifier or supplement. Check for hollow elements and for verbless clauses, which lack a verb altogether.

In *She wanted to arrange for the committee to review the proposal before the deadline*, *wanted* takes the to-infinitival complement *to arrange ...*. *Arrange* takes the for-complex complement *for the committee to review the proposal*. *For* introduces the subject of the infinitival, and *review* takes *the proposal* as object.

Non-finite clauses have three main form-types: infinitival, gerund-participial and past-participial. Infinitivals can be to or bare, and for introduces an overt subject. Modal auxiliaries and supportive do are excluded from non-finite clauses.

Catenative constructions chain verbs through non-finite complements. Hollow clauses lack a non-subject element, subjectless clauses lack an overt subject, and verbless clauses lack a verb. Non-finite clauses also function as ordinary subjects, objects, complements, modifiers and supplements.

key_terms.definition: A clause whose verb is infinitival or participial rather than a primary finite form.
A non-finite clause with a plain-form verb, either with to or bare.
An infinitival clause introduced by the subordinator to.
An infinitival clause with a plain-form verb and no to.
A non-finite clause headed by a gerund-participle in -ing.
A non-finite clause headed by a past participle.
A to-infinitival with an overt subject introduced by for.
A non-finite clause missing a non-subject element that is recovered from context.
A non-finite clause with no overt subject, interpreted from context.
A construction in which a verb takes a non-finite complement, often recursively.
A verb that licenses a catenative complement.
A non-finite complement that cannot be reduced to an object, predicative complement or PP complement.
A catenative construction with no intervening NP between the matrix and subordinate verbs.
A catenative construction with an intervening NP between the matrix and subordinate verbs.
A complex catenative construction with an intervening NP that is not introduced by a preposition.
A complex catenative construction in which for introduces the subject of the infinitival.
A complex catenative construction in which the intervening NP is the complement of a preposition.
A gerund-participial complement with a passive meaning, as in The house needs painting.
An intervening NP that is syntactically associated with the matrix verb but semantically associated with the subordinate verb.
A construction such as John is easy to please, with a hollow infinitival complement.
A non-finite or finite clause placed after dummy it in subject function.
A clause placed after dummy it in object function.
A complement ascribing a property to a predicand, which can be a non-finite clause.
An infinitival clause with interrogative type, as in whether to go.
An infinitival clause functioning as a relative modifier, as in a place to stay.
A clause with no verb, often functioning as an adjunct or supplement.
A verb phrase used before a noun that does not constitute a full non-finite clause.
The interpretation of an understood subject through another expression in the construction.

lessons.title: Coordination and supplementation

outcomes.text: Explain the main ideas in Coordination and supplementation.
Recognise the patterns in real sentences.
Use the ideas when you read and write.

lessons.reviewed_by: Owner-waived AI content check (2026-11-15); not human instructor sign-off

teaching.text: Say *Kim and Pat speak excellent French* and the subject is two people joined on equal footing, neither leaning on the other the way a modifier leans on its head. Try *The tourists — most of them exhausted — got into the bus* and a phrase sits beside the clause, describing the tourists without being part of its grammar. English extends clauses in these two quite different ways, and the contrast between them runs through the chapter.

The first half works through coordination: what a coordinate is, how coordinators attach, and how binary and multiple, marked and unmarked, single and repeated marking differ. Layering, scope, joint readings and gapping follow, along with the surprisingly wide range of things that can be coordinated. The second half turns to supplements — appositives, parentheticals, relative clauses, dislocations — and to what detachment buys a speaker.

One distinction is worth carrying from the start. Coordinates are equal yet integrated: they form a unit together, and the coordinator travels with the coordinate it introduces. Supplements are related to an anchor but not integrated, held in place by prosody and discourse rather than by dependency. Equality and attachment are separate questions, and keeping them apart prevents most of the usual confusions.

Say *Kim and Pat speak excellent French* and the subject is not one person but two, joined on equal terms. Neither name governs the other; remove either and a subject remains. Now try *He can see you this afternoon or on Tuesday*, where the alternatives are not even the same kind of phrase. English lets such things stand side by side, and the result belongs to neither category: it is an NP/PP-coordination, a construction in its own right.

Nothing inside it acts as a centre of gravity. *Kim’s father* is a phrase about the father, and the possessor merely locates him; *Kim and Pat* is not about either name in that way. That is what non-headed means, and it is why the pair cannot be filed as an NP with two heads. The whole is a coordination of NPs, and the category of the whole is the coordination itself.

Reverse the names and the structure survives: *Pat and Kim* is the same kind of subject. Either name can often stand for the pair, as when *Kim and Pat* gives way to *they*. Neither test is a law, though. *Kim and Pat are a happy couple* will not accept one name in place of the pair, because the couple is precisely what the predicate is about — a reminder that equal status does not mean interchangeable meaning.
Coordination and subordination
Headedness | Non-headed | Head plus dependent
Status of parts | Coordinates of equal status | Head and dependent
Category of whole | Coordination category | Category of the head
Typical markers | and, or, but | Subordinators, prepositions
Example | Kim and Pat | Kim’s father

Listen to where the coordinator sits. In *Kim and Pat* the natural break comes before *and*, not after it, and the same grouping shows up when the phrase moves: *And Pat* travels with its coordinator attached, while *Pat* is what remains once the linking material is stripped away. Hence the two labels. The expanded coordinate includes coordinator and modifiers; the bare coordinate is the core that is left.

Three observations point the same way. The second coordinate shifts position together with its coordinator; coordinators can open a sentence, as in *And so did her mother*; and the prosodic break falls before the coordinator rather than after it. Each is small on its own. Together they make it hard to treat *and* as a free-standing hinge between two equals.

Modifiers can expand a coordinate just as coordinators do. *He offended the guests and indeed his family too* dresses its second coordinate in *and*, *indeed* and *too*, so the unit set against *the guests* is larger than the noun phrase *his family* at its core. Equality of status survives the extra clothing: there are still two coordinates, and one of them simply wears more.
Kim and Pat — And Pat is the expanded second coordinate; Pat is the bare coordinate.
He offended the guests and indeed his family too. — The second coordinate is expanded by a coordinator and two modifiers.
And so did her mother. — Sentence-initial coordinator forms a unit with its coordinate.

Count the coordinates and a first contrast appears. *Kim wrote a letter and Ed watched TV* has two, one clause on each side of the coordinator. *She wants to live in Sydney, London, or Paris* has three, and with three a new question arises: which of them carry a coordinator in front? Binary coordination never has to answer it. Multiple coordination always does.

Marking is the next variable. *He invited all his colleagues and all his students* announces its join; drop the *and* and the same list still coordinates, silently. A multiple coordination with a coordinator before the final coordinate only is simple-syndetic; one marked before every coordinate after the first is polysyndetic. The difference is audible in *Sydney, London, or Paris* set against *Sydney or London or Paris*.

Paired markers add a further layer. *Both ... and* and *either ... or* signal from the first coordinate that a second is coming; the initial word is a determinative, while *and* or *or* does the coordinating. Within a single layer of multiple coordination the medial coordinates must then be treated alike — all bare or all marked. Mix the two treatments and the structure has to be layered, which is the puzzle of the next section.
Structural contrasts
Number | Binary: Kim and Pat | Multiple: Kim, Pat, and Alex
Marking | Syndetic: Kim and Pat | Asyndetic: Kim, Pat
Multiple marking | Simple-syndetic: Kim, Pat, or Alex | Polysyndetic: Kim or Pat or Alex
Initial marker | Non-correlative: Kim and Pat | Correlative: both Kim and Pat
Kim wrote a letter and Ed watched TV. — Binary syndetic coordination.
She wants to live in Sydney, London, or Paris. — Multiple simple-syndetic coordination.
She wants to live in Sydney or London or Paris. — Multiple polysyndetic coordination.
He invited both his father and his uncle. — Correlative coordination with both.

One coordination can sit inside another. *We should invite Kim and either Pat or Alex* invites Kim, then offers a choice between two others, so the *either ... or* pair is the second coordinate of a larger NP-coordination. Word order announces nothing. The brackets come from the sense.

*Egg and bacon or stew* can be read two ways, and the readings describe different dinners. Either the choice is between an egg-and-bacon dish and stew, or the choice is between egg and a bacon-or-stew dish. The words stay put; the structure shifts. Prosody and context tell a hearer which brackets to hear.

A single layer also demands consistency. *Kim, Tom and Pat, and your parents* leaves one medial coordinate bare and marks the other, so it cannot be a flat list of four; the comma before the last *and* signals a coordination nested inside a coordination. *Kim and Tom and Pat and your parents* can be either flat or layered, and punctuation or intonation decides which.
Layered structures
Kim and either Pat or Alex | Kim + (either Pat or Alex) | Choice within the second coordinate
Egg and bacon or stew | (egg and bacon) or stew | Choice between a pair and stew
Egg and bacon or stew | egg and (bacon or stew) | Choice within the second coordinate
Kim, Tom and Pat, and your parents | Layered | Medial marking forces layering
We should invite Kim and either Pat or Alex. — The lower either-or coordination is the second coordinate.
Egg and bacon or stew — Ambiguous between two scope relations.
Kim, Tom and Pat, and your parents — Inconsistent medial marking forces a layered analysis.

*I left the room and Pat followed me* joins two clauses, each with its own subject and predicate. *Kim and Pat speak excellent French* joins two names inside a single clause, which then supplies one predicate for both. Same coordinator, very different sizes of unit. Grammars keep the levels apart because the consequences differ.

At clause level each coordinate carries its own tense, subject and polarity. At subclausal level the coordinates share the clause’s remaining machinery, so agreement and scope have to be settled for the pair together. *Kim and Pat are a happy couple* shows how far that can go: the predicate does not apply to Kim and to Pat separately but to the two as a unit.

That last point opens a second distinction, between joint and distributed readings. *Kim and Pat are a happy couple* treats the pair as one entity; *Kim and Pat are tall* hands the property to each of them. The subject looks identical in both. The predicate chooses the reading.
I left the room and Pat followed me. — Clausal coordination.
Kim and Pat speak excellent French. — Subclausal NP-coordination; the predicate applies to both.
Kim and Pat are a happy couple. — Joint coordination: the pair is treated as one entity.

Reverse a coordination and the grammar usually shrugs. *Kim and Pat* and *Pat and Kim* are equally good subjects, one reason coordinations look so unlike head-dependent phrases. This time the shrug is not universal. *They got married and had a baby* does not say what *They had a baby and got married* says, although the same two events are named.

Order carries meaning whenever the relation between coordinates is temporal, causal or rhetorical. *He got up and had breakfast* narrates a sequence; swap the clauses and the morning changes. *Hurry up or we’ll be late* offers no free choice at all — it threatens a consequence. The coordinates remain equal in status while the relation between them is anything but symmetrical.

There is a processing side as well. Complex or heavy coordinates tend to land late, where a reader or hearer can absorb them, and a contrastive coordinate may be held back for prominence. Syntax permits the reversal; discourse decides whether it earns its keep.
Kim and Pat arrived. — Reversal is structurally and semantically neutral.
They got married and had a baby. — Temporal sequence is part of the interpretation.
Hurry up or we’ll be late. — Asymmetric consequence relation.

*And* joins, *or* divides — the schoolroom version, which logic sharpens: *and* needs both propositions true, *or* needs at least one. English then goes its own way. *He got up and had breakfast* is not a pair of independent facts but a sequence, and *Hurry up or we’ll be late* is a condition wearing the clothes of a choice.

Negation drags *and* and *or* into each other’s territory. De Morgan’s equivalences equate *not (A and B)* with *not A or not B*, and *not (A or B)* with *not A and not B*. Natural language adds a wrinkle: *not* can take scope over an entire coordination, so *He didn’t buy the report or the magazine* may deny both purchases or deny only the joint one, depending on how the coordination is bracketed.

One curious use of *and* builds meaning by repetition rather than conjunction. *Louder and louder*, *dozens and dozens*, *again and again* assert no pair of propositions; they convey increase, plurality or recurrence. The coordinator is doing aspectual work, and calling the result a simple conjunction misses what it is for.
He got up and had breakfast. — Asymmetric sequence.
Hurry up or we’ll be late. — Asymmetric consequence.
The sound grew louder and louder. — Coordinator-marked reduplication expressing gradual change.
He didn’t buy the report or the magazine. — Negation can scope over the coordination.

The paired markers come in fixed partnerships. *Both* looks ahead to *and*, *either* to *or*, *neither* to *nor*. In each pair the first word is a determinative announcing that another coordinate is on its way, and the coordinator arrives with the second coordinate to complete the job. Break the partnership — *both ... or*, *neither ... and* — and the sentence stumbles.

Negative pairing needs care. *Neither ... nor* is already negative, so *Neither Kim nor Pat came* needs no further *not*, and the pair can stand where clausal negation would otherwise go. *Nor* also works alone after a negative clause, continuing the negation as a connective: *He didn’t come, nor did she*.

Contrast and focus come from *but* and its relatives. *But* sets one coordinate against another or carves out an exception, as in *They allowed the others but not me*. *Not only* raises the first coordinate into prominence and usually calls for *but also* to finish the move: *She not only sings but also dances*, where the second coordinate, not the first, carries the surprise.
Both Kim and Pat agreed. — Both correlates with and.
Either Kim or Pat will attend. — Either correlates with or.
Neither Kim nor Pat attended. — Negative coordination with neither ... nor.
She not only sings but also dances. — Not only ... but also adds a focused coordinate.

Not every linker is a coordinator, and the comparison-based ones show why. *As well as*, *rather than*, *more than* and *less than* join material while keeping their comparative sense. *She plays the piano as well as the violin* adds a second accomplishment; *rather than* sets one option aside instead of merely adding another to it.

Addition and inclusion have a small family of their own: *including*, *instead of*, *plus*, *besides*, *along with*. Their behaviour is not uniform. Some take noun phrase complements, some prefer gerund-participials, and some behave like prepositions that happen to sit between two items. Calling them all coordinators would flatten real differences.

Connective adverbs are the clearest impostors. *So*, *yet*, *however* and *therefore* link clauses or sentences in discourse, but they form no coordination: they are supplements or connective adjuncts, and they can move. *For*, *only* and resultative *so ... that* have specialised linking jobs of their own, each distinct from what a coordinator does.
Linkers and their status
as well as | She plays piano as well as violin. | Comparison-based linker
rather than | They chose tea rather than coffee. | Alternative linker
including | Everyone, including Kim, agreed. | Inclusion preposition
plus | The rent plus bills is high. | Additive linker
however | However, nobody objected. | Connective adverb
for | He left, for he was tired. | Formal linking word

Coordination does not insist on matching categories. *He can see you this afternoon or on Tuesday* sets a noun phrase beside a prepositional phrase because both can say when. The result is an NP/PP-coordination, and what licenses it is the shared function, not a shared label.

The tolerance reaches further than one might expect. Grammaticised words coordinate when they share a role, as in *the before and after photographs* or *the up and down movement*; genitives coordinate in *Kim’s and Pat’s reports*; even clause types can be mismatched, as in *Come around six, or is that too early for you?*, where an imperative is followed by an interrogative.

Level matters throughout. The same string can be analysed as a coordination of words, phrases, clauses or whole sentences, and the choice changes what counts as agreeing, what falls within the scope of a modifier, and what the sentence commits its speaker to.
He can see you this afternoon or on Tuesday. — NP/PP-coordination with a shared adjunct function.
the before and after photographs — Coordination of grammaticised words.
Kim’s and Pat’s reports — Coordination of genitives.
Come around six, or is that too early for you? — Coordination of an imperative and a closed interrogative.

Some coordinations do not wear their structure on the surface. Expansion is the mildest case: a coordinate padded with modifiers, as in *The guests and indeed his family too*. Gapping cuts deeper. *Kim is an engineer and Pat a barrister* drops the verb from the second coordinate, and the missing *is* is recovered from the first: two predications, one verb.

Others coordinate sequences that are not phrases at all. *I gave $10 to Kim and $5 to Pat* pairs *$10 to Kim* with *$5 to Pat* — right-hand runs that never function as constituents elsewhere, hence the name right nonce-constituent coordination. Delayed right constituent coordination goes the other way, holding a shared phrase until both coordinates have passed: *I knew of but never mentioned my work*.

End-attachment coordination simply hangs the second coordinate on the end of the clause: *They had found Kim guilty, but not Pat*. What makes such patterns valuable is also what makes them tricky. A stretch of words that can be coordinated with a matching stretch is probably a constituent, so coordination probes clause structure; but nonce constituents show that the construction can also manufacture units for its own purposes.
Kim is an engineer and Pat a barrister. — Gapped coordination with the verb omitted from the second coordinate.
I gave $10 to Kim and $5 to Pat. — Right nonce-constituent coordination.
I knew of but never mentioned my work. — Delayed right constituent coordination.
They had found Kim guilty, but not Pat. — End-attachment coordination.

*The tourists — most of them exhausted — got into the bus.* The clause is complete without the interruption, yet the interruption is not noise: *most of them exhausted* describes the tourists, and the dashes mark it off as something said beside the clause rather than inside it. That detached constituent is a supplement, and *the tourists* is its anchor.

Integration separates a supplement from a dependent. A dependent belongs to its head’s syntax — *the exhausted tourists* cannot lose *exhausted* without losing part of the noun phrase. A supplement hangs on by discourse and prosody instead. It may elaborate, comment, evaluate, attribute or identify, but it does so from outside the dependency structure of the clause.

Supplements come in many shapes, from NPs and adjective phrases through PPs to finite and non-finite clauses. The noun phrase in *My friend, a doctor* identifies its anchor; an adverb may instead evaluate the clause, and a relative clause may add a comment without restricting it. What they share is the comma, the dash or the parenthesis — and the freedom to be lifted out.
Supplements and dependents
Integration | Detached | Integrated
Anchor | Related to an anchor | Licensed by a head
Prosody | Set off | Within the prosodic phrase
Typical forms | NP, AdjP, PP, clause | Varied by head
Example | The tourists – most exhausted – left. | The exhausted tourists left.

Function and form cross-cut in supplements. *My friend, a doctor, called* elaborates an anchor; *Fortunately, nobody was hurt* comments on a clause; *The report, according to Kim, was leaked* attributes a claim; *The report, which was leaked, caused a scandal* adds a relative clause. One detached position accommodates all four, and the punctuation carries much of the signal.

Appositives are the central case, because the supplement and its anchor name the same thing twice. *My friend, a doctor* characterises or identifies; either part could stand alone, and the comma tells the reader to take them together. Parentheticals comment rather than rename — *The plan, I think, will work* — while dislocations move an NP to the edge and leave a pronoun behind to hold its place: *Kim, I like her*.

It would be a mistake to file supplements as optional dependents. Optionality is not the issue; integration is. The same content can sit inside the clause or beside it, and the difference shows in syntax and in how the information is presented. *The exhausted tourists left* makes exhaustion part of who left; *The tourists, exhausted, left* offers it as an aside.
My friend, a doctor, called. — Appositive supplement identifying my friend.
Fortunately, nobody was hurt. — Evaluative supplement commenting on the clause.
The report, according to Kim, was leaked. — Attribution supplement.
The report, which was leaked, caused a scandal. — Supplementary relative clause.
Kim, I like her. — Dislocation with a resumptive pronoun.

Coordination has long served as a probe for constituent structure. If a stretch of words can be coordinated with a matching stretch, it behaves like a unit, and units are what clauses are built from. The probe is powerful, but it is not mechanical: nonce constituents and end-attachment show that coordination can also create units which do not exist independently.

Scope ambiguity is where the machinery gets interesting. *Long poems and essays* can mean long poems and long essays, or long poems together with essays of any length; *new and second-hand books* can describe books that are new or second-hand, or a collection composed of two kinds. The words are identical and the structures are not, so prosody, context and the predicate must decide.

Nonce constituents complicate the picture further. *I gave $10 to Kim and $5 to Pat* coordinates right-hand sequences that are not ordinary phrases; delayed right constituent coordination holds the shared phrase until after both coordinates, as in *I knew of but never mentioned my work*; end-attachment adds the second coordinate at the end, as in *They had found Kim guilty, but not Pat*.

The analyst therefore faces three questions rather than one. What are the coordinates? What material do they share? What scope does the coordination have? A sentence may be grammatical under more than one answer, and the work lies in seeing which answers the evidence actually supports.

*Kim, I like her.* The name sits outside the clause, and the pronoun inside does the grammatical work. Move the name to the other end and the mirror image appears: *I like her, Kim*. In the first, left dislocation, the NP opens the utterance; in the second, right dislocation, it arrives after the clause as an afterthought or clarification.

Parentheticals are close relatives with a different job. *The plan, I think, will work* and *The report, according to Kim, was leaked* interrupt or follow the clause in order to comment on it, hedge it or attribute it. They carry modal, evidential or attributive meaning, and they are not dependents of the verb.

What unites the two is detachment. Dislocation leaves a pronoun to fill the gap; parentheticals leave the clause intact and add a voice beside it. In both cases the relation to the anchor runs through discourse and prosody rather than through head-dependent syntax.

Take *Kim, I like her*: *Kim* is not the object of *like*; *her* is, and the verb takes its object from the pronoun. *The plan, I think, will work* is different: *I think* comments on the clause without making *I* the subject of *work*. Each piece keeps its own structure.

Two coordinates, no head, equal status: that is the shape coordination keeps. The coordinates may be two or many, marked or unmarked, linked by a single final coordinator or by one before every coordinate after the first, plain or paired with a correlative. The coordinator travels with the coordinate that follows it, and a coordinate may be bare or dressed up with modifiers.

The structures can nest. Coordinations layer inside one another, join clauses or smaller units, take joint or distributed readings, and survive gapping and the other non-basic patterns. Categories need not match so long as functions do. *And* and *or* carry logical and asymmetric senses; *both/either*, *neither/nor*, *but*, *not only* and the comparison-based linkers extend the inventory.

Supplementation works from the other direction. A supplement is detached from its anchor — an appositive, a parenthetical, a relative clause, an evaluation or a dislocation — and relates to it through discourse and prosody. Coordination integrates equals; supplementation leaves a companion standing beside the clause.

A coordination checklist: Identify the coordinates and the coordinator. Decide whether the coordination is binary or multiple, syndetic or asyndetic. Check for layering, gapping or nonce constituents. Then ask whether the relation is clausal or subclausal, joint or distributed, and whether a supplement rather than a coordination is involved.

Take *The guests and indeed most of the family stayed late, but the band had already packed up*. The first coordination is *The guests and indeed most of the family*, an NP-coordination functioning as subject. The second coordinate is expanded by *indeed*, and the whole coordination is joined by *but* to the clause *the band had already packed up*.

The example contains both subclausal and clausal coordination: the NP-coordination is the subject of the first clause, and the two clauses are coordinated by *but*. The coordinator belongs with the following coordinate in each case, and the second coordinate of the subject is expanded by a modifier.

Identify the coordinates and the coordinator. Check whether the coordination is binary or multiple, syndetic or asyndetic. If multiple, decide whether it is simple-syndetic or polysyndetic, and check for correlative markers.

Look for layering, gapping, nonce constituents and end-attachment. Then decide whether the coordination is clausal or subclausal, joint or distributed. The same sequence may have more than one structure, so use prosody and meaning to resolve the ambiguity.

For supplementation, identify the anchor and the supplement. Check whether the supplement is an appositive, parenthetical, relative clause, evaluation or dislocation. Supplements are detached, so do not analyse them as ordinary dependents.

In *The guests and indeed most of the family stayed late, but the band had already packed up*, the subject is an NP-coordination of *the guests* and *indeed most of the family*. *But* coordinates that clause with *the band had already packed up*. The second subject coordinate is expanded by *indeed*.

Coordination is non-headed and joins equal coordinates. It can be binary or multiple, syndetic or asyndetic, simple-syndetic or polysyndetic, correlative or non-correlative. Coordinators belong with the following coordinate, and coordinates can be bare or expanded.

Layering, gapping and nonce constituents show that coordination can be structurally complex. Supplementation relates a detached expression to an anchor and includes appositives, parentheticals, relative clauses and dislocations.

teaching.text: Put *Kim wrote the letter* beside *The letter was written by Kim* and nothing in the world has changed: same letter, same writer, same event. What has changed is where the attention falls and which participant gets to be subject. English keeps a whole repertoire of such moves — preposing, postposing, inversion, existentials, extraposition, dislocation, clefts and the passive — and this chapter works through them.

The repertoire divides roughly in two. Some constructions shuffle the order of elements; others realign the grammatical functions, so that an object becomes a subject or a clause steps out of the subject position. Running alongside that division is a set of information concepts — old and new, focus and presupposition — that explain why a speaker would bother to shuffle anything at all.

One caution runs throughout. Packaging generally leaves truth conditions and illocutionary force alone, but not always: move a quantifier across a negation and the clause can change what it claims. Nor does every non-canonical version have a comfortable basic counterpart. This is a family of related constructions, not a single transformation applied over and over.

Start with two ways of saying one thing. *Kim wrote the letter* and *The letter was written by Kim* report the same event, but the first puts Kim in the subject slot and the second puts the letter there. Set *Two doctors were on the plane* beside *There were two doctors on the plane* and the difference is more than order: a dummy *there* has appeared, and the phrase that would have been subject now follows the verb.

The inventory is longer than those two examples suggest. Preposing fronts a complement, postposing holds a heavy constituent back, and subject-dependent inversion puts a dependent first. Existentials, extraposition, left and right dislocation, clefts and the passive each add a twist of their own. The table below sets out each construction with its basic counterpart.

A rough division helps. Preposing, postposing and inversion mostly rearrange what is already there. Existential, extraposition, dislocation, cleft and passive add structure or change which participant occupies which function. The line is one of degree rather than a wall: an inversion that introduces a new entity is doing presentational work, and a passive that merely moves the object leftward still reshuffles functions.
Packaging constructions and their basic counterparts
Preposing | This one she accepted. | She accepted this one.
Postposing | I made without delay all the changes you wanted. | I made all the changes you wanted without delay.
Inversion | On board were two nurses. | Two nurses were on board.
Existential | There is a frog in the pool. | A frog is in the pool.
Extraposition | It is clear that he’s guilty. | That he’s guilty is clear.
Cleft | It was you who broke it. | You broke it.
Passive | The car was taken by Kim. | Kim took the car.

*This one she accepted* has the same subject and the same object as *She accepted this one*; only the object has moved forward, and every grammatical function stays where it was. That is reordering. Subject-dependent inversion works the same way on the subject and a dependent of the verb, which is why both patterns feel like rearrangements rather than rebuildings.

Passivise a clause and something more drastic happens than a change of order: the active object takes over the subject function while the active subject retreats into a *by* phrase or disappears. Form an existential and the basic subject becomes a displaced subject after the verb while dummy *there* occupies the subject slot. The participants are the same; their grammatical jobs are not.

The usual claim is that packaging preserves truth conditions and illocutionary force. *Many MPs weren’t in the House* and *There weren’t many MPs in the House* are the exception that keeps the claim honest. The first says that many members were absent; the second says that the number present was small. A quantifier has changed places with a negation, and the scope has changed with it.
Kim wrote the letter. / The letter was written by Kim. — Passive realigns subject and object.
This one she accepted. — Preposing changes order.
There were two doctors on the plane. — Existential adds dummy there and displaces the subject.
Many MPs weren’t in the House. — Many has scope over negation: many were absent.

*Two letters arrived for Jill; she will pick them up.* The phrase *two letters* is discourse-new, introduced for the first time; by the second clause it has become old, already on the table, and *them* points back to it. That is discourse status: not a property of the words themselves but of where they sit in the conversation.

Addressee familiarity is a different measure. *The President is giving the State of the Union address* can treat *the President* as known even in a conversation that has never mentioned him, because shared national knowledge supplies the referent. Discourse-old and addressee-old usually coincide, but they are not the same test.

Focus is where the informational weight lands. Say *Mary bought RICE yesterday* and the remainder — *Mary bought x yesterday* — becomes the frame against which *rice* stands out. That frame is the focus-frame; the presupposition is what the sentence takes for granted. Different packaging constructions offer different partitions of the same content, which is the whole reason for choosing among them.
Information status
Discourse-old | Has it been introduced or inferred? | them after two letters
Discourse-new | Is it being introduced now? | two letters
Addressee-old | Does the addressee already know it? | the President
Focus | What is most prominent? | RICE
Presupposition | What is taken for granted? | Mary bought something

*This one she accepted.* The object has left its post-verbal home and turned up in front, and the clause still parses because the missing object is understood. Preposing is no mechanical movement rule, though. The fronted phrase does work — linking back, setting a topic, carrying a contrast — and the rest of the clause comments on it.

When the preposed element is not the focus, it usually serves as a link or a frame. *That money I gave her, it must have disappeared* opens with a phrase the hearer can locate, and the clause then says something about it. Topic preposing of this kind keeps the sentence tied to what has already been said.

Focus preposing puts the weight at the front. *THAT I can believe* works when *that* is the point of contention, and the stress tells the hearer so. Proposition assessment preposing evaluates rather than topicalises: *That she was right I never doubted* passes a verdict on a whole proposition. One syntactic position serves several discourse jobs, and intonation and context sort them out.
This one she accepted. — Object preposed as a topic.
That I can believe. — Focus preposing with contrastive stress.
That she was right I never doubted. — Proposition assessment preposing.

*I made without delay all the changes you wanted* saves its longest phrase for the end and drops a short adjunct into the middle. The object has not changed function; it has simply been held back. The motive is processing: a heavy phrase is easier to unpack when nothing has to follow it.

Subjects get postponed too. *There arrived a letter from the bank* leaves the subject after the verb, and the effect is presentational — the letter arrives into the discourse as news. Postposed material is usually newer or heavier than what precedes it, which is another way of saying that the end of the clause is where the informative payload tends to land.

Postposing is not extraposition, though the two are easily confused. Extraposition installs dummy *it* or *there* and moves a clause or NP into a later slot; postposing leaves the original function in place and changes only the order. The difference shows when you try to undo them: remove the dummy and extraposition collapses, while a postposed constituent can usually go home.
I made without delay all the changes you wanted. — Heavy object postponed to the end.
There arrived a letter from the bank. — Subject postponed after the verb.
She gave a brilliant performance last night. — The object is in its default position; the adjunct follows.

*On board were two nurses.* The phrase that would normally follow the verb comes first, the subject follows the verb, and no auxiliary is involved. That last point separates this construction from the inversion that forms questions. Here the verb is a full lexical verb, often *be*, *stand*, *sit*, *lie*, *come* or *go*, and the preposed element is a dependent of that verb.

The pattern is choosy about context. The fronted dependent usually links to what has just been said or sets a scene, and the subject that follows is usually new. *On the stool was a large parcel* sits comfortably after *I walked into the kitchen*; *On an overcoat was a large parcel* does not, because nothing has prepared the hearer for an overcoat as a location.

Inversion of this kind often introduces an entity, which makes it a close relative of the presentational constructions. The verb can be semantically thin — *be* does little beyond holding the position — while the preposed phrase carries the scene and the postposed subject carries the news.
On board were two nurses. — Locative dependent preposed; subject postponed.
In the corner stood a small table. — Scene-setting inversion with stand.
On the stool was a large parcel. — Natural after mention of the kitchen and stool.
On an overcoat was a large parcel. — Infelicitous because the relation to the prior scene is not salient.

*There is a frog in the pool.* Nothing is being pointed at; the clause simply announces that a frog exists in a place. Dummy *there* fills the subject position, *a frog* follows the verb as displaced subject, and the basic counterpart would be *A frog is in the pool*. The existential lets English introduce something without pretending it is the topic.

The construction is constrained on both sides. The displaced subject is normally indefinite or quantificational, and a definite NP resists the slot unless context grants it a special reading. In formal standard English, agreement follows the displaced subject: *There are two frogs*, *There is a frog*.

Presentational clauses with *here* and *there* are cousins rather than twins. *Here comes the bus* and *There goes the last train* introduce an entity or an event, and they use inversion rather than a dummy subject. The deictic word ties the presentation to the speech situation: *here* towards the speaker, *there* away from the speaker or towards a salient spot.
There is a frog in the pool. — Existential with dummy there and displaced subject a frog.
There are two frogs in the pool. — Agreement with the displaced subject.
Here comes the bus. — Presentational construction with deictic here.
There goes the last train. — Presentational construction with there.

*It is clear that he’s guilty.* The clause carrying the content sits at the end, and a dummy *it* holds the subject position it has vacated. Reverse the operation and you get *That he’s guilty is clear* — grammatical, but heavier, and the weight is exactly why speakers extrapose.

The moved material need not be finite. *It was natural to be worried* and *It would help to close the valve* extrapose infinitival clauses, and the pattern reaches objects as well: *I found it distressing to see her so ill*. In each case the extraposed element is semantically the subject or object while the dummy occupies the syntactic slot.

Extraposition is favoured when the clause is long and the predicate short: the heavy material goes to the end, where end weight wants it anyway. It also combines with other packaging, as when *It was assumed by everyone that Jill would win* wraps extraposition inside a passive. What it is not is a simple movement, because the dummy *it* is added along the way.
It is clear that he’s guilty. — Extraposed subject.
It was natural to be worried. — Infinitival extraposed subject.
I found it distressing to see her so ill. — Extraposed object.
It was assumed by everyone that Jill would win. — Passive plus extraposition.

*That money I gave her, it must have disappeared.* The phrase at the front is picked up again inside the clause by a pronoun, and the clause would be grammatical without the phrase. Move it to the other end and you get *They’re still here, the people from next door* — the mirror image, with the NP trailing after the clause. Put the phrase first and you have left dislocation; put it last and you have right dislocation.

The pronoun is not decoration. In the left-dislocation example, *it* is the subject of *must have disappeared*, and *that money* is the anchor the pronoun points back to. In the right-dislocation example, *they* is the subject and the trailing NP tells the hearer who *they* are. Take the pronoun away and the construction falls apart.

Dislocation is packaging in the plainest sense: it foregrounds or backgrounds an NP without making it a constituent of the clause. Left dislocation tends to set a topic; right dislocation tends to clarify or remind. Both belong to speech more than to formal writing, and both can nest inside other packaging constructions.
That money I gave her, it must have disappeared. — Left dislocation with resumptive it.
They’re still here, the people from next door. — Right dislocation with resumptive they.
Kim, I like her. — Left dislocation in a simple clause.

*It was Kim who broke it.* The clause splits in two: a foregrounded phrase after *it was*, and a relative clause carrying the background. The basic counterpart, *Kim broke it*, asserts the same thing, but the cleft divides the labour — Kim as focus, the breaking as presupposition.

Pseudo-clefts reverse the arrangement with a fused relative. *What helped was closing the valve* makes *what helped* the subject and *closing the valve* the identifying complement; the reverse pseudo-cleft, *Closing the valve was what helped*, puts the fused relative after *be*. The content is stable, but the information structure is not.

Presupposition is where clefts earn their keep. An it-cleft with an old presupposition treats the background as already established and spotlights the focus; one with a new presupposition introduces the background too. Pseudo-clefts often present the value as new and the variable as given. Choosing among these shapes is choosing how much the hearer is assumed to know.
Cleft constructions
It-cleft | It was Kim who broke it. | Kim
Pseudo-cleft | What helped was closing the valve. | closing the valve
Reverse pseudo-cleft | Closing the valve was what helped. | closing the valve
It-cleft with new presupposition | It was Kim who broke it, not Pat. | Kim, with background introduced

*Kim took the car* becomes *The car was taken by Kim*: the object climbs into the subject position, the subject drops into a *by* phrase, and the verb takes *be* plus a past participle. Leave the *by* phrase out and you have the short passive, much the commoner form in real text.

The *by* phrase sits outside the passive verb phrase, which is why it can be dropped without breaking anything. The construction does not stop at ordinary transitive objects. Prepositional passives promote the object of a preposition — *The bed was slept in* — and ditransitives let either object take the subject role: *Pat was given the key* beside *The key was given to Pat*.

Not every passive is the same passive. *The vase was broken deliberately* describes an event and takes an agent-oriented adverb comfortably; *The vase looked broken* describes a state and behaves like an adjective. *Get*-passives add a third flavour by using *get* in place of *be*: *He got arrested* often suggests an event that befalls its subject, sometimes with an adversative edge.
The car was taken by Kim. — Long passive with by phrase.
The car was taken. — Short passive without by phrase.
The bed was slept in. — Prepositional passive.
He got arrested. — Get-passive.

*The door was very opened* is odd in a way that *The door was wide open* is not, and the oddness is a clue. Degree modifiers like *very* attach to adjectives, so a passive that tolerates them is behaving adjectivally. *The vase was broken* can go either way, and the company it keeps — a *by* phrase, *deliberately*, a degree word — tells you which reading is intended.

*Get*-passives belong mostly to informal English and typically report an event that changes the subject’s situation: *He got arrested*, *She got promoted*. They can sound adversative, and they suggest that something happened to someone rather than that someone did something. They are not freely interchangeable with *be*-passives.

Why choose a passive at all? Because it lets the speaker put the affected participant first and leave the agent out or push it to the end. That is useful when the agent is unknown, unimportant or already recoverable, and when the patient is what the discourse is about. End weight and the flow of given and new information pull in the same direction.
The vase was broken deliberately. — Verbal passive: an event with an agent.
The vase looked broken. — Adjectival passive: a state.
He got promoted. — Get-passive with a change of state.
The report was leaked. — Agent omitted because unknown or unimportant.

*Here comes the bus.* The deictic word points, the verb of motion follows, and the subject arrives last — the opposite of ordinary declarative order. That shape is what makes the clause presentational: it does not so much describe a state of affairs as announce something into the scene.

The deictic element does the anchoring. *Here* points towards the speaker and *there* away from the speaker or towards a salient location, and the verb is usually one of motion, existence or appearance. The postposed NP is typically new, which is why the construction suits arrivals, discoveries and announcements.

Presentational clauses are not existentials, though the two are easy to confuse. The existential puts dummy *there* in the subject position and a displaced subject after the verb; the presentational clause uses a deictic adverb and a postposed subject. *There is a bus coming* is existential; *Here comes the bus* is presentational, and the difference is audible in the first word.
Here comes the bus. — Deictic here with a postposed subject.
There goes the last train. — Deictic there with a postposed subject.
Here is your coffee. — Presentational here with be.
There is a bus coming. — Existential, not the same construction.

*It was Kim who broke it* divides a proposition into a focus and a background, and the background arrives as a presupposition: someone broke it is taken for granted, and Kim is asserted as the someone. Whether that background is old or new in the conversation changes what the cleft accomplishes.

When the presupposition is old, the cleft is little more than a spotlight. Say *It was KIM who broke it* after the window has already been discussed, and the only new information is the identity. When the presupposition is new, the cleft must establish the background and the focus at once: *It was Kim who broke it, not Pat* can introduce the event and the contrast together.

Pseudo-clefts often run the information the other way. *What helped was closing the valve* puts the value last, as new, and treats *what helped* as the given variable. The reverse pseudo-cleft, *Closing the valve was what helped*, can shift the emphasis back to the variable, which is useful when the hearer knows what was done but not why it mattered.
It was KIM who broke it. — Focus on Kim; the breaking is presupposed.
It was Kim who broke it, not Pat. — Contrastive focus with the background introduced.
What helped was closing the valve. — Pseudo-cleft with the value as complement.
Closing the valve was what helped. — Reverse pseudo-cleft.

Packaging constructions can stack when their requirements do not conflict. *Some of them she found offensive, my mother* preposes an object and then adds a right-dislocated NP; *It was assumed by everyone that Jill would win* wraps extraposition inside a passive. Each layer does its own work, and the result is still a single clause.

Other combinations fail, and the failures are informative. Existential formation needs a non-clausal displaced subject, while subject extraposition needs a clause in the subject position; put the two requirements together and nothing can satisfy both. *There is that he is guilty clear* is not so much a bad sentence as an impossible assembly.

Combination is therefore a probe in its own right. *Kim it was who had been interviewed by the police* stacks passive, cleft and preposing: the passive realigns the functions, the cleft foregrounds Kim, and the preposing moves her to the front. The order in which the layers apply shapes the final sentence, which is why some orders work and others collapse.
Some of them she found offensive, my mother. — Preposing plus right dislocation.
It was assumed by everyone that Jill would win. — Passive plus extraposition.
Kim it was who had been interviewed by the police. — Passive plus cleft plus preposing.

The family is familiar by now: preposing, postposing, subject-dependent inversion, existential, extraposition, dislocation, cleft and passive. Some reorder, others realign, and most preserve truth conditions and illocutionary force.

Discourse status drives the choices. Old and new information, addressee familiarity, focus and presupposition explain why a speaker fronts a phrase, holds one back, introduces an entity with *there*, or splits a clause into focus and background. End weight and the flow of the surrounding text do the rest.

The passive earns its prominence: it realigns subject and object, comes in verbal, adjectival and *get* varieties, and is chosen for topicality, agent recoverability, weight and register. Constructions combine where their structures allow it, and the places where they refuse to combine are as revealing as the places where they do.

A packaging checklist: Identify the basic counterpart. Decide whether the construction changes order or realigns functions. Check what is old or new, what is focused, and what is presupposed. Then ask whether the difference affects truth conditions, and whether the construction can combine with another packaging type.

Take *It was the committee’s decision that surprised everyone, but the report itself was never published*. The first clause is an it-cleft: *the committee’s decision* is foregrounded, and *that surprised everyone* is the backgrounded relative clause. The second clause is a passive: *the report itself* is subject, and the agent is omitted.

The example combines cleft and passive packaging. The cleft presents the decision as the focus and presupposes that something surprised everyone. The passive presents the report as topic and backgrounds the publisher. Both constructions reorganise information without changing the basic events.

Find the basic counterpart and compare it with the packaged version. Decide whether the difference is primarily order or alignment of functions. Then identify what is old, new, focused and presupposed.

For preposing, inversion and postposing, check the discourse link and end weight. For existentials and presentationals, identify the displaced subject. For extraposition and clefts, identify the dummy element and the clause function.

For passives, identify the active subject and object, the by phrase, and whether the passive is verbal, adjectival or get. Then ask why the writer chose that packaging: topic, agent recoverability, end weight, register or discourse flow.

In *It was the committee’s decision that surprised everyone, but the report itself was never published*, the first clause is an it-cleft focusing *the committee’s decision*; the second is a short passive with *the report itself* as subject and the agent omitted.

Information packaging includes reordering constructions and realignment constructions. It is shaped by discourse familiarity, focus, presupposition and end weight. Truth conditions are usually preserved, but quantifier scope can differ.

Preposing, postposing, inversion, existentials, extraposition, dislocation, clefts and passives each reorganise the clause in a distinct way. The passive is a central realignment construction with verbal, adjectival and get variants.

key_terms.definition: The organisation of a clause’s content for discourse, often by non-canonical syntax.
The syntactically more basic version of an information-packaging construction.
Placement of a complement in front of the nucleus clause, as in This one she accepted.
Placement of a constituent later than its default position, often for weight or focus.
Inversion of the subject with a dependent of the verb, as in On board were two nurses.
A construction with dummy there and a displaced subject, as in There is a frog in the pool.
The NP that follows the verb in an existential construction and corresponds to the basic subject.
A construction introducing an entity into the discourse, often with here/there + verb + NP.
Placement of a clause after dummy it rather than in its default subject or object position.
Placement of an NP at the left edge with a resumptive pronoun in the clause.
Placement of an NP at the right edge after a resumptive pronoun.
A pronoun in the clause that corresponds to a dislocated NP.
A cleft construction with foregrounded complement after it was and a relative clause, as in It was Kim who called.
A specifying construction with a fused relative, as in What helped was closing the valve.
A pseudo-cleft with the fused relative after be, as in Closing the valve was what helped.
A construction in which the object of the active becomes subject and the verb is be + past participle.
The optional PP in a passive that expresses the internalised agent.
A passive-like form functioning as an adjective, often describing a state.
A passive formed with get rather than be, often with an event or adversative nuance.
Information already introduced or inferable from the prior discourse.
Information not yet introduced or inferable from the prior discourse.
Information the speaker assumes the addressee already knows.
The constituent bearing the main informational prominence in a clause.
The open proposition left when the focus is replaced by a variable.
A proposition treated as already assumed in an utterance.
A packaging difference that mainly changes linear order, as in preposing and inversion.
A packaging difference that changes the alignment of semantic roles and syntactic functions.
The tendency to place heavier or more complex constituents later in the clause.
