lessons.title: Deixis and anaphora

outcomes.text: Explain the main ideas in Deixis and anaphora.
Recognise the patterns in real sentences.
Use the ideas when you read and write.

lessons.reviewed_by: Owner-waived AI content check (2026-11-15); not human instructor sign-off

teaching.text: Stand in a cluttered room and say *Put this with those boxes over there*. Every italicised word asks the listener to look outward: *this* and *those* divide the space by distance from the speaker, while *there* points beyond immediate reach. Quote the same sentence in an email and the instructions lose their targets. That dependence on who is speaking, where and when is deixis. A pronoun such as *they* can instead send the listener back to an earlier phrase, and that backward dependence is anaphora. The two relations often meet in a single form.

The chapter begins with that contrast, then follows it through personal pronouns, reflexives, reciprocals and demonstratives. Reduced noun phrases and verb phrases come next, including *one*, *do so* and *so*, together with ellipsis and gapping. The closing sections turn to spatial and temporal deixis, and to what happens when the deictic centre shifts from speaker to addressee or to a reported participant.

The question to keep asking is where an interpretation comes from: from the utterance situation, from an earlier expression, or from material omitted but recoverable. The interesting cases draw on more than one source.

*Could you pick this up and put it with those boxes?* The request works only if you know who is being addressed, which object *this* picks out, and which boxes *those* marks as relatively distant. Person, place and time all enter the interpretation. When reference depends on such features of the utterance-act, the expression is deictic.

Deictic expressions change referent from utterance to utterance, but they do so systematically: the first person pronoun belongs to whoever is speaking, a place adverb such as *here* names a region containing the speaker, and *yesterday* picks out the day before the utterance. *I bought a new stereo yesterday* shows person and time working together in one short sentence. A proper name can vary in reference too, yet its meaning does not build in that relation to the utterance-act.

A deictic expression may contain a smaller deictic marker. The whole noun phrase *those boxes* is the expression, while *those* carries the meaning ‘relatively distant from the speaker’. *Last week* splits the same way: the phrase locates a span, and *last* supplies the orientation.
Types of deixis
Person | I, you, we, they | Speaker and addressee
Place | here, there, this, that | Location of utterance
Time | now, then, yesterday, tomorrow | Time of utterance
Discourse | this point, the following section | Position in the text
Social | you, sir, madam | Social relation and addressee

*Max claims he wasn’t told.* Who is *he*? The natural answer is Max, and that answer comes not from the situation but from an earlier expression in the same sentence. The pronoun is an anaphor, *Max* its antecedent, and the relation between them is anaphora.

The antecedent need not sit in the same clause, or even the same sentence. In *I’ve just been talking to Max. I understand that Ed has told Frank that the report has exonerated him*, the pronoun could point to Max, Ed or Frank. Grammar leaves the options open; context, emphasis and careful writing close them down. A reader who has to stop and ask who *him* is has met the cost of an unresolved chain.

Order matters. Put the pronoun after its antecedent — *When the headmaster saw the damage, he called the police* — and resolution is immediate. Put it first, as in *When he saw the damage, the headmaster called the police*, and the listener must hold a pronoun in mind until the noun arrives. The second pattern, anticipatory anaphora, is possible but more restricted.
Anaphora and related terms
Anaphor | he in Max claims he left | Interpreted through Max
Antecedent | Max in Max claims he left | Supplies the interpretation
Retrospective | Max left because he was tired. | Anaphor follows antecedent
Anticipatory | Because he was tired, Max left. | Anaphor precedes antecedent
Pro-form | so in I think so | Stands for a clause or proposition

Say *I’ll be there* and *I* picks out whoever is speaking; say *You left it there* and *you* picks out the addressee. These are the primary uses of the first and second person. The first person covers *I*, *me*, *my*, *mine*, *myself* and the plurals *we*, *us*, *our*, *ours*, *ourselves*; the second covers *you*, *your*, *yours*, *yourself* and *yourselves*. Everything else falls into the third person, the unmarked category.

Both persons stretch beyond their primary use. An authorial *we* may include the writer and exclude the reader, or invite the reader in; *We’re going to be late* can do either. *You* can mean people in general, as in *You can’t tell these days*. The examples below keep those secondary uses visible.

*She said, ‘I am tired’* keeps *I* with the original speaker; *She said she was tired* shifts the pronoun to the reporter’s perspective. Because first and second person are anchored to the utterance, they move when speech is reported. The deictic centre is not always the current speaker, and free indirect style exploits exactly that instability.
I bought a new stereo. — I refers to the speaker.
You can’t tell these days. — Generic you: people in general.
We’re going to be late. — We may include or exclude the addressee.
She said, ‘I am tired.’ — I refers to the original speaker in direct report.

*They say it will rain.* Who are they? No identifiable group need be involved. The pronoun is neither pointing to a situation nor picking up an antecedent; it is generic. Third person is the default category, and it can also be anaphoric, as in *Max left because he was tired*, or deictic, as in *He’s the one over there*. The form alone does not settle the relation.

*Max thinks he is clever* normally has *he* mean Max; *Max thinks his brother is clever* does not. Where an antecedent is available, the semantic link can be identity, inclusion or exclusion. *His* can include Max in the possessive relation, but the person said to be clever is the brother. Number and gender narrow the search, yet neither determines it.

*When he saw the damage, the headmaster called the police* is acceptable; pushing the pronoun deeper into embedded structure makes the sentence harder to process. Anticipatory anaphora is permitted under narrower conditions, especially when the pronoun sits in a subordinate clause and its antecedent in the matrix. Syntax, discourse structure and the type of pronoun all bear on the result.
Max left because he was tired. — Anaphoric he refers to Max.
He’s the one over there. — Deictic he refers to a person in the situation.
They say it will rain. — Generic they; no specific antecedent.
When he saw the damage, the headmaster called the police. — Anticipatory anaphora under restricted conditions.

English prefers to name a referent before pronominalising it. *When the headmaster saw the damage, he called the police* runs with that preference: the noun phrase arrives first, and *he* collects it. Reverse the two, as in *When he saw the damage, the headmaster called the police*, and the sentence still works, but the listener must wait for the noun to settle who *he* is.

*When he saw the damage, the headmaster called the police* is easy enough; bury the pronoun deeper and the sentence becomes harder to process. The reversed order is not free. Anticipatory anaphora is easiest when the pronoun is in a subordinate clause and the antecedent in the matrix. The type of antecedent matters too: a definite noun phrase in a prominent position is easier to anticipate than an indefinite one buried in a modifier.

Processing pressure explains part of the pattern. A retrospective pronoun resolves against material already heard; an anticipatory one creates a temporary gap that the rest of the sentence must fill. Writers exploit it when syntax narrows the possibilities sharply enough to make the delay safe.
When the headmaster saw the damage, he called the police. — Retrospective: he follows the headmaster.
When he saw the damage, the headmaster called the police. — Anticipatory: he precedes the headmaster.
Because she was tired, the manager went home. — Anticipatory anaphora in a subordinate clause.

*It’s raining.* What is *it*? Nothing in the situation answers the question, and no earlier phrase supplies a referent. Weather *it* is a subject without an entity behind it. The same form does refer in *I found the key and put it in my pocket*, where it picks up *the key*, and it can name an abstract situation in *It was a mistake*.

*It is clear that he’s guilty* gives *it* no referent of its own. The clause *that he’s guilty* is the extraposed subject, and *it* merely holds the subject slot until the clause arrives. Clefts use the same pronoun for a different job: *It was Kim who called* foregrounds Kim by splitting one proposition into two parts.
Anaphoric *it* needs an antecedent; weather *it* does not; dummy *it* has no referent at all and exists because the clause requires a subject. These uses are not interchangeable.
I found the key and put it in my pocket. — Anaphoric it refers to the key.
It’s raining. — Weather it.
It is clear that he’s guilty. — Dummy it with extraposed subject.
It was Kim who called. — Cleft it.

*She hurt herself* and *She hurt her* differ by more than emphasis. The reflexive points back to the subject of its own clause; the ordinary pronoun points elsewhere. English uses *myself*, *yourself*, *himself*, *herself*, *itself*, *ourselves*, *yourselves* and *themselves* for this local anaphora, typically in complement function.

The antecedent normally sits in the same local domain, often the same clause. *She hurt herself* satisfies that condition; *She said that I hurt herself* does not, because *herself* would need an antecedent within the embedded clause, and *I* cannot supply it. Noun phrases and dual-head constructions can be domains too, so proximity on the page does not decide the boundary.

Some reflexives appear where a plain pronoun would be expected. *They elected the president himself* and *The manager spoke to Kim and myself* add emphasis or mark a particular point of view; these are override reflexives. Emphatic reflexives form a related but distinct pattern, as in *She herself wrote the letter*, where the reflexive reinforces a noun phrase rather than filling a complement.
She hurt herself. — Basic reflexive with a local antecedent.
They blamed themselves. — Reflexive complement with plural antecedent.
She herself wrote the letter. — Emphatic reflexive.
The manager spoke to Kim and myself. — Override reflexive in a coordinated phrase.

*She hurt herself* is grammatical because the reflexive and its antecedent share a clause. *She said that I hurt herself* fails because *herself* looks for an antecedent inside the embedded clause, and the only candidate there is *I*. Binding is easiest to see in that contrast.

*The teacher spoke to the student about herself* can point to the teacher or the student, depending on context and structure. The antecedent is often the subject of the local domain, but not always. Syntax constrains the search without always producing one answer.

Override reflexives sit outside the basic pattern. They occur where a non-reflexive pronoun would be expected, as in *They elected the president himself* or *The manager spoke to Kim and myself*, and they usually add emphasis or signal a point of view. Emphatic reflexives such as *She herself wrote the letter* are a separate use, related by form rather than by complement structure.
She hurt herself. — Reflexive bound within the local clause.
She said that I hurt myself. — Myself is bound by I within the embedded clause.
They elected the president himself. — Override reflexive adding emphasis.
She herself wrote the letter. — Emphatic reflexive.

*They helped each other* describes a relation running in both directions: each member of the group helped and was helped. *Each other* and *one another* are the reciprocal pronouns, and both require a plural or group antecedent. The relation holds among members of that group, not between one antecedent and one anaphor.
Reciprocals occupy many of the positions reflexives do: object (*They distrust each other*), prepositional complement (*They spoke to each other*), and genitive (*They read each other’s work*).

*They followed each other* can describe a line in which each person follows the one ahead, not a pair who follow one another simultaneously. Mutuality is not always symmetrical. The predicate and the context decide whether the relation is pairwise, collective or sequential, which is why reciprocal meaning cannot be read off the pronoun alone.
They helped each other. — Pairwise mutual help.
The two theories support one another. — Mutual support between the theories.
They read each other’s work. — Reciprocal genitive.

Put two bowls on a table and say *This bowl holds more than that one*. The demonstratives divide the space around the speaker: *this* is relatively close, *that* relatively distant. The same forms also point backward in discourse. *He wants $30, but that’s too much* uses *that* for the price just mentioned, not for an object in the room.

*This report* uses a demonstrative as a determiner; *This is important* uses one as a pronoun. *These* and *those* agree with plural nouns, and the deictic meaning can be spatial, temporal or discourse-based.

Even anaphoric demonstratives keep a trace of that spatial meaning. *That* can suggest distance from the speaker’s current focus; *this* can suggest closeness. Grammar does not dictate the choice. It tells the reader how the speaker is positioning the referent, and that positioning is part of the meaning.
This bowl holds more than that one. — Spatial deixis: near versus far.
He wants $30, but that’s too much. — Anaphoric that refers to the price.
These reports are ready. — Plural determiner use.
This is important. — Pronoun use.

*I need a pen; do you have one?* The second *one* does not introduce a new pen; it stands for the kind of thing already mentioned. This is the pro-nominal use of *one*, an anaphoric device that often appears in fused-head constructions such as *the red one* or *a good one*. *One* can also be a numeral or a generic pronoun, so the construction has to be identified before the meaning is fixed.

*Other* has a similar double life. In *I’ll take this one and you take the other*, it is pro-nominal and depends on an antecedent set; in *Other people disagreed*, it is a determinative modifying a noun. The pro-nominal use typically contrasts one member or subset with another.

*The rich* packs two functions into one form; *I’ll take the red one* leaves a gap for context to fill. Fused heads and ellipsis are related but not identical. In a fused head, one expression performs the head function together with a dependent function. In ellipsis, material is left out but recovered.
I need a pen; do you have one? — Pro-nominal one stands for a pen.
I’ll take this one and you take the other. — One and other are pro-nominal.
The rich are not always happy. — Fused modifier-head NP.
I’ll take the red one. — One is a pro-nominal; red modifies it.

A stranded auxiliary can carry a whole predicate. Ask *Can you finish by Friday?* and the answer *I could* means *I could finish by Friday*. The auxiliary remains, the rest of the verb phrase disappears, and the context supplies what is missing. *She has* and *They won’t* work the same way.

*She left and I did so too* lets *did so* carry the earlier verb phrase. *Do it* and *do that* contain a pronoun object and usually point to a specific action, as in *I’ll do it tomorrow*. The forms look similar, but they differ in what they can replace and in how specific their reference is.

*I think so*, *I hope so* and *They said so* use *so* as a pro-form for a clause or proposition. It has other lives too: deictic in *Hold it just so*, connective in *So we left*. Only the construction tells you which *so* you are dealing with.
I could. — Auxiliary stranding for a full predicate.
She left and I did so too. — Do so replaces the verb phrase.
I’ll do it tomorrow. — Do it with a specific action pronoun.
I think so. — So is a clause pro-form.

*Hope you’re well* drops *I* and the auxiliary from the start of a main clause. An open interrogative can shrink to *Why?*, a declarative response to *Me too*, and a coordination to *Kim likes tea and Pat coffee*. In each case the missing material is recoverable from context.

*Kim likes tea and Pat coffee* is understood as *Kim likes tea and Pat likes coffee*: the verb is absent from the second conjunct, while its subject and object remain. Gapping is the coordination case. Listeners restore the verb from the structure of the coordination.

A pro-form supplies an overt replacement; ellipsis leaves a gap. Ellipsis is not the same as a pro-form. The two can combine when an auxiliary is stranded and the rest of the predicate is ellipted, as in *I could*.
Hope you’re well. — Ellipsis of the initial subject and auxiliary.
Why? — Radical ellipsis in an open interrogative.
Me too. — Radical ellipsis in a response.
Kim likes tea and Pat coffee. — Gapping: the verb is omitted from the second coordinate.

*I was born in London and have lived here all my life.* The *here* refers to London, but not because *here* means London. It means a place containing the speaker at the time of speaking, and the antecedent supplies London as the value. The expression is deictic in its meaning and anaphoric in its resolution.

*Come* and *go* carry a similar orientation. *Come here* describes movement towards the speaker or addressee; *Go there* describes movement away. Which end counts as the centre depends on who is speaking and who is being addressed, so the same verb can reverse direction when the perspective changes.

Spatial expressions can also take their source from the discourse. *She lived too far away* means away from the speaker, or away from a place already mentioned; the context decides. The expression keeps its relational meaning even when the reference point is recovered anaphorically.
I live here. — Here includes the speaker’s location.
Put it over there. — There is relatively distant from the speaker.
Come here. — Come describes movement towards the speaker.
She lived too far away. — Away is interpreted relative to a contextually supplied source.

*I’ll do it now* places the action at a time that includes the utterance. *Now* and *then* are the basic temporal deictics — *then* pointing to a time relatively distant or supplied by the discourse — and they are joined by *today*, *yesterday*, *tomorrow*, *last week* and *ago*, all of which locate a time relative to the moment of speaking.

Temporal expressions can also be anaphoric. *She was stunned, but soon recovered* interprets *soon* relative to the being stunned, not to the utterance. *He left at least a week ago* may be measured from the utterance or from a reported perspective.

The deictic centre can shift. A public notice reading *Now wash your hands* means the time of reading, not the time of writing; reported speech can locate temporal expressions at the reported participant’s viewpoint. Once the centre moves, every deictic in the sentence may move with it.
I’ll do it now. — Now includes the utterance time.
She was stunned, but soon recovered. — Soon is interpreted relative to being stunned.
Now wash your hands. — In a public notice, now refers to reading time.
She realised Ed must have left at least a week ago. — Ago can be interpreted relative to her realisation.

*She is taller than her brother* contains more than it appears to. The comparative clause *than her brother* is reduced: it is understood as *than her brother is tall*, with the adjective and its degree recovered from the matrix. The single noun phrase stands in for a whole clause, and the missing material is supplied by the matrix rather than guessed from context.

Reduction can leave only a single element. *Bob is as generous as Sue* keeps just the second term, and *She is taller than him* does the same. Case forms vary: formal writing may prefer *than I*, informal speech usually has *than me*, and both are interpreted through the reduced clause.

Not every comparative clause can be filled out. *She wrote more plays than he wrote five novels* fails because the measure corresponding to *more* must stay empty in the comparative clause; the clause is structurally reduced, not a full clause with a numeral added.
She is taller than her brother. — Understood as than her brother is tall.
Bob is as generous as Sue. — Reduced to a single NP.
She is taller than I. — Formal nominative in the reduced clause.
She is taller than me. — Informal accusative in the reduced clause.

*Two letters arrived for Jill; she will pick them up.* The pronoun *she* reaches back to Jill, and *them* to the letters. Reference here is not confined to one sentence: it is a thread running through the discourse, and the reader follows it by keeping track of what has already been introduced.

*She* and *them* are enough once Jill and the letters are established. Discourse-old information is easy to pronominalise. Discourse-new information usually needs a fuller noun phrase, especially when it is the focus of the sentence. A writer who pronominalises too early leaves the reader searching for an antecedent that has not yet arrived.

Ambiguity appears when several antecedents remain available. *I’ve just been talking to Max. I understand that Ed has told Frank that the report has exonerated him* allows Max, Ed or Frank. Grammar permits all three; context may favour one.

Topic and focus shape the choice as well. A pronoun is easiest to resolve when its antecedent is the current topic or a salient participant. A change of topic often calls for a full noun phrase, and a long-distance pronoun can stay ambiguous even when syntax permits only one structural antecedent.

A pronoun can look outward to the situation or backward to a phrase, and the difference between those directions organises the chapter. Deixis anchors reference to the utterance-act: person, place and time. A deictic expression may contain a smaller marker, an indexing act may help identify the referent, and the deictic centre normally sits with the speaker — though it can move to the addressee or a reported participant.

The relation is retrospective when the anaphor follows its antecedent, anticipatory when it precedes it. Anaphora can also coexist with deixis, as *here* does when it means the place just named. Personal pronouns, reflexives, reciprocals and demonstratives each bring their own patterns of local and long-distance dependence.

Reduced noun phrases and verb phrases rely on pro-forms and ellipsis. *One*, *other*, *do so*, *do it* and *so* stand in for larger expressions; ellipsis omits recoverable material, including the gapped verb of a coordination. Spatial and temporal deixis complete the system, with *here* and *there*, *come* and *go*, *now* and *then*, and the shifts of centre that keep the apparatus flexible.

A reference checklist: Ask where the interpretation comes from: the utterance situation (deixis), an antecedent (anaphora), or omitted recoverable material (ellipsis). Identify the deictic centre and any indexing act. For anaphora, locate the antecedent and decide whether the relation is retrospective or anticipatory.

Take *She left her keys here yesterday, but now they are over there*. *She* and *her* are anaphoric to a contextually salient person; *here* and *there* are locative deictics; *yesterday* and *now* are temporal deictics. *They* is anaphoric to *her keys*.

The example shows deixis and anaphora interacting. *Here* is deictic because it is anchored to the speaker’s location, and it may also be anaphoric if the discourse has established a place. *Now* contrasts with *yesterday* deictically, while *they* depends on the antecedent *her keys*. The interpretation requires both the utterance situation and the discourse context.

For each referring expression, ask where its interpretation comes from. If it depends on the speaker, addressee, time or place of utterance, it is deictic. If it depends on an antecedent, it is anaphoric. If it depends on omitted recoverable material, it is elliptical or a pro-form.

Identify the deictic centre and any shift. In ordinary conversation it is the speaker; in a notice it may be the reader; in reported speech it may be a reported participant. Check for indexing acts such as gestures or written arrows.

For anaphora, locate the antecedent and decide whether the relation is retrospective or anticipatory. For reflexives and reciprocals, check the local domain and the type of relation. For reduced VPs, identify what the pro-form or ellipsis stands for.

In *She left her keys here yesterday, but now they are over there*, *here* and *there* are locative deictics, *yesterday* and *now* are temporal deictics, *she/her* are anaphoric to a salient person, and *they* is anaphoric to *her keys*. The deictic centre is the speaker’s current situation.

Deixis anchors reference to the utterance-act; anaphora anchors it to an antecedent. Deictic expressions can contain deictic markers, and indexing acts can clarify reference. The deictic centre is usually the speaker but can shift.

Pronouns, reflexives, reciprocals and demonstratives have distinct anaphoric and deictic uses. Pro-forms and ellipsis reduce NPs and VPs, and spatial and temporal deixis organise location and time around the utterance.

key_terms.definition: Reference determined by features of the utterance-act, such as speaker, addressee, time and place.
An expression whose reference is fixed in relation to the utterance-act.
The word within a larger expression that carries the deictic meaning.
A gesture, gaze or written device that helps identify a deictic referent.
The perspective from which deictic expressions are interpreted, usually the speaker’s.
Deixis involving the speaker, addressee or third parties, expressed by personal pronouns.
Deixis of place, expressed by here, there, this, that and related expressions.
Deixis of time, expressed by now, then, yesterday and tense.
The relation in which an expression receives its interpretation from an antecedent.
An expression interpreted through an antecedent.
The expression that supplies the interpretation of an anaphor.
Anaphora in which the anaphor follows its antecedent.
Anaphora in which the anaphor precedes its antecedent.
A reduced expression that stands for a larger expression or clause.
A form such as herself or themselves used for local anaphora or emphasis.
A form such as each other or one another expressing a mutual relation.
A determinative or pronoun such as this or that used for deixis or anaphora.
The pronoun one used to stand for a nominal expression.
An expression that performs the head function together with a dependent function.
Omission of material that is recoverable from context.
Use of an auxiliary alone as a reduced predicate, as in I could.
A pro-form replacing a verb phrase, as in She left and I did so too.
A pro-form with a pronoun object, often referring to a specific action.
So used as a pro-form for a clause or proposition.
Ellipsis of a repeated verb in a coordination, as in Kim likes tea and Pat coffee.
Deixis of location and movement, as with here, there, come and go.
Interpretation of a time expression through an antecedent time in the discourse.
A shift of the deictic perspective from speaker to addressee or a reported participant.
A pronoun used for people in general rather than a specific referent, as in You can’t tell.

lessons.title: Inflectional morphology and related matters

outcomes.text: Explain the main ideas in Inflectional morphology and related matters.
Recognise the patterns in real sentences.
Use the ideas when you read and write.

lessons.reviewed_by: Owner-waived AI content check (2026-11-15); not human instructor sign-off

teaching.text: *The children’s folders were left on the shelves, but the boxes had already been moved.* Four plurals sit in that sentence, and they do not behave alike. *Children* changes the base; *shelves* changes a final consonant; *boxes* adds a suffix with a spelling adjustment. Then *children’s* adds a genitive on top of the irregular plural. Inflectional morphology is the part of grammar that describes these form changes, while lexical word-formation creates new vocabulary items such as *simplify* or *simpleton*.

The chapter starts with lexical bases and the operations that build inflected forms, then turns to alternation, regularity and syncretism. It compares speech with writing, surveys phonological and spelling alternations, and works through grade, noun plurals, genitives and verb paradigms. Complex bases and negative auxiliaries lead into weak forms, clitics, the incorporation of *to* and liaison.

Form and meaning rarely line up one-to-one. A single suffix may have several pronunciations or spellings, distinct categories may share one form, and a form that looks irregular in writing may be perfectly regular in speech. The description has to cover the system and the alternations that keep it from looking tidy.

Are *simpler* and *simplify* the same kind of word? Both contain *simple*, but only one belongs to the paradigm of *simple*. *Simple*, *simpler* and *simplest* are inflectional forms of one lexeme; *simplify* and *simpleton* are different lexemes created by lexical word-formation. The fact that *simpleton* contains *simple* has no bearing on its syntax: it behaves like *fool*, not like an inflected adjective.

*This is simpler than that* requires the comparative form of *simple*; *This is the simplest of them all* requires the superlative. The lexeme is the vocabulary item, and these are the shapes it takes in different grammatical contexts. Swap in another adjective and the same pattern appears, which is what makes the formation general rather than lexeme-specific.

*At* has a strong form in *What are you looking at?* and a weak form in *Look at this!* The difference is conditioned by grammatical context, but it is phonological reduction, not a new inflectional category.
Inflection and derivation
Inflection | simple, simpler, simplest | Forms of one lexeme
Derivation | simple → simplify | Creates a new lexeme
Derivation | simple → simpleton | Creates a new lexeme
Compounding | blackbird | Creates a new lexeme

Take *dog* and *worker*. *Worker* divides into *work* and *·er*, so its base is complex rather than simple, yet both nouns take the same plural: *dogs*, *workers*. The distinction between simple and complex bases matters for word-formation, not for the inflectional pattern.

*Dregs* has no singular, yet its base is *dreg*; *sheep* has several forms identical with the base. The base is not always an independent inflectional form. Base and inflectional form are therefore separate notions, and a description that equates them will misrepresent defective and invariant lexemes.

*Teeth* changes the vowel of *tooth*, *rang* changes the vowel of *ring*, and *knives* combines a suffix with a modified base. Suffixation is the main operation, but it is not the only one. Some forms take two steps: the genitive *children’s* is built from the plural *children*, and *trodden* from the preterite *trod*.
Morphological operations
Suffixation | dog → dogs | Add ·s
Internal change | tooth → teeth | Change the vowel
Combined | knife → knives | Suffix plus base modification
Two-step | child → children → children’s | Genitive from the plural
Two-step | tread → trod → trodden | Participle from the preterite

Nouns mark number and case; pronouns mark nominative, accusative, genitive and reflexive; adjectives and some adverbs mark grade; verbs mark tense and person and have participle forms. English inflection covers less ground than the inflection of many languages, but what it covers is not simple. The list of categories is short, while the alternations within them are not.

*Dog*, *dog’s*, *dogs* and *dogs’* show the noun paradigm: singular and plural, plain and genitive. Pronouns carry a richer paradigm, with case, dependent and independent genitives, and reflexive forms built from *self* or *selves*. That compound structure is why *myself* and *themselves* look unlike the personal pronouns they relate to.

Grade applies to many adjectives and a few adverbs, giving plain, comparative and superlative forms. Verbs have six main forms plus negative auxiliaries, and their plain present and plain form usually match the lexical base; *be* is the suppletive exception.
Inflectional categories
Noun | Singular/plural; plain/genitive | dog, dogs, dog’s, dogs’
Pronoun | Nominative, accusative, genitive, reflexive | I, me, my, mine, myself
Adjective | Plain, comparative, superlative | weak, weaker, weakest
Adverb | Plain, comparative, superlative | soon, sooner, soonest
Verb | Plain present, 3rd singular, preterite, plain, gerund-participle, past participle | take, takes, took, take, taking, taken

The plural ending looks stable in writing and shifts constantly in speech. *Cats* ends in *s*, *boxes* in *es*; pronounced, the suffix is /s/, /z/ or /iz/ depending on the final sound of the base. The variation is regular, but a description that recognises only one form will miss it.
*Cats* and *boxes* are regular plurals; *talked* is a regular preterite and participle. *Children*, *bought* and *thieves* are not: they need lexeme-specific information in the lexicon.

Regularity can be partial. *Thieves* uses the general plural suffix, but the base changes from *thief* to *thieve-*, and that change is specific to the lexeme; *chieves* is not the plural of *chief*. The whole form counts as irregular even though the suffixation is regular, because the base modification is not general.

*Sheep* is both singular and plural; *hit* is both present and past. One form serves two distinct categories, which is syncretism. It is not the same as a base plural, because it describes a relation between paradigm cells rather than the shape of a single form.
Regularity and syncretism
Regular alternation | cats, boxes | General rule for plural suffix
Irregular form | children | Lexeme-specific plural
Modified base | thieves | Regular suffix on a special base
Syncretism | sheep (singular/plural) | One form, two paradigm cells
Syncretism | hit (present/past) | One form, two tense cells
*Sighed*, *kissed* and *waited* all end in *·ed* on the page, but the spoken suffixes are /d/, /t/ and /id/. The writing hides a three-way alternation that every speaker controls.

*Churches* has /iz/ and *es*; *stomachs* has /s/ and *s*, because the *ch* is pronounced /k/, not /tʃ/. In several cases the written rule is derivative. The spelling follows the sound rather than the other way round.

Written and spoken classes usually match, but the exceptions are instructive. *Say* has a regular written third singular *says* and an irregular spoken vowel. *Pay* has a regular spoken preterite /peid/ and an irregular written *paid*. *House* has a regular written plural and an irregular spoken plural with voicing.
sighed / kissed / waited — Same written ·ed; different spoken suffixes.
churches / stomachs — The spelling follows the pronunciation.
say / says — Regular in writing, irregular in speech.
pay / paid — Regular in speech, irregular in writing.

The sibilant suffixes have three spoken shapes. *Horses* takes /iz/, *cats* takes /s/, and *dogs* takes /z/. The final sound of the base decides which one, not the spelling. The same alternation appears in the third singular present and in the genitive, which is one reason the categories are worth describing together.

The preterite and past participle suffix also has three shapes: /id/ in *waited*, /t/ in *kissed*, /d/ in *sighed*. Alveolar plosives trigger /id/; voiceless consonants trigger /t/; voiced sounds trigger /d/. This is a phonological rule, not a lexical one.

Bases ending in syllabic /l/ can show a vowel before the suffix, and non-rhotic accents develop special patterns with final /r/. Other alternations involve syllabic /l/ and post-vocalic /r/. These are general phonological adjustments, not facts stored with individual lexemes.
horses / cats / dogs — Plural suffix /iz/, /s/, /z/.
waited / kissed / sighed — Past suffix /id/, /t/, /d/.
The plural of bus is buses. — Sibilant base takes /iz/ and written es.

English spelling has regular alternations of its own. A final consonant may double before a suffix (*bat* → *batting*, *fit* → *fitted*), a final *e* may be deleted (*like* → *liking*, *subdue* → *subduing*), and a final *y* may become *i* (*silly* → *sillier*, *try* → *tries*). None of these changes creates a new lexeme; they keep the written form in line with pronunciation and with the spelling system.

The *·s/·es* alternation in plurals and the third singular present is also a spelling rule, but it follows the pronunciation. *Boxes*, *bushes* and *churches* take *es* because they end in sibilants; *cats*, *dogs* and *stomachs* take *s*. The written pattern is a consequence of the spoken one.

Spelling can make a regular form look irregular. *Fitted* doubles the final *t*, but the doubling is general, so the form is regular; *knitted* is regular for the same reason. *Thieves* is irregular for a different reason: the base change is lexeme-specific, not a spelling convention.
bat → batting — Consonant doubling.
like → liking — E-deletion.
silly → sillier — Y-replacement.
box → boxes — Sibilant base takes es.

*Weak*, *weaker*, *weakest* and *soon*, *sooner*, *soonest* show grade at work. The plain form matches the lexical base, and the other two are formed by suffixation for the bases that allow it. The three-form system is general enough to feel natural and restricted enough to need description.

Not every base takes the suffix. *Careful* forms *more careful* and *most careful*, not *carefuller* and *carefullest*. The choice between inflectional and analytic grade is partly phonological, partly lexical and partly stylistic.

*Good, better, best*; *bad, worse, worst*; *far, farther/further, farthest/furthest* are the irregulars. A few grade forms are irregular and have to be listed in the lexicon. The regular pattern still covers the majority of adjectives, which is why the irregulars stand out.
weak, weaker, weakest — Inflectional grade.
careful, more careful, most careful — Analytic grade.
good, better, best — Irregular grade.
soon, sooner, soonest — Inflectional grade on an adverb.

*Cats*, *dogs* and *horses* show the usual plural pattern: a suffix written *s* or *es* and pronounced /s/, /z/ or /iz/. A smaller group modifies the base before adding the suffix: *wife* → *wives*, *mouth* → *mouths* with voicing, *house* → *houses*.

Some nouns use a base plural, where the plural is identical with the base: *cod*, *bison*, *series*, *Chinese*, *craft*. Others change the vowel (*tooth* → *teeth*, *mouse* → *mice*, *man* → *men*), and a small class adds *·en* (*oxen*, *children*, *brethren*). None of these patterns follows from the noun’s meaning, so each class has to be learned as part of the lexeme’s entry.

Foreign plurals retain borrowed patterns: *formulae*, *curricula*, *phenomena*, *crises*. Some nouns have both a foreign and an anglicised plural. Compound nouns usually pluralise the first element or the head (*grown-ups*, *commanders-in-chief*), and proper nouns form plurals regularly (*Joneses*, *Marys*).
Noun plural types
Regular ·s | cats, dogs | General suffix
Modified base | wives, houses | Suffix plus base change
Base plural | sheep, series | Plural identical with base
Vowel change | teeth, mice, men | Internal vowel change
·en plural | oxen, children | En suffix
Foreign plural | formulae, phenomena | Borrowed pattern

*Dog* gives *dog’s* and *dogs* gives *dogs’*, so the genitive is built from the non-genitive form. The plural genitive comes from the plural, not from the base, which is why *children* → *children’s* and not *child’s* for the plural. That makes the form a two-step formation, one of several in English inflection.

The marker attaches at the end of the genitive noun phrase, even when a post-head dependent intervenes: *the people next door’s behaviour*. In writing, the apostrophe separates singular and plural genitives for many nouns; in speech, the two forms may be identical. The written distinction is useful, but it is not a difference in pronunciation.

Genitive formation interacts with plural formation and syncretism. *Sheep’s* can be singular or plural genitive, and *children’s* is a plural genitive built on the plural. The apostrophe is a spelling convention, not a separate morpheme that a speaker pronounces.
dog’s / dogs’ — Singular and plural genitive.
children’s — Plural genitive formed from children.
the people next door’s behaviour — Genitive marker on the final word of the NP.

Take *talk*: *talk*, *talks*, *talked*, *talk*, *talking*, *talked*. Those are the six inflectional forms most verbs carry — plain present, third singular present, preterite, plain form, gerund-participle and past participle. Regular verbs use *·ed* for the preterite and past participle. The identity of the plain present and plain form is a feature of English, not an accident of the example.

*Be* has *am*, *is* and *are*; *have* has *has*; *do* has *does*; *say* has *says*, with a vowel change in speech. Irregular present forms are few. The regular third singular suffix is *·s*, and it shows the same phonological alternations as the plural suffix.

Irregular preterites and past participles fall into several classes. One class uses a secondary *·ed* formation (*burn*, *keep*, *hit*, *lose*), another vowel alternation (*drink*, *dig*, *find*, *come*), a third adds *·en* for the participle (*see*, *ride*, *take*), and a fourth collects other formations (*flee*, *hear*, *stand*, *buy*, *can*). The classes are descriptive groupings, not rules that generate the forms.
Verb inflection
Regular | talk, talked | ·ed preterite and participle
Irregular present | be, am, is, are | Suppletion
Class 1 | keep, kept | Secondary ·ed formation
Class 2 | drink, drank, drunk | Vowel alternation
Class 3 | take, took, taken | ·en participle
Class 4 | buy, bought | Other formations

A complex base inflects like a simple one. *Underpin* gives *underpins* and *underpinned*; *become* gives *becomes*, *became* and *become*. The internal structure of the base may affect meaning and the lexical entry, but it does not change the inflectional pattern.

*Won’t* bears little resemblance to *will*, yet it belongs to the same auxiliary paradigm. Auxiliary verbs have negative forms: *isn’t*, *aren’t*, *wasn’t*, *weren’t*, *hasn’t*, *haven’t*, *don’t*, *doesn’t*, *didn’t*, *can’t*, *won’t*, *shan’t*, *couldn’t*, *mightn’t*, *mustn’t*, *needn’t*. Some are irregular in pronunciation and spelling, and *won’t* is the clearest case.

Negative forms can be cliticised onto the auxiliary or written as separate words. *Isn’t* is a clitic form; *is not* is a full form. The choice is stylistic and syntactic. The negatives belong to the auxiliary paradigm, not to a separate lexical class.
underpin, underpins, underpinned — Complex base inflects regularly.
become, becomes, became, become — Complex base with irregular preterite.
isn’t / is not — Clitic and full negative forms.
won’t / will not — Irregular negative form.

*At* is /æt/ in *What are you looking at?* and /ət/ in *Look at this!* Many grammaticised words behave this way, with strong and weak forms. Pronouns, prepositions, auxiliaries and determiners reduce in connected speech, and stress along with grammatical context decides which form appears.

Auxiliary verbs have clitic versions: *I’m*, *you’re*, *he’s*, *we’ve*, *they’ll*, *she’d*. These attach to the preceding word and are not separate words in the way full forms are. Their distribution is sensitive to syntax and style, so a description has to say where they can attach, not merely list them.

The infinitival marker *to* can be incorporated into the preceding verb in speech: *gonna*, *wanna*, *hafta*. This is phonological reduction, not a new inflectional category. Liaison links sounds across word boundaries, as in *an apple* or, in non-rhotic accents, *far away*.
Look at this! — Weak form of at.
I’m / you’re / they’ll — Clitic auxiliaries.
gonna / wanna — Incorporation of to in informal speech.
an apple — Liaison across the word boundary.

One lexeme can wear many forms, and the difference between those forms and a new lexeme runs through the chapter. Inflectional morphology describes the forms a lexeme takes when syntax requires them; lexical word-formation creates new lexemes. The lexical base is the starting point for inflection and is not identical with any particular inflected form, as defective and invariant lexemes show.

Suffixation, internal change and combined operations produce the forms. Alternation, regularity and syncretism describe how form relates to category, and speech and writing often diverge, with the spoken rules frequently the more basic.

Grade, noun plurals and genitives, verb paradigms, complex bases and negative auxiliaries show the system in detail. Weak forms, clitics, the incorporation of *to* and liaison describe non-inflectional variation in connected speech.

A morphology checklist: Identify the lexeme and its lexical base. Decide whether the form is inflectional or derivational. Check the operation: suffixation, internal change or a combination. Then check whether the form is regular or lexeme-specific, and whether speech and writing diverge.

Take *The children’s folders were left on the shelves, but the boxes had already been moved*. *Children’s* is a two-step genitive: the plural *children* is formed from the base *child*, and the genitive is formed from the plural. *Shelves* is an irregular plural with base modification, and *boxes* is a regular plural with the /iz/ suffix and *es* spelling.

The example shows inflection, alternation and syncretism at work. *Children* is irregular, *shelves* modifies the base, and *boxes* follows the regular sibilant pattern. The genitive and plural categories are distinct, but they interact in the form *children’s*.

Identify the lexeme and its lexical base. Decide whether the form is inflectional or a new lexeme. Then identify the operation: suffixation, internal change, or a combination. Check whether the form is regular or requires lexeme-specific information.

For spelling and pronunciation, separate the two levels. A form can be regular in writing but irregular in speech, or vice versa. The sibilant and alveolar-plosive suffixes have predictable alternations based on the final sound of the base.

For noun and verb paradigms, check the plural or preterite class, the genitive formation, and any two-step processes. For connected speech, distinguish weak forms, clitics and incorporation from inflectional morphology.

In *The children’s folders were left on the shelves, but the boxes had already been moved*, *children’s* is a plural genitive formed from the irregular plural *children*. *Shelves* is an irregular plural with base modification. *Boxes* is a regular plural whose *es* spelling reflects the /iz/ pronunciation.

Inflectional morphology describes the forms of a lexeme; lexical word-formation creates new lexemes. The lexical base is distinct from particular inflectional forms, and operations include suffixation, internal change and combined processes.

Regularity, alternation and syncretism describe how forms relate to categories. Speech and writing can diverge, and the spoken rules are often primary. Noun plurals, genitives, verb paradigms, negative auxiliaries, weak forms and clitics show the system in detail.

key_terms.definition: The part of grammar concerned with the form of words.
A form change marking a grammatical distinction such as plural, tense or case.
The creation of new lexemes by derivation or compounding.
A vocabulary item whose forms are related by inflection.
The starting form to which inflectional operations apply.
The addition of a suffix to a base.
A morphological operation that changes a vowel or consonant inside the base.
Different realisations of a morphological unit depending on context.
An inflectional form produced by a general rule not specific to a lexeme.
An inflectional form requiring lexeme-specific information.
Identity of form between distinct inflectional categories.
A lexeme lacking some inflectional forms found in its category.
The system of plain, comparative and superlative forms.
A comparative formed with -er, as in cheaper.
A comparative formed with more or less, as in more careful.
The number form used for more than one entity.
The case form marked by ’s or a possessive pronoun.
A plural identical in form to the lexical base, as in sheep.
A plural formed by changing the base vowel, as in teeth.
A plural retaining a borrowed morphological pattern, as in formulae.
The primary past-tense verb form.
The verb form used after perfect have and passive be.
A reduced pronunciation of a grammaticised word in connected speech.
A reduced form attached prosodically to a neighbouring word.
The linking of sounds across word boundaries in connected speech.
A negative form of an auxiliary, such as isn’t or won’t.
Doubling of a final consonant before a suffix, as in batting.
Deletion of final e before a suffix, as in liking.

teaching.text: Say *ungentlemanly* slowly and you can feel the seams: a negative prefix outside, an adjective-making suffix within, a compound underneath that. English keeps building words this way, and speakers keep accepting some of the results while letting others pass. Lexical word-formation is the study of that construction — the shaping of new bases and new lexemes — where inflection only reshapes words that already exist.

The account opens with the gap between a word a dictionary lists and a word the grammar merely permits, then examines the internal anatomy of complex words and the reasons why one pattern keeps minting new items while another survives only in what it has already made. From there it works through the minor processes — clipping, blending, back-formation, conversion — before settling into compounding and the affixation patterns that do most of the labour: negation, evaluation, gender, place, nominalisation, adjectivalisation, verbalisation, numerals.

Two questions run underneath everything. Is the form grammatical, and is it established? They have different answers and different kinds of evidence, and holding them apart is most of the analytical discipline the chapter asks for.

*Kingdom* and *bishopric* sit in the dictionary, and so do *unfaithfulness* and *infidelity*, even though those two look nothing alike inside. These are established words: items a speaker knows individually and a dictionary lists. The match is imperfect: dictionaries also carry multiword expressions whose meaning is idiomatic, so dictionary entries and morphological words are not the same inventory.

Now try *policeability*. Nothing in it is strange — *police* takes *-able*, and *-able* takes a nominalising suffix — yet it will not be in the dictionary. That is a potential word: morphologically well formed, not established. *Priestric* and *pick-basket* fail differently. The *-ric* of *bishopric* no longer forms new words, and the verb-plus-object pattern behind *pick-basket* is closed as well, so these strings are not merely unused but unavailable.

A nonce-word goes one step further into use: coined on a particular occasion, understood in context, never adopted. Every nonce-word is a potential word, but most potential words have never been uttered at all. And disliking a well-formed coinage settles nothing about its grammar. That is a judgement of taste, not of morphology.
Word status
Established | kingdom | Familiar vocabulary item
Potential | policeability | Well formed but not established
Nonce | a one-off coinage | Used but not established
Ungrammatical | priestric | Does not conform to current rules
Multiword dictionary item | give in | Listed but not a morphological word

*Mouse-trap*, *child-care* and *elephant-tusk* come apart into two bases each; *entrap*, *childish* and *elephantine* come apart into a base plus an affix. That is the first cut to make. A complex word can be analysed into smaller units, a simple word cannot, and the units doing the central work are bases — with affixes as the bound elements that attach to them.

Most English bases stand alone, which is exactly why the bound ones are easy to miss. *Dur-* in *durable*, *aggress-* in *aggressive*, the bases of *pre-empt* and *disperse*. None stands alone, yet each fills the base slot and takes the affixes a base takes. Their Latin and French provenance explains the oddity: they arrived already attached.

Classical combining forms are the strangest members of the family: *anglo-*, *aster-*, *auto-*, *electro-*, *pseudo-*. They are bound, so they cannot stand alone, and they lean towards affix-like behaviour. But they pair with other combining forms, as in *electrolysis*, or with free bases, as in *electromagnet*, and they bring lexical meaning of their own rather than grammatical modification.
Morphological units
Free base | trap, child | Can stand alone
Bound base | dur-, aggress- | Cannot stand alone
Combining form | electro-, pseudo- | Classical bound base
Prefix | en-, un-, pre- | Before the base
Suffix | -ish, -ly, -able | After the base

Where does the first cut fall in *ungentlemanly*? Not between *ungentleman* and *ly*, since there is no such base, but between *un* and *gentlemanly*. *Gentlemanly* divides again into *gentleman* + *ly*, and *gentleman* into *gentle* + *man*. Only one ordering matches how the word is built, and only that ordering predicts which pieces behave alike.

That ordering is the word’s constituent structure, and it tells you what sort of base each layer is. *Gentleman* is a compound base, because its immediate constituents are bases; *gentlemanly* is a derivative base, because one immediate constituent is an affix; *gentle* and *man* are simple. A lexical base, finally, is not contained in any larger base formed by word-formation.

The same string changes job with its surroundings. *Gentleman* is a word in *He behaves like a gentleman*, but inside *gentlemanly* it is only a base; *gentle* and *man* are bases within *gentleman* and are not words there. Wordhood belongs to a use, not to a permanent label attached to a sequence of letters.
un + gentlemanly — The first division is prefix plus derivative base.
gentleman + ly — Gentlemanly is a derivative base.
gentle + man — Gentleman is a compound base.
dis + interested + ness — Layered derivation with a compound-like base.

Why does *policeability* feel available while *priestric* feels shut? Both are assembled from real pieces. The difference is productivity: *-able* and *-ness* still recruit new bases, whereas *-ric* survives only in formations already made. Availability, not shape, is what a productive pattern offers.

Establishment can also bury a formation’s parts. Anyone can parse *blackmail* into *black* and *mail*, and nobody predicts its sense from them. *Blackguard* has travelled further still: the compound is no longer recoverable, so the word is now a simple base. Lexicalisation names that drift — a formation settling into a lexical item with a meaning and history of its own.

Patterns run from wide open through semi-productive to a closed list of survivors; productivity is not a switch. Blocking can keep a well-formed newcomer out when an established synonym already covers the ground. Frequency, register and fashion sort the remainder.
police + able + ity — Potential word formed by productive suffixes.
bishop + ric — Established word with a non-productive suffix.
blackmail — Morphologically analysable but semantically opaque.
blackguard — Historically compound, now a simple base.

Some new words arrive without any morphology worth the name. *Kodak* was invented outright; *Xerox* began as a brand. Initialisms press the opening letters of a phrase into service, whether read letter by letter, as in *BBC*, or as a word, as in *NATO* and *aids*. Clipping simply cuts: *advertisement* to *ad*, *gymnasium* to *gym*, *influenza* to *flu*.

Clipping can also dress up what it leaves. *Comfortable* becomes *comfy*, *television* becomes *telly*, a suffix or a fresh ending doing the cosmetic work. Blending welds two words at the seam — *smoke* and *fog* give *smog*, *breakfast* and *lunch* give *brunch* — while back-formation runs derivation backwards and strips an affix that was never really an affix: *editor* yields *edit*, *burglar* yields *burgle*.

A smaller set works on sound rather than structure. *Teeny* trims and raises *tiny*; *flip-flop* and *ping-pong* echo themselves. These sit at the margin of derivation and compounding, and yet each is productive in its own narrow domain.
Minor processes
Manufacture | Kodak | Invented brand name
Initialism | BBC | Initial letters
Clipping | ad | Shortened word
Embellished clipping | comfy | Clipping plus ending
Blending | smog | Parts of two words
Back-formation | edit | Remove an affix
Phonological modification | teeny | Sound change

Nothing is added and nothing removed. *Google* becomes *to google*, *email* becomes *to email*, *empty* becomes *to empty*: the written form holds still while the category and the meaning move. Conversion, as the name says, moves a word from one class to another with no affix to show for it.

Direction shapes the sense. Nouns turning into verbs usually gain an activity or instrument reading — *to bottle*, *to shelve*, *to network* — and verbs turning into nouns often name an instance or a result: *a run*, *a build*, *a reply*. Adjective-to-noun conversion can be fully institutionalised, as with *the poor*, or flicker in and out of context, as with *the rich*.

Pronunciation sometimes carries a contrast that spelling hides. The noun *permit* and the verb *permit* look identical on the page, and *record* behaves the same way; in speech the stress differs, and with the stress goes the grammar. The change is lexical and syntactic, not inflectional; no paradigm is involved.
Google → to google — Noun to verb.
bottle → to bottle — Noun to verb.
run → a run — Verb to noun.
empty → to empty — Adjective to verb.

Two bases can fuse into a single lexical unit whose meaning is narrower than its parts suggest. *Bedroom*, *blackbird*, *language teacher*, *passer-by*: a *blackbird* names a species, not any bird that happens to be black. The compound names a category, which is not the same as describing a scene.

Most compound nouns are built around a noun head — *bedroom*, *mouse-trap*, *child-care* — but verbs get in as well. *Pickpocket*, *breakwater* and *drawbridge* each contain one, and *pickpocket* names a person rather than a thing, which is the compound’s own doing rather than anything the head predicts. The head still fixes the category and usually the core meaning.

Spelling will not settle compound status. The same formation may be written solid, hyphenated or open, and the choice shifts with fashion. Stress and meaning are better guides. *A blackbird* takes its main stress on the first element; *a black bird* takes it on the adjective: one is a word, the other a phrase.
bedroom — Noun-centred compound.
mouse-trap — Noun-centred compound with a trap head.
pickpocket — Verb-object compound naming a person.
passer-by — Compound with a verb-derived head.

In *well-known*, *heart-breaking* and *blue-eyed*, the second element is an adjective or a participle and the first modifies or completes it. Compound verbs are thinner on the ground and usually formed by conversion or back-formation from nouns: *to babysit*, *to proofread*, *to overdo*.

Neo-classical compounds assemble scientific and technical vocabulary out of classical combining forms: *biography*, *geology*, *telephone*, *photograph*. The forms are bound, but in composition they behave like bases, which is why the pattern keeps turning out new technical terms.

One last group takes its cue from rhythm rather than grammar. *Flip-flop*, *ping-pong* and *tick-tock* pair their halves by sound, and what results is a lexical item with a fixed sense rather than a transparent relation between two parts.
well-known — Compound adjective.
blue-eyed — Compound adjective with a participial head.
to babysit — Compound verb.
biography — Neo-classical compound.
ping-pong — Phonologically motivated compound.

Most English compounds are headed, and the head normally comes last. *Bedroom* is a kind of room, *blackbird* a kind of bird, *well-known* an adjective because *known* is. Remove the head and the category goes with it, which is the quickest test for finding one.

What the head cannot tell you is how the parts relate. *A language teacher* teaches a language, or speaks several; the string alone does not choose. *A coffee table* is not made of coffee. Conventional knowledge and context settle what the grammar leaves open.

Some compounds refuse the pattern altogether. *Pickpocket* denotes a person, not a pocket; *turncoat* denotes a person, not a coat. These are exocentric: the whole is not a kind of its head. Meanings of this sort are learned rather than computed, which is why they tend to fossilise.
bedroom — Endocentric: a kind of room.
blackbird — A kind of bird, not simply a black bird.
pickpocket — Exocentric: a person, not a pocket.
turncoat — Exocentric: a person who changes allegiance.

English derivation runs mostly on affixation. Prefixes normally rework meaning and leave the category alone — *unkind*, *rewrite*, *preview* — while suffixes usually change category as well: *kindness*, *modernise*, *readable*. The tendency is a useful first guess, not a rule.

Class I affixes attach close to the base and often disturb its phonology; Class II affixes sit further out, behave more like independent words, and leave stress where they found it. Hence *electric* beside *electricity*, *photograph* beside *photography*, with the stress migrating in each pair. The division is gradient, but its predictions are testable.

Derivation drags spelling along with it. *Happy* becomes *happiness* with *y* turning to *i*; *able* becomes *ability* with one suffix replacing another. Seen from outside these look like irregularity. Seen by affix class, they are the ordinary behaviour of the forms involved.
un-kind — Prefix changes meaning.
kind-ness — Suffix changes category.
read-able — Adjective-forming suffix.
electric → electricity — Morphophonological alternation with a Class I suffix.

*Electric* ends in a /k/ and *electricity* in an /s/; *photograph* stresses its first syllable and *photography* its second. Neither shift is a slip. Each follows regularly from adding a particular suffix to a particular base.

Class I suffixes characteristically retune the base — its vowels, its consonants, its stress — and Class II suffixes characteristically leave it alone. *-ity* and *-ic* belong with the retuners; *-ness* and *-less* do not. The classification is gradient, but it earns its keep by predicting where alternations fall.

Spelling keeps pace. *Happy* → *happiness* turns *y* into *i*, *hope* → *hopeful* keeps its *e*, *make* → *making* drops one before *-ing*. Whole suffixes can be swapped as well: *able* → *ability*, *curious* → *curiosity*. Once the affix class is known, none of this needs a list of exceptions.
electric → electricity — Final /k/ alternates with /s/.
photograph → photography — Stress shift with a Class I suffix.
happy → happiness — Y changes to i.
able → ability — Affix replacement.

English can make a thing smaller or dearer with a suffix. *-let* gives *booklet*, *-ling* gives *duckling*, *-ette* gives *kitchenette*, *-y* gives *doggy*. Augmentation is less grammaticalised: *mega-*, *super-* and *over-* do that work, often with a borrowed air.

Gender marking is vestigial. *Actor/actress*, *waiter/waitress*, *hero/heroine* are pairs inherited from a system English no longer runs, and they are lexical and stylistic rather than grammatical. Many have been abandoned for neutral forms, and that abandonment is a social decision as much as a linguistic one.

Place and time get their own small inventory of affixes: *fore-*, *pre-*, *post-*, *sub-*, *inter-*, and the suffix *-ward*. *Forecast*, *preview*, *postpone*, *submarine*, *international*, *homeward* each locate something in space or in time, productively but not without limit.
booklet — Diminutive with -let.
duckling — Diminutive with -ling.
actress — Feminine suffix, now often replaced.
preview — Temporal prefix pre-.

English denies with a family of prefixes that overlap without being interchangeable: *un-* in *unhappy*, *in-* in *impossible*, *non-* in *non-negotiable*, *dis-* in *dishonest*, *a-* in *atypical*. Which one attaches where is largely a matter of the lexeme’s history, and the members of the family differ in how freely they recruit new bases.

Not every such prefix denies a property. Reversatives undo an action — *unlock*, *untie*, *devalue*, *disconnect* — and removal prefixes take something away, as in *defrost*, *dethrone*, *unmask*. Opposition prefixes set one thing against another: *anti-war*, *counter-argument*, *pro-choice*.

The categories leak into one another and the base decides the reading. *Dis-* can deny, reverse or oppose; *un-* can negate a quality or undo an act. So one prefix may be fully productive in one use and fossilised in another, and no single gloss will cover both.
unhappy — Negative un-.
non-negotiable — Negative non-.
unlock — Reversative un-.
anti-war — Oppositional anti-.

Names slide into ordinary vocabulary with surprising ease. *Shakespearean*, *Victorian*, *Darwinian*, *Thatcherite*, *Londoner*: the suffix contributes ‘relating to’ or ‘a person associated with’, and the result can drift well beyond the name’s original bearer.

Derivatives from places form a large and untidy family — *American*, *European*, *Asian*, *African* — serving as adjectives or nouns, and their formation resists a single rule. *-an*, *-ian*, *-ese*, *-ish*, *-ic* and a bare zero ending all occur, and which ending a name takes is a fact about that name.

Some derivatives shed the name almost entirely. *A sandwich*, *a boycott*, *a diesel*, *a hoover* began as eponyms and now name ordinary things. Etymology records where they came from; morphology describes what they are now, and the two accounts must not be folded together.
Shakespearean — Adjective from a proper name.
Londoner — Noun from a place name.
European — Adjective or noun from a continent name.
sandwich — Lexicalised common noun from a proper name.

Verbs and adjectives turn into nouns by several routes. *-er*, *-or* and *-ant* typically name a person or an instrument — *driver*, *actor*, *assistant* — while *-tion*, *-ment*, *-ance*, *-ness* and *-ity* name an action, a state or a process: *destruction*, *movement*, *performance*, *happiness*, *ability*.

Some nominalisations stay transparent to their base and some do not. *Happiness* is see-through. *Destruction* is related to *destroy* but has its own shape and its own history. Meaning can drift as well, which is why *a building* usually names a structure rather than the act of building it.

Academic and technical prose leans on nominalisation heavily, and the habit has costs. Packing an action into a noun makes the writing abstract and slows the reader. Choosing between *they decided* and *the decision* is a rhetorical decision as much as a morphological one, and worth making on purpose.
driver — Person nominalisation with -er.
actor — Person nominalisation with -or.
destruction — Action nominalisation with -tion.
happiness — State nominalisation with -ness.

Adjectives come from nouns and verbs through a familiar set of suffixes: *childish*, *hopeful*, *readable*, *economic*, with *-ish*, *-ful*, *-able*, *-ic*, *-ous* and *-al* doing the work. What comes out may be gradable, relational or classificatory, and the difference shows in what the adjective will combine with.

Verbs form the same way from nouns and adjectives: *modernise*, *legalise*, *simplify*, *strengthen*, *computerise*, using *-ise/-ize*, *-ify*, *-en* or no affix at all. The usual sense is ‘make or become’ whatever the base names, though the details vary from suffix to suffix.

Conversion and derivation meet at this point. *To empty* adds nothing to *empty*; *to modernise* adds a suffix. Both produce verbs, yet a question about the productivity of one is not a question about the other.
childish — Adjective from a noun with -ish.
readable — Adjective from a verb with -able.
modernise — Verb from an adjective with -ise.
strengthen — Verb from an adjective with -en.

Cardinals name numbers — *one*, *two*, *three*, *ten*, *hundred*, *thousand* — and they combine recursively into *three hundred and forty-two* or *two thousand five hundred*. The system generates indefinitely and still has to be learned in places.

Ordinals rank (*first*, *second*, *third*, *fourth*), fractions divide (*half*, *quarter*, *third*, *two-fifths*), and dates run numerals together with calendar convention: *the third of May*, *May 3rd*, *twenty twenty-six*.

Numerals also enter compounds. *Two-door*, *three-piece*, *four-wheel-drive*, *ten-year-old* use the numeral as a modifier, and the unit noun stays singular inside: *a ten-year-old child*, never *a ten-years-old child*. The compound has frozen the singular while the meaning stays plural.
three hundred and forty-two — Composite cardinal numeral.
first, second, third — Ordinal numerals.
two-fifths — Fraction.
a ten-year-old child — Numerical compound with singular year.

Vocabulary grows along several routes at once. Borrowing takes a word from another language, semantic change gives an old word a new sense, coinage invents a form outright, and word-formation builds one from pieces already in the language. These routes interact, and a single item may travel more than one of them.

*Policeability* is well formed and unlisted. Whether it becomes established depends on usage — frequency, acceptance, fashion — not on its morphology. A nonce-word may never spread. Dictionaries record what has been established; they do not fix the limits of what is possible.

Productivity itself moves. *-ric* built *bishopric* and then stopped; *-able* and *-ness* are still in service. Borrowed patterns behave the same way, with foreign plurals persisting, fading or settling into a division of labour with native forms.
policeability — Potential word from productive suffixes.
priestric — Not admitted because -ric is no longer productive.
smog — Blend that became established.
sandwich — Lexicalised common noun from a proper name.

English has taken words from Latin, French, Greek, Norse and many other sources, and the borrowed forms do not stay foreign. *Nation* supports *national*, *nationalise* and *nationalisation*, running through productive English patterns like any native base. Borrowing is not itself a morphological process, but it supplies the material that morphology works on.

Classical combining forms carry much of the technical vocabulary: *bio-*, *geo-*, *tele-*, *photo-*, *graph-*, *-ology*, *-graphy*. They pair with one another in *biography* and *geology* and with free bases in *photograph* and *telephone*. Their meanings are usually more specific than those of native affixes, which is why they suit technical coinage.

Borrowed plurals and derivational patterns can be irregular or semi-productive. *Formulae*, *curricula* and *phenomena* keep their foreign plurals while other borrowings have been anglicised, and one and the same item may support both forms with a difference of register or sense.
nation → national → nationalise — Borrowed base in productive derivation.
biography — Neo-classical compound.
geology — Classical combining forms.
formulae / formulas — Foreign and anglicised plurals.

Three questions organise everything in this chapter. Is the form grammatical? Is it established? And if it is both, what internal structure does it have? *Kingdom* is established, *policeability* is grammatical without being established, and a nonce-word is the second kind, used once and dropped. None of those verdicts is about taste.

Complex words are bases and affixes arranged in layers, and the arrangement explains behaviour that a flat list of pieces cannot. Productivity and lexicalisation account for the gap between a pattern that still makes words and a formation surviving only in what it has already made. Around the edges sit manufacture, initialism, clipping, blending, back-formation and phonological modification.

Conversion shifts a word between categories without changing its form. Compounding joins bases into nouns, adjectives and verbs, classical combining forms included. Derivation supplies negation, evaluation, gender, location, nominalisation, adjectivalisation, verbalisation and the numeral patterns — most of the vocabulary-building machinery English has.

A word-formation checklist: Identify the base and the process: conversion, compounding, derivation, clipping, blending or back-formation. Check whether the pattern is productive and whether the result is established, potential or nonce. Then analyse the constituent structure and the meaning relation between the parts.

Take *The editor’s useful guide was republished after a surprisingly readable rewrite*. *Editor* is an established person nominalisation; *useful* is an adjective formed with *-ful*; *republished* contains the prefix *re-*; *readable* is a potential or established adjective formed with *-able*; *rewrite* is a conversion from verb to noun with the prefix *re-*.

The example shows several word-formation processes at once: derivation, prefixation, conversion and nominalisation. Each form has a base and an affix or a converted category, and each contributes to the meaning of the sentence. The distinction between established and potential words matters for deciding which forms belong to the vocabulary and which are merely possible.

Identify the base and the process. Is the word simple or complex? Is it formed by conversion, compounding, derivation, clipping, blending or back-formation? Then analyse the constituent structure and the meaning relation between the parts.

Decide whether the formation is established, potential or nonce. Check whether the pattern is productive and whether an established synonym blocks it. Do not confuse a stylistic preference with a morphological ungrammaticality.

For derivation, identify the affix class and any morphophonological or spelling alternation. For compounds, identify the head and the relation between the elements. For numerals and proper-name derivatives, check the conventional patterns and any lexicalised meanings.

In *The editor’s useful guide was republished after a surprisingly readable rewrite*, *editor* is a person nominalisation, *useful* is an adjective with *-ful*, *republished* contains *re-*, *readable* contains *-able*, and *rewrite* is a converted noun. The forms illustrate derivation, prefixation, conversion and nominalisation.

Lexical word-formation creates new lexemes. Established, potential and nonce-words differ in vocabulary status, not simply in grammaticality. Complex words have hierarchical base-affix structure, and productivity determines which patterns can create new forms.

Minor processes, conversion and compounding extend the vocabulary alongside derivation. Affixation covers negation, evaluation, gender, location, nominalisation, adjectivalisation, verbalisation and numerals. Morphological analysis must distinguish form, meaning, productivity and lexical status.
